News.title: Totley Rail Tunnel live - trains continue to face 'severe delays' after tunnel fire
News.content:
Four fire crews raced to Totley Rail Tunnel in Sheffield, with rail services through the Peak District halted and locals warned there is 'a lot of smoke in the area'

Trains will continue to face 'severe delays' until the end of the day after a fire broke out close to a set of train tracks between Sheffield and Derbyshire, halting all services through the Peak District.

Four fire crews raced to the Totley Rail Tunnel in Sheffield, where South Yorkshire Fire & Rescue warned there was "a lot of smoke in the area". Local residents were urged to avoid the area and keep their windows and doors closed.

The blaze between Totley and Grindleford, in Derbyshire's Hope Valley, caused all lines through the Peak District to close. And while services have now reopened, commuters have been warned they could face 'severe' disruption until the end of the day.

The affected services included East Midlands Railway (EMR) trains between Liverpool Lime Street and Nottingham/Norwich, Northern services between Manchester Piccadilly and Sheffield, and TransPennine Express between Liverpool Lime Street and Cleethorpes.

News.title: Andy Burnham vows to tackle issues ‘ignored by Westminster’ including rough sleeping and fly-tipping
News.content:
Andy Burnham vows to tackle issues ‘ignored by Westminster’ including rough sleeping and fly-tipping

Next week the Prime Minister will speak with the public about ending rough sleeping and resolving the 'toxic dump, fly-tipping and environmental vandalism scandal'

View 2 Images The PM vowed to tackle the scourge of fly-tipping (Image: Anita Maric / SWNS)

Andy Burnham is set to look at issues “ignored by Westminster for too long” during the second week of his summer tour of the UK.

‌



Next week the PM will speak with the public about ending rough sleeping and resolving the “toxic dump, fly-tipping and environmental vandalism scandal”.

‌



Mr Burnham had pledged to tour the country after replacing Keir Starmer to hear directly from the country about the issues facing their communities.

‌



A Downing Street spokesperson said: “The Prime Minister wants to bring back hope that we can finally fix the difficult issues facing the country that have been ignored by Westminster for too long.

“This includes taking on issues that others have said are intractable, like ending rough sleeping and resolving the toxic dump, fly-tipping and environmental vandalism scandal that is blighting communities across the UK.

Met Office issues weather maps and names 15 areas to face rain on Saturday - see full list READ MORE :

View 2 Images Andy Burnham wil continue his tour of the country next week (Image: Getty Images)

‌



“The coming week will see the Prime Minister take on some of these issues as he continues his tour around the UK, which will inform his upcoming 10-year plan to make Britain better off.”

It comes as Mr Burnham unveiled a £65 million funding package for farmers, amid fears hot, dry weather could see supermarket food prices soar.

Mr Burnham visited a family-run potato farm near Truro, Cornwall, on Saturday that has been affected by the drought and met National Farmers’ Union president Tom Bradshaw.

‌



Speaking at Colwyn farm, Mr Burnham said: “I realise we’ve got a long way to go to build back trust with the farming community across the country. I think it’s probably been the hardest summer for British farming in a generation.

“I see food and farming as part of national resilience, national infrastructure.We need to be able to guarantee our own food production going forward.”

In his first week of travelling around the country, the new PM visited Derbyshire, the West Midlands, Devon, and Cornwall to hear from local people and businesses.

Article continues below

He also announced a series of policies to give families breathing space, including “easy to exit” rules to help cancel subscriptions and a ban on retailers making misleading claims about discounts.

Mr Burnham has also promised to give councils new powers to block vape and betting shops in a bid to save Britain’s “hollowed-out high streets”.

News.title: Trains services blocked between Bristol and Devon after person hit by train
News.content:
Trains services blocked between Bristol and Devon after person hit by train

Rail passengers have been warned to expect 'major disruption' between Bristol and Devon, just south of Taunton, this evening after a person was struck by a train

View Image National Rail says major disruption will continue into the evening (Image: PA)

A person has been struck by a train between Bristol and Devon, just south of Taunton, with all services on the route blocked.

‌



National Rail has warned passengers to expect "major disruption" until at least 11pm this evening as emergency services continue working at the scene.

‌



Great Western Railway (GWR) and Cross Country say passengers trying to get between Taunton and Exeter St Davids may have to cancel plans to travel or face long delays.

‌



Trains between these stations may be cancelled or delayed by up to 70 minutes.

A GWR spokesperson said: "A person has been struck by a train, leading to all lines being blocked. It is necessary to bring all trains in the affected area to an immediate stop.

‌



"If you are onboard one of the services in this incident and have been affected by this incident or know someone else who needs support, there is always someone to talk to.

"Contact a Samaritan on 116 123 for free, any time, on any phone. Help is only a phone call away."

The firm says it is working alongside Network Rail to gather more information and understand how the incident will affect its services.

Article continues below

A spokesperson for Network Rail: "The emergency services are currently dealing with an incident between Taunton and Exeter St Davids. So that they can safely carry out their work, all lines are closed.

"As a result, trains between these stations may be cancelled or delayed by up to 70 minutes. Major disruption is expected until 23:00."

Samaritans (116 123 in UK and Ireland) operates a 24-hour service available every day of the year. If you prefer to write down how you're feeling, or if you're worried about being overheard on the phone, you can email Samaritans at jo@samaritans.org

News.title: Teenager Alex McKee who died in Greece 'may have been electrocuted by faulty shower'
News.content:
Teenager Alex McKee who died in Greece 'may have been electrocuted by faulty shower'

Irish student Alex McKee, 17, may have been electrocuted to death by faulty shower equipment while on a family holiday to the Greek island of Kimolos, authorities say

View 2 Images Alex McKee, 17, was on holiday with family when the tragic accident unfolded

An Irish teenager who died on a family holiday to Greece may have been electrocuted by faulty shower equipment, authorities have said.

‌



Alex McKee, 17, tragically died last Sunday at a residential property on the island of Kimolos, where his mother is from. The student had been on holiday with his family when the tragic accident unfolded.

‌



His body was taken to the Greek mainland where a post-mortem examination at the Piraeus Forensic Medical Service confirmed his cause of death to be electrocution.

‌



Greek authorities have suggested this may have been caused by faulty shower equipment.

A doctor based in Kimolos, Agapitos Xanthis, told how Alex's mother had also felt an electrical sensation while showering at the property, adding "we are lucky there weren't two deaths as a result of electrocution."

View 2 Images Alex was on holiday with his family on the Greek island of Kimolos (Image: UCG/Universal Images Group via Getty Images)

‌



A Greek police inquiry is now looking into the building's water heater to locate a possible wiring fault, according to The Guardian.

An officer said a fusebox at the property may have had an issue with a safety valve. An electrical installation certificate reportedly signed by an electrician in 2024 is also being investigated.

Alex was part of an award-winning Irish Young Scientist and Technology Exhibition project, which gained national acclaim earlier this year, reports the Irish Mirror.

‌



Alongside two classmates, the teenager developed 'Bumblebee,' a communication system for people with nonverbal autism.

The project won first place in its category, as well as a Special Award from the Ombudsman for Children's Office.

Cork North TD Colm Burke, who met Alex just months ago during the Young Scientist and Technology Exhibition, told Cork Beo how the tragic death of such a bright and talented young man has devastated the community.

‌



"It's extremely sad to hear that someone so young has died so tragically," he said.

"He was a really talented young person with his whole life and huge career ahead of him. Earlier this year, he put a huge effort into getting to that stage in the Young Scientist and Technology Exhibition and was awarded for his efforts.

"It is devastating news for his family, the community and his school colleagues."

Article continues below

Ireland's Department of Foreign Affairs is assisting following the tragedy.

A spokesperson for the Department said: "The Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade is aware of this case and is providing consular assistance. As with all consular cases, the Department does not comment on the details of individual cases."

News.title: TikTok star jumps fence to help fight Birmingham fire and raises £11,000 for victims
News.content:
TikTok star jumps fence to help fight Birmingham fire and raises £11,000 for victims

A TikTok star known as Ringz N Tiingz was one of the first at the scene of a fire in Gorleston Road, Birmingham, on Thursday as it ripped through people's homes, later calling the scene 'overwhelming'

View 2 Images Fire damaged properties on Gorleston Road (Image: Emma Trimble / SWNS)

A TikTok star has revealed how he leapt over a garden fence in a bid to prevent fire from spreading between properties and help those caught up in the blaze.

The 35-year-old TikToker, known as Ringz N Tiingz, said he was one of the first on the scene of a fire in Gorleston Road, Birmingham, on Thursday, as it tore through residents' homes.

Ringz N Tiingz said he was on his way to the shops when he noticed "unusual, thick smoke" in the air, and followed it to a small field.

He said: "I went into the field, and I could see everything on fire. There was a row of houses you can see from from the field, and the grass and everything was just on fire."

View 2 Images Residents in the houses and a nearby care home were evacuated (Image: Sophie Robinson/PA Wire)

Fire service says what you must NOT do if you spot people barbecuing in heatwave ban READ MORE :

Emergency phone alert chaos as fire services make plea after being inundated with calls about neighbours' BBQs READ MORE :

Ringz N Tiingz said he started livestreaming the fire before making the decision to get "actively involved" in helping people.

He said: "As the fire was spreading, I just ran just before the fire (reached me), jumped over this fence to go check if people's all right.

"I'd seen they was evacuating the building, so I left them to do it. But then a bit further down, I've seen someone else run into the fence. So I just ran to the fence, and I've seen someone come running out the back door.

"But then he's ran back into his house, because on the one side there was fire, and then on the other side there was the fire just started.

"So me and him was in the garden. We're trying to put out this fire, but it was just too big. It was too hot, so we've ended up kicking down this back gate, jumping back over the fence, and then just trying to stop the fire from spreading."

He revealed that he and another man rushed to a nearby care home in search of fire extinguishers to help bring the blaze under control.

He said: "The care home was getting evacuated, and we just stopped the fire from spreading, because if the fire would have carried on spreading, the bushes would have went up, the trees would have went up, and then eventually that care home would have went up as well."

He described watching elderly residents being brought out of the care home – some in their beds or wheelchairs, others connected to medical equipment.

"If I'm honest, it felt overwhelming, as in it was emotional," Ringz N Tingz said. "It was just like, 'Oh my God... these are people's houses'. People are screaming... shouting. It was crazy. It was absolutely hectic."

He added: "These people have got nothing. They've been living there for 30 years. They've got generational photos, that's all gone.

"The jewellery, everything's just gone. They've got nothing. One lady, bless her, the only items what she's got is the clothes what she was wearing. It's so sad."

Some 4-5,000 people tuned into the livestream to watch the events unfold, the TikToker said.

To support those displaced from their homes in Gorleston Road, Ringz N Tingz has launched a fundraising page, urging his followers to contribute. "While we were doing what we were doing, towards the end of the night we could see the damage what's been caused, so we decided to set up a GoFundMe," he said. "We managed to raise £11,000 in the space of 24 hours."

The appeal is just one of numerous campaigns on the crowdfunding platform that has been launched to support wildfire victims. GoFundMe estimates that more than £110,000 has been raised across the various appeals combined.

News.title: Trump's alarming week as he won't rule out declaring a national emergency
News.content:
Trump's alarming week as he won't rule out declaring a national emergency

Donald Trump is facing his most humiliating electoral catastrophe since he lost to Joe Biden - and some wildly antidemocratic methods of clinging on to power are apparently on the table

Trump's $10billion BBC lawsuit gets even funnier because... less than 300 WATCHED it in the US

There are now 80 days to go until Donald Trump faces his most humiliating electoral catastrophe since he lost to Joe Biden.

‌



A year ago, when Democrats looked forward to the midterms, the most they'd let themselves hope for was to retake the House. Since then Donald Trump has embroiled America in a lengthy war that nobody asked for, and for which there is no end in sight. The war has contributed to skyrocketing oil prices - which in turn has increased the price of petrol, the one thing you never want to be blamed for if you're a politician in America. Meanwhile, his team is slowly falling apart - with attack dogs like Jeannine Pirro, who Trump set up as state attorneys to prosecute his enemies - have singularly failed to do so. And his attack dog in chief - press secretary Karoline Leavitt - is leaving the administration, possibly because of the unreasonable demands put on her family by Trump. It's been a rough week to be Donald Trump. Let's catch you up with what's happened.

‌



Trump won't rule out declaring a national emergency to take over the Midterms

In a terrifying preview of what many people think is exactly what's going to happen in 81 days time, Trump wouldn't rule out declaring a state of emergency in order to seize control of November's midterm elections. Interviewing the President on Real America's Voice, a propaganda outlet with former aide Steve Bannon as its figurehead, host Wayne Allyn Root suggested: "If you declare a national security emergency as the president of the United States, they can't challenge it. It can only be overturned by a two-thirds vote by both houses of Congress. So if you do this in the next month, we will get photo ID, proof of citizenship (for voter registration) and a limit to mail-in ballots." These measures are included in the "SAVE America Act", the draconian voter suppression bill Trump has tried and failed to get Congress to sign off for months. Trump was coy about it, but indicated it was on the table. "Let me just say that stranger things have happened, OK?" Trump said. "I'll leave it at that."

‌



Content cannot be displayed without consent

Todd Blanche has some brass neck

Speaking ahead of Trump's speech at a police academy on Long Island, Todd Blanche - Donald Trump's newly minted full-time Attorney General - promised, apparently seriously, that law enforcement officers would be protected on his watch. "In my Department of Justice," he said, "if anybody touches a federal law enforcement officer in any way inappropriate, we will prosecute them to the fullest extent of the law." This is quite the pledge for the man who, not a couple of months ago, was helping Trump arrange a slush fund to pay out millions of dollars in cash to reward the loyalty of people convicted of being involved in the January 6th attempted coup, who were then pardoned by his boss on his first day back in office. Including those who battered police officers.

Content cannot be displayed without consent

‌



Trump has big plans for the Strait of Hormuz

Donald Trump threatened to make the Strait of Hormuz a "territory of the United States" if he defeats Iran. He said he would "pretty soon" claim the waterway for America, despite dwindling hopes of victory in the conflict. Speaking at the aforementioned police academy, he said: "After we finish defeating Iran, which is being very badly defeated, pretty soon I'll be declaring the Hormuz strait a territory of the United States." He added: "Essentially, that's what it is. We have the blockade. No ships get through unless we want them to." It's unclear whether Trump meant his vow to claim the strait as a serious policy announcement, or if he was just engaging in one of his trademark "weaves" - an unplanned detour from prepared remarks. Iran's Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi was characteristically withering in response, saying on X: "This strait will be opened and closed only under Iran's command, and so long as you do not accept the reality of defeat and stop indulging in fantasies, Iran will continue to enforce the blockade."

Content cannot be displayed without consent

Trump will not apologise for making petrol more expensive

Trump also said during his speech that Americans should accept paying a "tiny little bit more" for petrol because of his Iran war. Refusing to apologise for starting the war, Trump said: "What we're doing is a great service for the world, not only for ourselves … and we're really doing a great job."

‌



Trump's war on the BBC got even funnier

There's an old rule of thumb in courtrooms. Never ask a question you don't know the answer to. Donald Trump just found out why. Regular readers will recall that last week Donald Trump had to have a mad scramble to rewrite his preposterous lawsuit against the BBC, because if he didn't, he'd have to send the BBC all his bank statements. The judge let him off the hook and earlier this week we saw the newly unsealed, rewritten lawsuit. It accuses the BBC of a "brazen" attempt to interfere in the 2024 election, because...about 300 Americans may have seen the Panorama episode with a slightly dodgy edit.

His TEN BILLION DOLLAR lawsuit is predicated on his reputation and political standing had been damaged by showing footage of him saying things he actually said - to an audience that would barely fill a medium sized pub. The docket includes a deposition from Richard Cooper, the BBC's director of digital distribution. He revealed the programme had been watched 570,000 times on iPlayer. But of those, only 285 are from IP addresses that could have been based in America. Not 285,000 - 285. And 34 of those were from Florida, where the case is being heard. And it somehow gets funnier. Cooper said the US-based IP addresses didn't necessarily mean the viewer was actually in the United States.

For example, of those 34 streams from Florida, most were traced back to an IP address in Slough, via the cruise ship company Carnival...which has its HQ in Florida. That 285 is also over the ENTIRE period the documentary was available online, which is about a year. And only a week of that was before the election.

‌



In case you're wondering, if you assume all 285 viewers were by American voters, which they weren't - the damages Trump's asking for per view comes to $35,078719.30 In proper money, that's £25,974,385.96. EACH.

Leavitt Out

View 2 Images She's off - but why? (Image: AP Photo/Julia Demaree Nikhinson)

Farewell, then, to Karoline Leavitt, who is stepping down as Donald Trump's Press Secretary at the end of the month. She has, of course, done a string of things a Press Secretary should never do. She has lied, repeatedly. She has berated and insulted members of the media from the podium. She presided over an influx of right-wing propagandists diluting the real reporters in the press room. And she was the face of the decision to exclude the Associated Press from some Trump events in retaliation for their refusal to change their stylebook to call the Gulf of Mexico the Gulf of America.

‌



But none of those was the reason she left. A source reportedly told CNN that when she took a month off in May following the birth of her daughter, Trump would often contact her "and, at times, asked when she planned to return". It would be a terrible shame if she had been forced out of the job because she had a young family, rather than for all of the manifest reasons she's a terrible Press Secretary.

Who will replace her? Anna Kelly would be among the obvious choices, to the point of being a bit boring. She is among Leavitt's deputies and would keep continuity. Steven Cheung, the White House Comms Director is one of the most combative people in the White House. In fact, he's one of the most combative people on Planet Earth outside of the UFC. He might be a bit noisy for the role. But the top bets on America's prediction markets are going on Alina Habba. A former Trump advisor and lawyer, she stepped down as acting US Attorney for New Jersey after an appeals court found she'd been continuing in the role despite her interim appointment having expired, and the Administration failing to get the Senate to confirm her. She's one of a string of "interim" Trump administration prosecutors who have had their appointments challenged.

Trump ripped up America's childhood vaccine regime

In an executive order this week, Trump made a bid to scale back the number of lifesaving vaccines given to children in America. The schedule of jabs for kids, for which there is no evidence of widespread harm, and huge amounts of evidence of efficacy and safety, is being torn up, the President said, "based on what I feel."

‌



Neither Donald Trump nor his health secretary, embarrassing nephew and croaky anti-vaccine advocate Robert F Kennedy Jr, are doctors. RFK Jr admitted in 2012 that a parasite "ate a portion" of his brain. But for well over a decade, Trump has expressed his view — against medical groups’ guidance — that childhood vaccines should be administered in smaller doses over a long period of time. The executive order sought to bear out that discredited theory. “This is based on what I feel,” Trump said last September when he called for splitting the measles, mumps and rubella, or MMR, vaccine into three single-disease vaccines. On Monday, he again pushed for separating the MMR shot into three, ordering the US Department of Health and Human Services to work on developing that option for children, since it doesn’t currently exist in the United States. Public health experts have warned that spacing out shots could increase the risk of infection with a vaccine-preventable disease before a child returns for the next visit.

Medical experts said Trump’s order is misguided and likely to stoke fear and confusion among parents at a time when measles is raging, immunisation rates are falling and children are heading back to school.

Trump downplays the strain on the sailors he sent to Hormuz

Trump on Friday downplayed the toll on American sailors enduring nearly nine months at sea on the USS Abraham Lincoln as concerns escalated about mental health and supply issues aboard the aircraft carrier supporting US operations against Iran. After reports emerged that sailors on the Lincoln are struggling with mental health concerns, the Navy said it has “not observed an increase in suicidal ideations or attempts aboard the ship,” though officials have declined to provide data, citing operational security and patient privacy concerns. A Navy official said a sailor aboard the Lincoln went overboard in early August but the person was quickly recovered, treated by the ship’s medical department and transferred off ship for follow-on care. The official would not say whether it was being considered a suicide attempt. In a brief exchange with reporters before flying to New York for an event to highlight falling violent crime rates across the US, Trump refuted that family members have raised concerns about the deployment’s length and even said that the deployment — which includes a record-setting uninterrupted time at sea of more than 240 days — is “not nearly long enough.”

Article continues below

"That ship is moving right now, or very shortly, and it’s being replaced with another very similar ship,” Trump said when asked about the lengthy deployment. The acting navy secretary, Hung Cao, said the Lincoln “will return home soon” in a social media post on Friday.

News.title: Joe Marler says 'I knew there would be backlash for interviewing Prince Harry'
News.content:
Few people can claim to have discussed everything from manscaping and ChuckleVision to fatherhood and trauma with a member of the royal family - but as of last month, Joe Marler can. His chat with the Duke of Sussex for his hugely popular podcast, Joe Marler Will See You Now, is just one of the many surreal moments the retired England rugby star has experienced since The Celebrity Traitors kicked-off his remarkable second act.

The series sees Joe, 36, and comedian co-host Jake Bhardwaj combine silliness with often surprisingly honest conversations about mental health and life’s difficult moments. And when Harry took his turn in the chair, the result was one of the podcast’s most unexpectedly candid – and hilarious – episodes yet.

“We put some prep in but it crept up on us and I was nervous, thinking about the whole thing and also the polarising public opinion of it,” he tells us. “Jake just said, ‘Calm down and think about what we want to achieve from having him as a guest.’ I knew I liked him. I was Team Harry, if there were teams or whatever."

View 6 Images Joe was surprised that talking to Prince Harry was 'like talking to a normal person' (Image: JOE MARLER WILL SEE YOU NOW PODCAST/SPOTIFY)

‌



He continues, “We were in the room waiting for him to arrive, thinking it’s going to be this big event, and he just comes straight in, said, ‘Hi guys, how you doing?’ And comes over and hugs me, and then hugs Jake. Within 90 seconds, it was like talking to a normal person so I thought let’s just treat him accordingly, and we did.”

The trio delved into everything – their grooming routines, Harry “squeezing his kids extra tight” on a hard day, the Invictus Games, and why “getting a sweat on” helps the royal stay mentally and physically healthy.

Harry, 41, also proved unexpectedly competitive and animated when finishing off classic ad slogans and singing the ChuckleVision theme tune.

“He was great, honestly, he was fantastic,” says Joe. “For him to be so generous with his time and give that up to us and be so open and up for a laugh, and also deal with topics like grief and trauma and what he’s so passionate about with JJ Chalmers and the Invictus Games was just incredible.”

‌



View 6 Images Joe plays the role of a pseudo-therapist on his Joe Marler Will See You Now podcast (Image: YouTube/ @Joe Marler Will See You Now)

After spending 17 years as a professional rugby player, the last few years have been a steep learning curve about public opinion and fame. “I knew that there would be some level of backlash to whatever question or whatever answer he gave,” he reflects.

“But I didn’t want that to stop me and Jake from being genuine and in the moment. I wanted him and us to be present and to have the experience. I didn’t want to overthink things or not ask a particular question because of how it might be received. But the level of vitriol that comes with him, the social media backlash... What is the matter with some people?”

The episode was an extraordinary moment in what has been an extraordinary year for Joe, who retired from international rugby in November 2024. His life is more focused around his wife Daisy and their children – and retirement has given him a chance to reflect on the sacrifices they made during his rugby career.

‌



View 6 Images Joe has now more time to spend with his wife Daisy and their four children (Image: Getty Images)

“You have to be incredibly selfish and self-driven, and you have to sacrifice a lot,” he shares. “And if you have a family they have to sacrifice a lot and get on board with it too. The only thing now is I probably have less time on my hands because I say yes to pretty much everything that sounds fun and exciting!”

He currently has “a couple of projects bubbling away”, including his imminent second book, Joe Marler Vs The World, and stepping into some Lycra as "Mauler", one of the new Gladiators - something his children are excited about.

“My kids love it, particularly my youngest boy. He’s probably the shyest of them, a Covid baby, and when I did Soccer Aid, we walked around the pitch and he wouldn’t let go of my hand, while the others just run off. We walked past Nitro and he says, ‘Daddy, it’s Nitro!’ He walked over like, ‘Hi, Nitro.’ And I’m like, ‘What? Who is this? You barely say hello to family members, but you’ve gone straight up to Nitro.’

‌



“So when the call came in to say, ‘We’d like you to be a Gladiator if you fancy it,’ it was a definite yes. But then I asked if I could be the first Gladiator to wear baggy clothes. They told me, ‘That’s not really how we do Gladiators here, mate.’ So, I’m going to need a little bit of time to get as close to Gladiator-ready as possible.”

View 6 Images Joe announced his retirement from international rugby in late 2024 (Image: PA)

Exercise still plays a huge role in not just Joe’s physical health but his mental health. In his 2020 autobiography, Loose Head: Confessions Of An (Un)Professional Rugby Player, he wrote about struggling with depression, anxiety and anger, and has since become a vocal campaigner for men’s mental health.

“It still blows my mind that suicide is the biggest killer of men under 40. It’s baffling. If I have a platform and the ability to nudge the dial in the direction to stop men killing themselves, why wouldn’t I do that?

‌



“And maybe selfishly, the more I talk about it, the more I can try to understand being a better role model to my kids, particularly my two boys. It also helps me try and keep a constant check in with myself, because I’m still f***ing it up and getting it wrong, and processing a lot of what I need to stay on top of.”

He’s now back into a good gym routine and taking his medications, and planning to find a therapist to help him “delve a bit deeper again”. He’s also determined to keep a handle on his workload and work-life balance, and to avoid adding unnecessary pressure or responsibilities.

View 6 Images Joe's Babybel Protein campaign is about making little changes that can make a big difference (Image: Will Ireland/PinPep)

That more realistic approach to self-improvement ties in neatly to the Babybel Protein campaign Joe’s currently fronting, encouraging people to focus on simple, achievable changes rather than “life-maxxing” and chasing perfection.

‌



“You don’t have to do a million different things,” he says. “You don’t have to take on the latest fad, there’s just small changes you can make to your life to make things easier and better.” It helps that the campaign fits his family life - his children are “absolutely obsessed” with Babybels.

While his post-Traitors life - with royal interviews and Gladiators - may still feel slightly surreal, Joe is determined not to take any of it for granted.

“It’s such a cliché and so minging to say out loud, but there’s no other way of putting it – Traitors changed my life,” he says. “The last 12 months have been wild.”

Joe Marler has teamed up with Babybel Protein for its ‘Fit It In’ campaign, encouraging Brits to embrace small, achievable healthy habits that fit into everyday life.

‌

News.title: Nigel Farage warned public 'deserve answers' over finances despite by-election win
News.content:
Nigel Farage warned public 'deserve answers' over finances despite by-election win

EXCLUSIVE:The Labour chair accused the Reform UK leader of delivering weeks of 'political theatre' rather than explain his £5 million ' gift' from Thai-based crypto billionaire Christopher Harborne.

View 2 Images Nigel Farage was warned the by-election doesn't change questions about his finances (Image: Victoria Jones/Shutterstock)

The public deserves answers over Nigel Farage’s finances and winning a by-election against a man dressed as a bin doesn’t ‘let him off the hook’, Bridget Phillipson has claimed.

‌



The Labour chair accused the Reform UK leader of delivering weeks of “political theatre”, rather than explain the “scandal” of his £5 million “gift” from Thai-based crypto billionaire Christopher Harborne.

‌



Since the farcical vote, which saw Mr Farage face off with Count Binface, the Reform chief has not been seen in public, and even failed to show up for the result of the £250,000 contest he triggered.

‌



Now Ms Phillipson has warned him nothing has changed, and that Labour won't stop fighting for the truth.

View 2 Images Bridget Phillipson vowed Labour would not let Nigel Farage 'off the hook' (Image: Wiktor Szymanowicz/Shutterstock)

‌



Writing for The Mirror, she said: “Nigel Farage wants this week’s by-election to draw a line under the questions surrounding his and Reform UK's finances.

“Spoiler alert: it does not. While he may have won a totally unnecessary by-election, the scandal he’s embroiled in will not magically disappear. Labour will not let him off the hook, because the public deserve to know where the money came from, what it was for, and why it wasn’t declared.

“Was it for security? Was it a reward for Brexit? Was it in exchange for something else? It should be a simple question for Farage to answer – yet his story keeps changing.”

‌



Just after Mr Farage's hollow victory, it emerged that the Parliamentary Commissioner for Standards probe into Mr Farage's £5million gift has resumed.

Ms Phillipson, the minister for women and equalities, said Mr Farage could have explained himself, but instead put the people of Clacton through a by-election for no reason.

In a firm warning to the former city banker, she said: “Unfortunately for Farage, despite his desperate attempts at distraction, the questions are not going away.

‌



“And Labour will not let him off the hook, because the public deserve to know where the money came from, what it was for, and why it wasn’t declared. Time is running out for Nigel Farage and Reform to come clean.”

Mr Farage has said the gift was not political and insisted he has done nothing wrong. The Reform leader also claimed did not attend the official count for the by-election because he had been advised by police to stay away due to a “credible threat” against him.

Ms Phillipson mocked Mr Farage over spending his summer “fighting with a bin”, and vowed Labour would keep working to bring back hope.

Article continues below

She added: “We know there is more to do. But while Farage and Reform continue to be mired with sleaze, scandal and questionable finances – Labour is fighting every day to build a fairer country, bring back hope and get Britain believing again."

News.title: Major incidents across UK putting firefighters under 'incredible pressure', fire chief says
News.content:
Eleven major fires in the past 48 hours and 43 new wildfires since Friday have left services under "incredible pressure", a fire boss has said.

Phil Garrigan from the National Fire Chief's Council (NFCC) said major incidents had been declared across the UK, including in Stourbridge, Sandwell, Pershore and Stoke-on-Trent in the West Midlands, as well as in Hampshire and South Wales.

In Stourbridge, 38 houses have been destroyed or damaged by the fires, with some residents left unable to return home.

West Midlands Fire Service set up a meeting point on Saturday where residents would be told if their house had been damaged or totally destroyed in the blaze and if it was safe to go back.

News.title: Jason Arday death 'tragedy on so many levels' says PM
News.content:
Speaking to BBC Newsnight, Professor of Black Studies Kehinde Andrews, a friend of Arday, described him as "very down" after resigning from Cambridge.

"He was very upset. He felt that there was no way out. He effectively wasn't leaving the house. He had lost a lot of weight," Andrews said.

"There should be a wakeup call to just how bad black academics actually have it in academia."

Labour MP Bell Ribeiro-Addy also told the programme "the idea that an academic would be dragged through this amount of media scrutiny is unheard of".

On Saturday Scotland's First Minister John Swinney said that people who "made many hard comments must now consider the impact of their words", describing it as a "deeply concerning and very sad case".

Prior to his appointment at Cambridge, Arday had worked as a professor at the University of Glasgow.

Shadow communities secretary Sir James Cleverly said he was angered by the "tragic" death and said "a number of people at a number of academic institutions have serious questions to answer".

When asked by the BBC on Saturday if the University of Cambridge needed to answer questions over its duty of care, Cleverly said the university should "ask themselves how he got into this position, how he ended up being in the eye of the storm, what could and should have happened to prevent this long before it got to this tragic situation".

Arday had denied plagiarism - but admitted errors in his work - and said the recent controversy had led to "an unrelenting level of public scrutiny and personal attack".

The row first erupted after another academic - self-defined "race realist" Nathan Cofnas, who was sacked from his Cambridge role in 2024 - said he found numerous instances of plagiarism in the professor's work.

Arday said some errors in his early academic work arose because of his autism, as he relied on using mimicry to make sense of information. Similar scrutiny would find similar errors in work by other academics, he said.

Questions were also raised about parts of his life story, including that he ran 600 miles in six days and that he had raised Â£5.5m for charity.

He later said the run was actually completed over a 12-day period to allow for rest days - and that the huge sum was raised with the help of others.

Arday's appointment as Cambridge's youngest ever black professor at the age of 37 in 2023 was hailed at the time.

Announcing his resignation last week, Arday said the "personal cost" of the scrutiny of him had become "too great".

He said: "While criticism is an inevitable part of academic life, what I have experienced has gone far beyond scholarly disagreement.

"The relentless accusations, speculation and public commentary have taken a profound toll on me and on those I love."

He stressed that his resignation should not "be mistaken for an acceptance of the narratives that have surrounded me".

Earlier this week, Cambridge announced an independent investigation around the circumstances of Arday's appointment.

Liverpool John Moores University - which awarded Arday his PhD in 2015 - concluded that he had not plagiarised work.

In a statement on Saturday, a spokesperson for the university said it was "saddened to hear of the tragic loss of Professor Jason Arday".

News.title: Powerful magnitude 7.7 earthquake kills at least 47 in Indonesia
News.content:
At least 47 people have been killed after a magnitude 7.7 earthquake struck Indonesia early on Saturday, the nation's disaster mitigation agency has said.

The official death toll has been rising as a search and rescue operation gets under way. The National Disaster Management Agency (BNPB) said several people had been injured to varying degrees.

Hundreds of buildings in the region have been damaged by the quake and the dozens of aftershocks that followed.

The quake struck the island of Flores shortly before 05:00 local time on Saturday (22:00 GMT on Friday). It had a depth of 15km, Indonesia's meteorology and geophysics agency stated.

The shallower an earthquake is, the more destructive its effects on the surface tend to be.

Aftershocks included a magnitude 6.4 earthquake in North Sumatra, located in western Indonesia, at a depth of 163km, BNPB announced. The US Geological Survey measured it at magnitude 6.9.

Video taken at the port in Maumere showed large chunks of concrete breaking off the terminal building onto passengers waiting to board an inter-island ferry. Some were thrown into the sea when the gangway to a ship collapsed.

Emanuel Melkiades Laka Lena, governor of East Nusa Tenggara province, told a news conference that they were killed in their sleep by collapsing rubble.

News.title: Met Police apologises for data breach involving alleged Al Fayed victims
News.content:
The Metropolitan Police has apologised after it inadvertently disclosed email addresses of around 140 people who say they were sexually abused by the late Harrods owner Mohamed Al Fayed.

Scotland Yard confirmed to the BBC it copied in all those who had signed up to receive a monthly email update for victims instead of blind copying them.

The update revealed a further three suspects in their 70s and 80s had been interviewed under caution, bringing the total number interviewed to seven.

The force said it had referred itself to the Information Commissioner's Office (ICO). It is considering providing further support to the victims along with additional safeguards.

A Met Police spokesperson told the BBC a monthly update sent to victims on 11 August regarding Operation Cornpoppy had contained details of progress in the investigation.

Operation Cornpoppy is the Metropolitan Police investigation into people who may have facilitated or enabled sexual offending by Al Fayed.

The spokesperson said: "Due to human error, recipients' email addresses were visible to others on the distribution list. The issue was identified quickly and immediate action was taken.

"We understand the impact this may have on victims and sincerely apologise. Everyone affected was contacted directly on the day of the incident.

"The incident is being investigated as a matter of priority, and we are reviewing our processes to help prevent a similar breach from happening again."

The force said the breach affected victims who had opted in to receive updates from the investigation team, but recipients had been split into smaller groups, meaning email addresses were only visible within those groups rather than across the entire cohort.

The BBC understands around 140 people have signed up to the updates.

The force has previously said 154 victims have reported allegations connected to Al Fayed and that supporting survivors remains at the heart of the investigation.

It said the incident had been formally recorded within the investigation records and they would continue to monitor the circumstances and impact of the breach, including reviewing alternative methods of updating victims that would reduce the risk of human error.

The force added that victim-survivors remained its priority and said it was committed to providing updates to those involved in the investigation.

News.title: Reform UK plan would overhaul welfare system with £50bn in savings
News.content:
Under the plans, Jenrick said they would invest in talking therapies, physiotherapy and employment support to move away from people claiming health Universal Credit (UC) payments and Personal Independent Payments (Pip).

People with "lower-level conditions" would no longer receive payments, instead accounts run by local councils and mayors will provide for needs such as transport and equipment.

Employers would see the creation of a return to work cover giving them a "strong economic incentive" to return an employee to work who has been off due to sickness.

Those claiming benefits and who had not returned to work in two years would face a "single, rigorous disability needs assessment", conducted in person to screen out fraudulent claims.

A new regularly reviewed payment will be in place for those that are considered "gravely ill and severely challenged".

Jenrick estimates after assessments of people already claiming, 2.16 million will keep their cash entitlement in full, while 2.89 million will see it modified or withdrawn.

Pip is paid to 3.7 million people with long-term physical or mental health conditions in England and Wales.

It is not linked to someone's savings or income and does not affect other benefits, or the benefit cap. People can get Pip if they are working.

Pip includes a daily living component and a mobility component. Claimants may be eligible for one or both.

"We will not pretend this is painless," Jenrick wrote of the changes, adding: "Dumping our young people onto welfare isn't compassion; it's neglect."

The party has previously said it would cut the benefits bill by billions if the party was in power, in order to offset the cost of keeping the triple lock state pension.

A Labour spokeswoman said: "Reform's Â£50 billion claim is fantasy economics, built on stripping support from disabled people and shifting costs onto employers."

She added that the Labour government's reforms to welfare "deliver credible, independently-costed savings, not arbitrary numbers with no credible plan behind them".

In March 2025, the government attempted to tighten the daily living assessments for both current and future claimants, but was forced to dial back after pressure from Labour MPs.

Jenrick described this as an attempt at "modest savings" gutted by backbenchers.

Last month, an interim report was published by Disability Minister Sir Stephen Timms, who has been leading a review into Pip, stating the benefit was "not fit for purpose" and requires a fundamental change.

Changes recently went ahead to UC which saw the health element of UC paid to new claimants halved for those with less severe conditions.

Jenrick also took aim at the Conservative Party, describing their proposals as "paper thin", adding that they would save more than double the Â£23bn proposed by Kemi Badenoch's party.

The Tories have proposed Â£23bn of savings from the welfare bill, through a package of measures including restricting benefits to UK citizens and ending access to sickness benefits for less serious mental health conditions.

In May, the Tories said they would reform the household benefit cap, meaning people receiving Pip would no longer be an automatic exemption.

The party said its proposals would deliver at least Â£1bn of savings annually.

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said the plans would "stop those who abuse the system getting almost unlimited welfare payments".

News.title: Thousands of Bonnie Tyler fans line the streets as coffin taken to Swansea home
News.content:
Legendary singer Bonnie Tyler has made a final journey to her Mumbles home, with thousands of emotional fans lining the streets to pay their respects.

The Total Eclipse of the Heart singer died "unexpectedly" on 8 July, aged 75, at a hospital in Portugal.

At the time, tributes poured in from a host of friends and stars including Catherine Zeta-Jones, Bryan Adams and Rod Stewart.

Despite Tyler's career taking her all over the world, she has been described by those living in the coastal suburb of Mumbles as a "Swansea girl through and through", and someone who "never forgot where she came from".

Huge crowds turned out as her coffin was driven through the place she called home.

News.title: Hunt wins third gold as Asher-Smith makes history
News.content:
Amy Hunt won her third gold medal of a potential historic quadruple and Dina Asher-Smith earned a spot in the record books as Great Britain's 4x100m relay stars put on a show at the European Championships.

Britain's new sprint sensation Hunt celebrated her third title in six days, following triumphs in the 100m and 200m, as the GB women's quartet claimed the hosts' second gold medal in a spectacular ending to Saturday's action in Birmingham.

The 24-year-old, who described her team-mates as "superwomen" and a "privilege to race with", will now attempt to become the first athlete to win four gold medals at a single edition in the event's 92-year history when the mixed 4x100m relay takes place on Sunday.

Team-mate Asher-Smith, meanwhile, achieved her seventh gold at the championships - 10 years after capturing her first.

With that, the 30-year-old matched the record tally also held by Norwayâs Jakob Ingebrigtsen and Croatian discus thrower Sandra Elkasevic.

Following her 200m bronze on Thursday, Asher-Smith also equalled Polish sprinter Irena Szewinska's overall record tally of 10 medals at the championships.

In an utterly dominant performance, Imani-Lara Lansiquot completed the job for a GB team which also featured 21-year-old student midwife Success Eduan, crossing the line in 42.05 seconds - more than a second clear of fellow medallists Switzerland (43.12) and Poland (43.15).

Hunt told BBC Sport: "I am stood next to the real life GOAT [greatest of all time]. She [Asher-Smith] is the most decorated European athlete in history.

"I am stood next to some amazing women. This girl [Eduan] is a midwife, she brings babies into the world. This girl [Lansiquot] wrote a play. We're all amazing.

"That was stunning to come together. I had the time of my life."

News.title: What's driving men to get penis fillers, despite the risks?
News.content:
Jason didn't want a "Coke can" â that's the nickname for a penis that has been enlarged with so much filler it resembles a stubby drink can.

"Some people go really overboard," Jason tells me when we meet in Manchester.

His procedure increased the girth of his penis by 16% - an amount he, and his partner, are really happy with. He says it has given him a "self-confidence boost".

"Everything still functions" as normal, Jason explains - just with "that extra little bit of width".

It is not clear how many men like Jason are having penis fillers. And you can't walk down the street and get a sense of it in the way you can visibly see the popularity of lip fillers. There is little regulation and there are no official records as anybody can start offering the procedure.

Penis fillers even became the topic of a bizarre conspiracy theory at the last Winter Olympics. Male ski jumpers were rumoured to be using fillers to increase the surface area of their suits so they could jump further.

However, some men have ended up in A&E with a penis turning black and skin "sloughing off" after a botched procedure. And the British Association of Urological Surgeons has issued warnings to men having these procedures.

So why are men doing it and what are the risks?

News.title: Analysis: Arday's death will send shockwaves through a divided academia
News.content:
There was another reason this row had such a high profile. Arday was a celebrity academic known as much for the remarkable life story he told, of an autistic child who didn't speak until 11, or learn to read and write until 18.

Other aspects of his personal narrative came under scrutiny, and he had to clarify that Â£5m raised for charity had been as part of a group effort, and that a 600 mile running challenge had taken twice as long as originally claimed.

Some who had signed a public letter of support quietly removed their names.

By the time he resigned his Cambridge position last week Arday said the "relentless accusations" had taken a "profound toll" on him and his family.

He suggested they had been racially motivated.

There are many unanswered questions which a coroner will no doubt be expected to consider about his circumstances and state of mind in the days before his death.

In the immediate aftermath of his death, his family said Arday had been subjected to a "campaign of misinformation" that was too much for this "gentle man".

Others think that he attracted so much scrutiny because he was a black man in a prominent position.

Sir Sadiq Khan, the mayor of London, said Arday had been "the victim of a pernicious public shaming that other people in his position simply wouldn't have faced. His death was a tragedy, but once again it should be a wake up call for all of us."

There has been deep unease among some academics of colour who feel the ferocity of the debate was due to Arday being a young black academic.

Professor of Black Studies Kehinde Andrews, a friend of Arday, told Newsnight in the wake of his death: "This is not just something that has happened in the past two weeks, we've seen the stories, this goes back three and a half years.

"The very day he got the position at Cambridge he had a Freedom of Information request asking about his credentials. He had all the right-wing people in America and the UK writing in to see if he was credible.

"Some people didn't believe a black man should be in that position at Cambridge.

"It's been a three-and-a-half-year toll which has come its head now."

What is certain is that Arday had sought to defend his reputation, using a high-profile firm of lawyers to send a letter to a journalist from Times Higher Education who first questioned his work.

The University of Cambridge initially robustly defended Arday then announced an investigation into his appointment and tenure amid growing disquiet.

In 2023, as an elite university which had been criticised for a lack of diversity, Cambridge had been keen to make some high-profile non-white appointments. It had already made a huge effort to ensure admission of students was more diverse.

Whoever was appointed into such a high profile post would have faced scrutiny and Arday had a slighter research track record than some others in the field.

Dr Jo Grady, general secretary of the University and College Union, described Jason Arday's death as "devastating".

"There are so many questions that need to be answered. The level of harassment he suffered and the racism he was subjected to, has been sickening. It must be investigated."

For the University of Cambridge now there will be the difficult task of holding together an academic community divided and shocked by the controversy and now the death of Jason Arday.

It had announced an investigation into his appointment and tenure at the university and a review of how senior staff are chosen.

Now all of that has been overtaken by his sudden and shocking death.

News.title: 'Fury' at Tarling death as cycling union calls for better helmets
News.content:
The cyclists' union has expressed "fury" over the death of British rider Fin Tarling during Friday's stage of the Volta a Portugal.

The 19-year-old NSN Cycling rider reportedly collided with a vehicle not involved in the race.

And the union's president Adam Hansen told BBC Sport there needs to be better helmet safety as cyclists hit record-breaking speeds during races.

"We are speechless and filled with anger," said the Cyclistes Professionnels Associes (CPA) on social media.

"It is not right that a young athlete's life should end this way, and we are furious that even today it is still not possible to prevent such serious accidents.

"We share in the grief of his family, friends, team, and everyone who knew Finlay. Rest in peace, young rider; we pray for you, and we will carry you in our hearts."

Tarling was the younger brother of Josh, a time trial specialist for British super team Netcompany Ineos, who has won a stage of the Giro d'Italia and a European Time Trial title.

Fin Tarling himself had finished strongly in the time trial a few days earlier in the race he would never finish.

He was part of a new generation of male and female British riders on the World Tour who grew up on the success of highly decorated road cyclists, such as Mark Cavendish, Chris Froome and Lizzie Deignan, during a golden decade for British participation in the sport from 2012.

Just like all young professionals, Fin spent hours every day trying to extract as much performance as possible. But he was known to love every element of cycling and was always in the saddle.

His parents, Michael and Dawn, frequently attended races and even set up their own team in their home in Ceredigion, west Wales.

BBC Sport understands organisers are considering a tribute to Tarling at the men's Tour of Britain, which starts on 2 September.

News.title: Military sent in to help emergency services fight wildfires across Wales
News.content:
The military has been deployed to help tackle wildfires across Wales.

Personnel and an Army helicopter are supporting firefighters in Cwmavon, Torfaen council has said.

People have been warned not to fly drones in the area because they will interfere with the military helicopter, and a fire service drone.

Meanwhile, police investigating a "deliberate fire" on the mountain near Pleasant Heights, Porth, said on Friday they had arrested four 14-year-old boys from Porth on suspicion of arson. They are on police bail.

The UK government issued an emergency alert to phones across England and Wales on Friday evening saying there was "a very high risk of wildfires nationally".

On Friday, Stephen Kinnock, Secretary of State for Wales, said military personnel had been deployed for logistical support and to help "ease the pressure on the ground".

Despite cooler temperatures on Saturday, crews across Wales are continuing to battle fires.

Mid & West Wales Fire and Rescue Service (MWWFRS) said crews had spent more than 90 hours on "operational incidents" in Llanwrtyd Wells, Merthyr Tydfil and Ebbw Vale.

"It has been tough, however, we have been overwhelmed by the support we have received during this time," the service said, thanking local businesses "that have kept us fuelled with food and drinks".

Residents had been evacuated from their homes after a fire near Llandovery, Carmarthenshire, with a councillor describing the situation as "scary", as the fire made its way towards the village.

News.title: Heathrow Airport roads reopen after mains burst
News.content:
All roads to Heathrow Airport have reopened after earlier disruption caused by flooding from a burst water main on a ring road.

The flooding along Inner Ring Road West prevented access to the central terminal area (CTA), which includes Terminals 2 and 3, a number of other buildings and the road network.

Heathrow Airport has confirmed the airport is now operating as normal and has apologised for the inconvenience after the road closures were made just before 06:00 BST.

Passengers are still being advised to use public transport where possible due to heavy congestion on the roads.

The travel disruption left some passengers struggling to get to their planes on time.

George Smyrniadis, 79, missed his flight to Frankfurt where he was headed for a school reunion on Saturday afternoon.

Smyrniadis, who got in touch via BBC's Your Voice, said: "I was upset. It's the first reunion I've missed since 1987.

"I was so downhearted I just wanted to get home.

"The whole airport seemed completely chaotic, but I got the impression the airlines just carried on as though nothing was wrong - and if you missed your flight you just missed it."

Smyrniadis said his trip from Portsmouth went well until he left the M4, at which point he was sat in traffic for 90 minutes travelling a distance which usually takes him about 10 minutes.

"By the time I got to security it was too late - it was already 09:30BST so they wouldn't let me go through any further."

News.title: Body found in search for UK student missing on Romania hike
News.content:
Tributes are being paid to an 18-year-old who went missing on a hiking trip to the Romanian mountains.

George Smyth, a University of Bristol student from Shropshire, had been missing since 23 November in the Bucegi mountains, despite daily searches, BraÈov Mountain Rescue said.

Avon and Somerset Police confirmed they had been notified by Romanian local authorities that a body had been found in the region. While formal identification has not yet taken place, the body is believed to be his.

"We are all devastated by George's death. He was the best of us and is deeply missed by his younger brothers, family and friends," his family said.

They added: "We want to thank Salvamont Mountain Rescue, who have worked tirelessly since November searching for George; despite very difficult and often dangerous conditions. They are an amazing team, and have remained in constant communication, helping us greatly throughout this awful time.

"We would also like to thank Avon and Somerset Police and University of Bristol, who have gone above and beyond to try and find George, and to support us as a family.

"Although this latest news is incredibly painful, the torture of waiting is finally over, so we can now focus on bringing George home and saying goodbye. We would appreciate privacy while we continue to come to terms with this loss."

News.title: Bride dazzles in thrifty wedding with £2 charity shop dress
News.content:
A couple tied the knot in a thrifty-themed wedding with the bride dazzling in a Â£2 charity shop wedding dress.

Gina and Jacob Dodds, from Hoole in Chester, said "I do" in a ceremony held at the city's Storyhouse arts and cultural centre on Wednesday.

Both Gina's dress and engagement ring were bought from the Hope House Children's Hospice outlet while guests were also invited to wear outfits sourced from charity shops - raising money for a range of good causes.

"If we were going to have a wedding then we wanted it to be about more than just us - we wanted it to be about helping other people," she said.

News.title: Woman allegedly tasered, raped and beaten by ex-partner, court hears
News.content:
A woman was allegedly tasered, raped and beaten in her home by her ex-partner, a court has heard.

In a special court sitting at Lisburn Magistrates' Court, a man aged in his 40s was charged with two counts of rape, three counts of sexual assault, threats to kill, non-fatal strangulation, entering as a trespasser to commit rape and assaults including causing actual bodily harm.

He cannot be identified to protect the identity of the woman.

The court heard the man had turned up at the woman's house on two previous occasions, once with a baseball bat, but it was "marked as a domestic".

Warning: This article contains details of sexual assault that some readers may find distressing.

A detective constable told the court on 14 August staff at the Ulster Hospital contacted police to report the woman had presented with significant injuries which she disclosed had been caused by her ex-partner who was also at the hospital.

Officers attended and the woman said she was asleep in bed when she woke to find the defendant was in the room having broken in and was holding a taser.

He physically assaulted the victim and attacked her with the taser.

She described him threatening to kill her and covering her mouth with his hand before raping her twice.

When he agreed to take her to hospital he stopped on a road and discarded the taser, which has also been recovered by police.

The woman sustained a broken nose and bruising to her face and neck.

The defendant was arrested at the hospital and provided a pre-prepared statement accepting that he let himself into the house but denying the offences insisting everything was consensual.

However, he could not account for the injuries.

News.title: Baby puffins make uninhabited island their new home
News.content:
Footage of a puffling - a baby puffin - bred on the Copeland Islands off the County Down coast has been captured for the first time.

The seabirds, synonymous with Rathlin Island off County Antrim, are not indigenous to the uninhabited Lighthouse Island, so no population existed there until an introduction scheme was launched around 2013.

There are now around 30 breeding pairs of puffins, which is being seen as a real success story.

They arrive to the island each April, and this year - in fact, just last month - trail cameras near their burrows in the ground filmed a young puffling out of its burrow, and an adult puffin bringing fish back to feed its young.

Attempts to attract puffins to Lighthouse Island included setting up fake "decoy" puffins, and a solar powered speaker system broadcasting its call.

News.title: Push to oust US ambassador from Canada expands - and ‘51st state’ could take up the issue in fall
News.content:

More than 170,000 Canadians have signed a petition demanding the removal of U.S. Ambassador Pete Hoekstra, after months of boycotting American goods and canceling trips in response to escalating trade disputes and talk of annexing the country.

Submitted on July 21 by a Calgary resident, the parliamentary petition urges the Canadian government to declare Hoekstra persona non grata under the Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations. It also calls for a parliamentary committee to investigate “U.S. diplomatic interference in Canadian domestic affairs.”

Under Canadian parliamentary rules, online petitions require only 500 validated signatures to earn a formal presentation on the floor of the House of Commons.

Because this filing far exceeded that threshold, Green Party Leader Elizabeth May is expected to bring the matter forward for parliamentary debate when lawmakers return this fall, The New York Times reported. Once presented, the federal government is required to lay a formal response on the table within 45 calendar days.

The petition follows a decline in relations between the two countries. A Pew survey released in June indicated that 35 percent of Canadians viewed the United States as a reliable partner, down from 82 percent in 2022. Canadian leisure travel to the U.S. has dropped by more than a quarter over the last year, while Canadian consumers have increasingly turned away from American products.

open image in gallery More than 170,000 Canadians have signed a petition calling for the removal of US Ambassador Pete Hoekstra, following months of consumer boycotts and canceled travel to America ( AFP/Getty )

Tensions have been high between the U.S. and its neighbor since President Donald Trump returned to office. He blasted the country and its trade with the U.S., threatened new tariffs and even talked about Canada becoming the “51st state.”

“If people wanted to play the game right, it would be 100 percent certain that they’d become a state,” Trump said early in his term.

After the U.S. administration imposed fresh tariffs on Canadian goods, Prime Minister Mark Carney warned at the World Economic Forum in January that global alliances faced “a rupture, not a transition.”

Tensions escalated further over Canadian objections to U.S. rhetoric regarding Greenland, as well as an Ontario-funded advertising campaign against tariffs that quoted former President Ronald Reagan.

Military cooperation has also faced strain. Following discussions regarding Canada’s procurement of American F-35 fighter jets, Hoekstra warned that changes to Ottawa’s purchase plans could affect North American Aerospace Defense Command operations.

“NORAD would have to be altered,” Hoekstra told CBC News.

The petition accuses Hoekstra, a former Republican representative from Michigan and former ambassador to the Netherlands, of harming bilateral relations and normalizing rhetoric regarding the annexation of Canada as a “51st state.” The petition also highlights social media posts by the ambassador referencing these annexation remarks, as well as statements dismissing Canadian public concern as “emotional.”

open image in gallery Hoekstra was appointed by President Donald Trump to oversee relations in Ottawa - which have soured because of the president’s rhetoric ( Getty )

The filing also alleges that Hoekstra engaged in improper political involvement by meeting with Alberta separatists, raising questions regarding U.S. positions on Canadian unity. The petition further cites his acquaintance with the developer of a voter ID application used by Alberta separatist groups. Hoekstra has denied allegations of improper engagement with separatist entities.

Despite the controversy, representatives from the cross-border business community have defended Hoekstra's work. Rick Tachuk, president of the American Chamber of Commerce in Canada, stated that Hoekstra remained accessible to business leaders and focused on trade relations, The New York Times reported.

“He at times can be blunt, but, in many respects, that is an advantage for us because he helps articulate the view of the president, and helps us understand what the challenges are,” Tachuk said.

No U.S. ambassador has ever been declared persona non grata by Canada, though foreign envoys have been expelled globally during historical diplomatic crises.

Canadian officials have not formally summoned Hoekstra, but other U.S. envoys in Europe — including those to France and Belgium — have recently been called in by host governments over comments about local affairs.

Cambridge University has defended its handling of Jason Arday and said he was provided with range of support before and after his resignation, The Times reports.

Prof Arday, who resigned earlier this month after a plagiarism row, was pronounced dead after emergency services were called an address in Battersea, south London, on Friday to reports that a man had been found unresponsive inside a property.

Prof Arday, a professor of sociology of education who became Cambridge’s youngest black professor in 2023, quit following a series of media reports alleging he plagiarised his PhD thesis – completed at Liverpool John Moores University – and other research.

Further questions were asked in the press about the truth of other claims he made, including saying he ran 600 miles in six days and that he had raised £5.5 million for charity.

open image in gallery ( St Mary's University Twickenham )

An investigation at Liverpool John Moores University cleared Prof Arday of wrongdoing.

Academics and politicians have argued that Cambridge failed to take Prof Arday’s vulnerability seriously when he was appointed to a senior public-facing role in 2023, despite allegations being raised at the time. The allegations resurfaced last month and were widely reported in the press.

In a statement released to The Times, a university spokesperson said Prof Arday was given “the provision of counselling, support and advice, and ­security measures, including the installation of panic alarms and the screening of racist emails and post.”

The spokesperson added: “Our support continued in the face of intense public and media ­scrutiny and after his resignation.”

Following news of Mr Arday’s death, his family said they were “in shock to have lost this amazing father, partner, brother, uncle and son”, in a statement issued through his publisher Simon & Schuster UK.

Reacting to news of his death, some MPs blamed the media for “hounding” Mr Arday, with Jeremy Corbyn saying the 41-year-old had been “turned into a pawn for vicious culture wars”.

But others, such as Conservative MP James Cleverly, said academic institutions had “serious questions to answer” for elevating Mr Arday into “positions he was clearly not qualified for”.

open image in gallery Jason Arday, a professor of sociology of education, became Cambridge’s youngest black professor in 2023 ( PA Archive )

Cambridge’s vice-chancellor Professor Deborah Prentice said on Saturday: “My thoughts and deepest condolences are with Jason’s family and loved ones who, as they said last night, have lost a father, partner, brother, uncle and son.

“My immediate thoughts are also with colleagues and students who worked with Jason in the Faculty of Education, and at Jesus College where he was a Fellow.”

Amy Hunt hailed her British quartet of “superwomen” after they successfully defended their European 4x100m relay title to keep Hunt on course for an historic quadruple in Birmingham on a night of back-to-back triumphs for the hosts.

Dina Asher-Smith moved joint-top of the all-time European Athletics Championships medal table with 10, the same as Polish sprinter Irena Szewinska – though the Briton has two more golds with seven and a chance, alongside Hunt, to add another from Sunday’s inaugural European mixed 4x100m relay.

Asher-Smith, Hunt, Success Eduan and Imani-Lara Lansiquot blitzed to the finish in 42.05 seconds ahead of Switzerland, who took silver in 43.12s, and bronze went to Poland in 43.15 seconds.

open image in gallery Amy Hunt won a third gold medal with the women’s 4x100m relay team (Mike Egerton/PA) ( PA Wire )

Hunt, who sealed a European sprint double earlier in the week, when asked about the possibility of becoming the first British athlete to win four golds in a single European Championships, said: “Hopefully! We’ll have to chat to the coaches about tomorrow, but I’m so, so happy for tonight.

“It was incredible to come together with these so inspiring ladies. Everyone had so much going on. We got a midwifery degree, psychology degree, history degree, and this girl (Lansiquot) wrote a play.

“It’s such a privilege to be able to step on the track with these ladies and the individual superpowers that we bring. It’s no joke. We’ve had all superwomen together out there, and yeah, it was so much fun.”

Asher-Smith said she would have to wait to see if she was selected for the new relay event, but appreciated she could become the outright top medal-winner in the 92-year history of the European Championships.

open image in gallery Dina Asher-Smith won a 10th European medal and seventh gold (Annabel Lee-Ellis/PA) ( PA Wire )

The 2019 200m world champion, who was runner-up to Hunt in Birmingham, said: “That was my aim, honestly, coming into this season. I knew that with the last European Championships, I was getting a bit close, so it was just in my vision board, but not in the forefront.

“I’m proud to have done it. It’s been over a decade of hard work with some incredible ladies and incredible championships. So yeah, I’m very happy.”

Jeremiah Azu, Louie Hinchliffe, Zharnel Hughes and Romell Glave also triumphed in their own 4x100m relay, beating Germany and Belgium to gold in 38.45s.

Azu, who claimed individual 100m silver on Tuesday in a British one-two with Glave, ran a 10.51s opener, while Hinchliffe, Hughes and Glave all dipped below 10 seconds in 9.22s, 9.57s and 9.15s respectively.

open image in gallery Jeremiah Azu, right, hugs Amy Hunt as they celebrate their relay gold medals (Annabel Lee-Ellis/PA) ( PA Wire )

Hinchliffe said: “The times don’t matter, getting the gold is the main thing so to get the gold, that’s job done. It was good to get out there and get a medal.

“For us to finish on both men and women getting gold medals in the relay, that’s special. It just shows we need to think bigger and replicate these results at bigger championships.”

Jake Heyward missed out on a medal by 0.16 seconds as the British trio of men’s 1500m finalists were shut out of the podium, and Katarina Johnson-Thompson was 21st of as many finishers in a heptathlon won by Ireland’s Kate O’Connor.

Bruce Willis made a rare appearance at his daughter Tallulah’s wedding this week, three years after being diagnosed with frontotemporal dementia.

The 71-year-old action star was among partygoers in Idaho as Tallulah married musician Justin Acee.

He was captured in a Vogue photo series, embracing his daughter while clasping hands with his new son-in-law.

Tallulah wrote in a caption: “A tender moment with my dad and Justin at the start of wedding weekend.”

Willis has largely kept a low profile since his dementia diagnosis. In January, his wife Emma Heming Willis said that the actor “doesn’t know” that he has the degenerative disease as one of the neurological symptoms includes anosognosia – which prevents a person from accurately recognizing their own illness.

Tallulah Willis and her father, action star Bruce Willis, who was diagnosed with frontotemporal dementia in 2023. Bruce made a rare public apperance to attend her wedding ( Getty )

Tallulah Willis, 32, is the youngest of the star’s three daughters with his former wife Demi Moore. Her elder sisters are Rumer, 37, and Scout, 35.

Heming Willis married the Die Hard actor in 2009, with the couple now parents to daughters Mabel, 14, and Evelyn, 12.

Earlier this month, Heming Willis revealed that she was torn over whether to mark her recent 50th birthday in June, saying that she has “not really been in the celebratory feelings of late” because of her husband’s condition.

“I was unsure if I really wanted to do anything, but I had a friend of mine who kept sort of pushing me and saying, ‘You know what, you don't want to miss out on your 50. You have to celebrate in some form or fashion.’ And I really sat with that and I thought about it,” she told Hoda Kotb on her Making Space podcast.

She added that she “always wrestles” with guilt, adding: “I think guilt is something that I am always carrying, but I've learned that it is really not helpful.”

“I always go back to: what would my husband want for me?” she continued. “And he would want me to have a big, fun bash. He would want me to celebrate my life with my friends and family. And that is sort of what I always think about when guilt of any sort comes in front of me.”

Last year, Heming Willis moved her husband out of their family home as his condition became progressively worse. She said in August: “Bruce would want that for our daughters. He would want them to be in a home that was more tailored to their needs, not his needs.” He currently lives with a full-time care team in a one-story home.
