Tyson Foods is shutting down or selling three beef facilities as an ongoing domestic cattle shortage continues to squeeze profit margins, the company announced.

The meat producer said it would end operations at its Joslin, Illinois, beef plant and its Eagle Mountain, Utah, case-ready facility. It is also seeking a buyer for its beef plant in Pasco, Washington.

The consolidation follows a $138 million operating loss in Tyson’s beef unit, as reported in its latest earnings update. Company executives noted that earlier cost-cutting measures — including the closure of a major processing plant in Lexington, Nebraska, last fall that displaced over 3,000 workers — proved insufficient to offset rising costs, according to Food Dive.

"I'm really heartbroken right now," Marydel Lewis, who worked at the plant, told KSL. "We thought we were going to get a bonus because it's our five-year anniversary."

Instead, she and other employees learned they were out of jobs in October.

open image in gallery Tyson Foods will close or sell three beef plants to streamline its manufacturing footprint as a persistent US cattle shortage drives up operating costs ( Getty Images )

"It's hard to take in," Lewis told the outlet. "It's like, is it true?"

High wholesale costs have driven retail beef prices to record levels, peaking at an average of $9.64 per pound in April, according to the American Farm Bureau Federation.

That price pressure has curbed demand. Total U.S. meat department sales dropped 2.3 percent in June, according to data from research firm Circana, as inflation-weary shoppers reduced purchases.

Tight cattle supplies will likely persist, Tyson officials said in their announcement, making plant consolidations necessary to protect overall processing capacity.

The Illinois shutdown alone is expected to result in roughly 2,500 union job losses, federal officials representing the state said in a news release, while more than 7000 employees will lose jobs at the Utah plant.

“Today’s news is devastating for the 2,500 skilled union workers impacted by the closure of the Tyson plant in Joslin, especially at a time when American families are struggling with the rising cost of living. In the coming weeks, we remain committed to supporting our union members during this transition and working with Tyson to ensure that they have access to resources that support their return to work,” Illinois Democrat Senator Tammy Duckworth said.

To absorb capacity from the affected sites, Tyson plans to shift production across its remaining network. The company will reinstate a second shift at its facility in Amarillo, Texas, where it had previously laid off about 1,760 workers during a consolidation effort late last year.

Moving forward, Tyson expects to anchor its primary beef processing operations in three central U.S. locations: Amarillo, Texas; Holcomb, Kansas; and Dakota City, Nebraska.

open image in gallery Cattle shortages pushed average beef costs to $9.64 per pound in Apri ( Getty Images )

U.S. cattle inventories have dropped to multi-decade lows due to lingering economic pressures and climate challenges that have left ranchers hesitant to rebuild herds, according to the USDA.

Supply concerns have been further complicated by a resurgence of the New World screwworm, a flesh-eating pest that has limited live cattle imports from Mexico. In an earnings call, Tyson CEO Donnie King noted that recent federal trade adjustments along the southern border will not fully offset current domestic supply deficits.

Meat processing competitors are facing similar pressures across the sector. Earlier this year, global meatpacking rival JBS announced the closure of two facilities and named a new chief executive after posting a $102 million second-quarter net loss attributed to elevated live cattle costs.

Problematic drug use in Israel has risen sharply following October 7, with prescription sedatives and opioids showing some of the steepest increases, according to new data from Israel’s Center on Addiction and Mental Health (ICA).

Professor Shauli Lev-Ran, co-founder and academic director of the ICA said that the centre's surveys, which have been conducted regularly since 2018, show a marked rise in addictive substance misuse.

Spiking in the months after the October 7 attacks by Hamas, the increase has failed to come down since, where problematic substance use has continued to affect around a quarter of the population from December 2023 onwards.

With such use often leading to addiction, “[Israel] may be facing another serious problem,” Lev-Ran warned.

Sedatives show the sharpest rise

The problematic use of sedatives and sleeping pills has risen from 3.8 per cent in 2022, to 10.2 per cent in 2025 — a steep 168 per cent increase.

Both opioid and stimulant use have also almost doubled.

open image in gallery Drug use in Israel has dramatically spiked ( AFP/Getty )

The proportion of respondents meeting the criteria for problematic use of at least one drug is now 20.8 per cent, according to the ICA.

When alcohol is included, this figure reaches 26.8 per cent, or 1 in 4 people — completely surpassing pre-October 7 levels.

What is Gen-Z using?

For Israel’s Gen-Z, the most popular substances are ketamine and 3-MMC (methylmethcathinone), known by the street names "Memsi" and "Doctor."

A dissociative drug commonly used as a horse tranquilliser, ketamine is taken recreationally for its hallucinogenic effects.

open image in gallery Ketamine and 3-MMC have emerged as the substances of choice for Israel’s Gen-Z ( AFP/Getty )

In Israel, its consumption has risen dramatically.

Speaking to The Independent, Yoav, 26, a former IDF serviceman, explained what he attributes to the increase: “After what happened at the Nova festival, I think we, as a society, really understood the fleetingness of life.

“After everything, rave culture in Israel really popped off. The ‘we will dance again’ movement is huge.

“Anyone I know could have been there [at Nova]; some people I know were there, and I think for many of us, knowing that it could all be over at any time has made us want to feel more alive, have more fun, and just party more — which has led to more people doing more drugs.”

open image in gallery People embrace next to memorials of victims of the 2023 October 7 attacks at the Nova Festival grounds in Reim ( AFP/Getty )

Referring to ketamine, Yoav said: “It’s everywhere — I’ve probably been offered it the most.”

Discussing the spike in its use after October 7, he explained: “I think for some people, it definitely can be a way to escape, or just forget about the s**t happening around us.”

3-MMC, a lesser-known substance, is a synthetic derivative of cathinone, the stimulant compound found in khat leaves.

While the Israeli government has not publicly released the number of deaths related to these drugs after 2022, ICA data largely indicates that this figure has only increased.

Higher rates among people with PTSD

The rise in drug abuse is even more extreme among Israelis experiencing symptoms of post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD).

According to ICA figures, problematic substance use in people with PTSD currently stands at 54.2 per cent — more than twice the rate seen in the general population.

The centre’s broader research also points towards a sharp spike in the severity of PTSD symptoms experienced by Israeli combatants post-October 7, where reports of soldiers describing their military instruction in Gaza as “illegal”, “not moral” and “wrong” continue to emerge en masse, according to testimonies obtained by Israeli veteran organisation, Breaking the Silence.

For Yoav, cases of PTSD-related drug abuse appear to be some of the most damaging.

“The people deployed to Gaza or Lebanon — I think it’s f***** them.

“Being a conscious person, being able to understand the value of human life, and then coming back — it’s really common for soldiers to be prescribed cannabis for their PTSD.

open image in gallery A boy sits near soldiers in Hebron ( AFP/Getty )

“But some of them end up needing the drugs just to be able to get through the day.”

As of February 2025, 15.5 per cent of respondents in the ICA's wider survey screened positive for potential PTSD, compared to the 12 per cent recorded in 2022.

The figures come as Israel enters the fourth year of its war on Gaza, with Netanyahu’s brutal military campaign placing growing pressure on health and social services.

The Israeli military was contacted for comment.

News.title: Rashford returns and Fernandes misses another penalty as Man Utd humbled by Amorim
News.content:
Manchester United 2 AC Milan 4

Bruno Fernandes missed a penalty for the second successive pre-season friendly as Manchester United were beaten 4-2 by former head coach Ruben Amorim’s AC Milan.

Fernandes, who rolled a spot-kick wide in a shoot-out against Leeds in midweek, was gifted the chance to open his pre-season account in Wroclaw, Poland.

His effort was on target this time, but Milan keeper Lorenzo Torriani dived to his right to beat the shot away.

Fernandes did at least get an assist, taking the second-minute corner which was powerfully headed home by Harry Maguire to give United the lead.

News.title: Newcastle kit fiasco sums up haphazard pre-season
News.content:
Newcastle United 1 Bayer Leverkusen 2

Newcastle’s pre-season friendly against Bayer Leverkusen at St James’ Park took a bizarre turn when a kit clash prompted the hosts to change shirts midway through the first half.

The German team’s white away kit with blue trim proved hard to distinguish from Newcastle’s home strip, which has a white back and blue stripes across the shoulders.

During the first-half hydration break, Newcastle decided to change into their lilac third kit, which improved the viewing experience for fans who took to social media to question the original choice of kits.

Newcastle would go on to lose the game 2-1 in new manager Matthias Jaissle’s first game at St James’, a result which followed a 3-1 reverse against Everton on Wednesday evening.

Leverkusen, the 2023-24 Bundesliga champions now managed by Spaniard Carles Martínez Novell, scored after just 44 seconds through a powerful Ibrahim Maza strike.

News.title: Raul Jimenez’s late penalty seals share of spoils for Wolves against Blackburn
News.content:
Cesar Peixoto wants Wolves to play with their heads rather than their hearts after the home side rescued a late point in the first game of the Championship season following relegation. Wolves replaced Rob Edwards with Portuguese coach Peixoto during the summer and he felt his side’s loss of organisation allowed Blackburn to take control of the game.

Peixoto said: “One point is not what we want, we want three points. We lost some organisation in the second half and played more with our hearts and not our heads and brains.

“We have to keep our mental stability during the 90 minutes because we’re better when we’re organised. We need to play our way with our identity. It’s a lesson for us to understand when we lose organisation it’s more difficult for us and more easy for the opposition.

“We’re working hard to bring more solutions [into the club] but we need to work hard with the players we have. It’s the first game, there’s a lot to work on and a lot to improve.”

Mowbray: It feels like a defeat

Tony Mowbray took charge of Blackburn in the league for the first time since returning to the club for a second stint in the dugout. Rovers recorded their lowest league finish since Mowbray’s first stint in charge of the club last term but the Blackburn boss is confident his side have enough to beat the drop and climb up the table this campaign.

Mowbray said: “Ultimately, it feels like a defeat, it’s a bit disappointing and a bit frustrating. I just felt a lot of decisions were starting to swing their way. It’s harsh to take, I don’t think they deserved a second goal. We asked the players to be brave and we were collectively very strong.

“Everybody has us relegated, probably on the back of finishing 20th last season and losing a couple of our better players and not spending much money, which is a good motivation for the team. We deserved to win the game, we showed there’s enough quality to give teams problems and I hope there’s help on the way [in the transfer window].”

The first chance of the season came the way of Blackburn as a cross-field pass found Alebiosu down the right, who floated a ball into the box only for an unmarked Oladipo Afolayan to head wide from eight-yards out.

However, Wolves scored the first goal of the new campaign when Fer Lopez played a defence-splitting through ball into the path of Munetsi, who coolly found the net with a first time effort from the edge of the penalty area.

News.title: How to have the perfect slow-paced holiday in Zakynthos
News.content:
Zakynthos, also known as Zante, is renowned for raucous nightlife, but there’s a far more authentic side to the Venetians “Fiore di Levante” (Flower of the East). For such a small island, scenery is extremely varied: the southern coastline – home to Laganas’ notorious nightlife strip – also encompasses the pristine beaches of Zakynthos Marine Park, where loggerhead sea turtles come to nest, while some of the island’s best-known attractions, including Navagio Beach on the cliff-lined northerly coast, can only be reached by boat.

Birthplace of the man who penned Greece’s national anthem, Zakynthos was also a magnet for literary greats: Byron lay in state here and philhellene Edgar Allan Poe wrote a sonnet to the island’s “verdant slopes”.

Last but not least, food is a powerful lure here: sit in a rustic sea view tavern sipping local Verdea white wine with a plate full of traditional kouneli stifado – a garlic and tomato-soaked rabbit stew – and you’ll be hooked.

News.title: Ebola doctors ‘step back’ from WHO in drug trial ethics row
News.content:
Two leading doctors have “stepped back” from long-held positions with the World Health Organization amid a row over the ethics of an Ebola drug trial underway in the Democratic Republic of Congo.

The randomised control trial, called Ebo-Pep, is testing whether an experimental antiviral is an effective post-exposure treatment.

But experts believe the study’s design puts healthcare workers on the frontline of the epidemic at risk, because it means medics exposed to Ebola might receive a placebo treatment.

“We owe them [healthcare workers] a duty of care to do the best possible thing, and a 50 per cent chance of getting a placebo tablet is not that,” said Prof Tom Fletcher, director of the Global Health Trials Unit at the Liverpool School of Tropical Medicine. The WHO’s health emergencies clinical unit has also deployed him to Ebola ‘Red Zones’ for more than a decade.

This week, Prof Fletcher and eight other experts based in the UK, US, Uganda, Rwanda, Sierra Leone and Canada published their concerns in Nature Africa, calling for a “careful reconsideration” of the trial protocol.

They said they are not against Ebo-Pep or randomised trials, but warned there are “additional ethical obligations” when including healthcare workers in studies like this, given the case fatality rate currently stands at 40 per cent.

Prof Fletcher said: “Ebo-Pep is a really good trial, it’s the trial we’ve talked about doing for years. But we’re talking about [protecting] the ‘one-per-centers’, the people who willingly step into one of the most dangerous environments in the world.”

News.title: Wildfire watch: Inside London’s fire control centre on the hottest day of the year
News.content:
“It’s been relentless, an immense number of calls,” says Yvonne Woodhams, control room commander at the London Fire Brigade’s headquarters on the morning of what turned out to be the hottest day of the year so far.

Inside a nondescript building in South-west London, dozens of fire brigade dispatchers field calls from the public and direct the city’s 5,000 or so firefighters across 102 stations to where they are most needed.

In the middle of another heatwave and on a day when temperatures rose to just above 38 degrees, the control room was busy – the scale and frequency of wildfires in London’s parks and grasslands are now considered unprecedented.

Above the dispatchers there is a live map, with red dots representing each active fire, sprawling from Enfield in the north to Purley in the south.

Wildfires nearly always have a human origin like dropped cigarette butts, glass bottles that magnifies the sunlight, or the now-temporarily banned portable barbecues.

But it’s the tinderbox that London has become which is worrying firefighters.

Scorching hot, low-humidity weather, a bit of wind, and tinder-dry vegetation can cause the smallest spark to ignite an inferno. Conditions like this have been described as “fire weather” by the author John Vaillant.

News.title: Inside the biggest collection of venomous snakes in Latin America
News.content:
On the outskirts of São Paulo, several secure serpentariums sit in forested parkland. They contain some of the most venomous creatures on earth and provide the fuel for Latin America’s biggest antivenom manufacturing and research facility.

In one corner of the grounds, huts on stilts house five of Brazil’s most endangered snakes. One, the golden lancehead, is so rare that poachers asked $20,000 for a single specimen. It is found only on a tiny uninhabited island off the South Atlantic coast.

Nearby, inside the campus’s oldest building, a dip worn into the stone floor shows wear from the original serum-producing horses housed here over a century ago. Around it hang old scientific drawings and shelves stacked with journals bound in snakeskin.

Founded in 1901 by physician Dr Vital Brazil, the institute pioneered the development of species-specific antivenoms Credit : Camila Svenson/The Telegraph

This is Brazil’s Butantan Institute. Founded in 1901 to fight an outbreak of bubonic plague, it now produces almost all of the country's antivenoms, supplying at least 350,000 vials annually. It is part of a public health system that has made snakebite in Latin America far less deadly than almost anywhere else in the world.

Now, having spent over a century perfecting antivenom at home, Brazil is expanding its global impact – sharing not just its lifesaving sera, but its world-leading snake research.

Specimens in a jar at the institute Credit : Camila Svenson/The Telegraph

More than five million people are bitten by snakes around the world each year. Between 82,000 and 138,000 die, while roughly three times as many suffer amputations or permanent disability, according to the World Health Organization (WHO).

The burden falls heaviest on poor rural communities in Asia (up to two million bites annually) and Africa (around 500,000), where farmers, women and children walk through dense vegetation without protective clothing or access to nearby hospitals.

Across the Americas, the incidence of bites is far smaller. Some 57,000 are bitten by snakes each year, with Brazil accounting for over 30,000, according to the country’s health ministry.

But what stands out is the survival rate. According to the Pan American Health Organization (Paho), the region’s fatality rate is just 0.6 per cent – compared to up to 12 per cent in some rural regions of Africa.

Latin American snakes are no less dangerous. Venom from bothrops, a genus of the pit viper known locally as “jaracas”, can dissolve blood vessels, stop clotting and cause severe flesh rot or necrosis. Bites from the viper account for up to 90 per cent of reported envenomings each year in Brazil.

One of the snakes housed by the Institute Credit : Camila Svenson/The Telegraph

Brazil’s constitution legally obliges the state to provide treatment regardless of cost, resulting in antivenom having come to be seen as an essential public right, rather than a commodity for profit.

For poor rural workers who cannot afford treatment, receiving free antivenom quickly is what prevents a bite from becoming fatal.

Regional biology helps too. Unlike in Asia or Africa, where dozens of disparate snake families complicate treatment, the dominance of the Bothrops in Brazil makes life easier.

It means that rural clinics only need to stock a few versatile antivenoms rather than dozens of hyper-specialised ones. The Butantan Institute makes roughly 400,000 vials annually, more than enough to meet demand.

Yet even such a well-designed system struggles with the country’s unforgiving geography.

The Butantan Institute is home to Latin America’s largest collection of venomous species Credit : Camila Svenson

Covering nearly half of Brazil, the Amazon rainforest has vast roadless expanses where travel relies on slow wooden boats. For isolated communities, reaching a stocked clinic can take 12 to 24 hours – often beyond the critical window to prevent amputation or death.

Part of the challenge lies in the treatment itself. Traditional liquid antivenom must be administered intravenously under strict medical supervision due to the risk of acute allergic reactions. Crucially, it also requires an unbroken cold chain.

When exposed to tropical heat, the therapeutic proteins quickly denature and clump together. This renders the serum useless or, in the worst cases, dangerous.

Dr Grazziotin holds a tiny snake Credit : Camila Svenson/The Telegraph

To overcome this, Brazil is increasingly deploying freeze-dried (lyophilised) antivenoms.

Though more expensive and complex to produce, these powder formulations withstand high heat and remain stable for years without cooling, needing only sterile water to reconstitute them for use.

The centuries-old process of creating antivenom is complex and relies on a method barely changed since its invention.

Reptiles at the Institute Credit : Camila Svenson/The Telegraph

Pioneered in 1895 by French physician Albert Calmette in Saigon (now Ho Chi Minh), Vietnam, the process begins by manually milking live snakes for their venom.

Small, non-lethal doses are then injected into horses over several months, prompting their immune systems to produce high concentrations of specialised antibodies.

Once levels peak, blood is drawn from the horses, and the plasma is separated and purified into concentrated vials of serum.

The new breakthrough lies in a technique of lyophilisation, or freeze drying, in which the liquid serum is converted into a heat-stable powder.

The antivenom is subjected to a temperature of -40 C inside a deep vacuum chamber. It leaves a fine powder that prevents antibody proteins from degrading or clumping.

Sealed in airtight vials, the powder can sit without refrigeration for years, needing only a splash of sterile water to become an active intravenous antivenom in seconds.

Dr Isabel Batista, Museum Director Credit : Camila Svenson/The Telegraph

Brazil’s antivenom infrastructure was the vision of one 19th-century physician.

The Institute’s origins trace back to 1899, when an outbreak of bubonic plague struck Santos, a major port city in the state of São Paulo, threatening Brazil’s coffee-dependent economy.

Officials turned to Dr Vital Brazil, a pioneering physician who set up a makeshift laboratory inside an old stable at Fazenda Butantan, a 400-hectare property outside the capital.

The Institute is not only sharing its life-saving sera, but its world-leading snake research Credit : Camila Svenson/The Telegraph

To test how the plague spread, he famously let himself be bitten by mosquitoes; when he didn’t fall ill, he (correctly) concluded rodents and fleas, rather than insects, were the vectors.

By 1901, the stables had officially become the Butantan Institute. The research facility was modelled on Paris’s Pasteur Institute – the “global gold-standard reference” of the era, according to Suzana Fernandes, director of the Butantan Center for Cultural Development.

“It was a model adapted here in Brazil for research, production, and the popularisation of science,” she says.

With the plague contained, Dr Brazil turned to a slower, but equally lethal threat: the pit vipers killing thousands of farmers across São Paulo’s booming coffee fields.

The snake conservation enclosure houses critically endangered species Credit : Camila Svenson/The Telegraph

While European authorities insisted a single antivenom could treat any bite, Dr Brazil proved serum must be tailored to the snake’s specific genus – a principle that remains foundational to antivenom science today.

To produce these species-specific antivenoms at scale, he devised an unconventional public barter network.

The Institute shipped wooden boxes and snake hooks to rural communities. In return, farmers captured live snakes and loaded them onto trains bound for São Paulo, where conductors guarded the locked crates in dedicated carts.

To seal the bargain, the Institute rewarded those participating with free vials of lifesaving antivenom. Between 1901 and 1977, the railway network delivered over 1.1 million live snakes to Butantan.

More than a century later, new snake lineages are still emerging from Brazil’s vast ecosystems. In 2022, for example, researchers formally described Bothrops jabrensis, a distinct species of pit viper discovered in the high-altitude forests of northeastern Paraíba.

Behind an unmarked door lies Butantan’s Herpetological Collection – one of Latin America’s most important archives of preserved reptiles.

Dr Felipe Grazziotin, curator of the Institute's herpetology collection Credit : Camila Svenson/The Telegraph

Dr Felipe Grazziotin, its curator, leads the way inside, revealing floor-to-ceiling shelves lined with stoppered glass jars. Suspended inside in pale-yellow ethanol are serpents, scorpions, and spiders – their intricate scale patterns and beady eyes frozen mid-glare.

Each jar has a handwritten label – a record of where a species was found, when and by whom. But in 2010, that priceless history was almost wiped out when a devastating fire swept through the Institute, severely damaging its collections.

Between 15,000 and 20,000 specimens were salvaged from the fire Credit : Marcelo Ribeiro Duarte/Laboratório de Coleções Zoológicas do Instituto Butantan.

Out of what was then the world’s largest snake collection – totaling nearly 100,000 specimens – scientists managed to salvage only 15,000 to 20,000. Most of the glass jars shattered in the intense heat and firefighting efforts.

“We lost more than 100 years of history about snakes in Brazil,” Dr Grazziotin says, adding that the news nearly brought him to tears at the time. “Without the label, a specimen loses its scientific meaning for us. We need to know exactly where it came from”.

A fire at the institute in 2010 severely damaged its herpetological and arachnological collections Credit : Marcelo Ribeiro Duarte/Laboratório de Coleções Zoológicas do Instituto Butantan.

He walks to the end of one of the solid metal shelves and spins a large mechanical wheel. With a low hum, the wall of jars parts down the middle, opening a new aisle.

As he steps between the banks, Dr Grazziotin points out that despite the devastation of 2010, certain parts of the collection survived the blaze remarkably intact.

“It was purely down to where they were stored in the building,” he says, gesturing toward a meticulously ordered section of jars containing some 8,000 South American rattlesnakes – an entire species’ record preserved against the odds.

Losing a century of history forced Butantan to completely rethink how it preserves its science.

Since the fire, the collection has been rebuilt inside a state-of-the-art facility with fire-suppression gas systems and shatterproof plastic containers.

In a nearby room, Dr Grazziotin proudly gestures toward a new $2 million (£1.5 million) machine: a sleek Micro-CT scanner, the only one of its kind in South America, he says.

The collection has been rebuilt inside a state-of-the-art facility with fire-suppression gas systems and shatterproof containers Credit : Camila Svenson

Rather than dissecting rare or historical specimens, it creates non-invasive “digital slices” of snake skulls and internal organs, producing detailed 3D models that can then be analysed online.

The ultimate goal, Dr Grazziotin adds, is to “digitise” the entire 120-year collection into an open-access platform.

The Butantan team is also building a network across Latin America, as well as partnerships with Portuguese-speaking African nations, including Angola and Mozambique.

“We share a language and shared experiences,” Dr Grazziotin says, lifting a nearly two-metre snake from its container. “We are bringing colleagues here to work alongside us, conducting fieldwork over there, and helping them build their own national collections”.

“The idea is to reduce regional disparities,” he adds. “If we can put all the information in our collection online, we can help scientists anywhere in the world”

Sports.title: Bowen staying, breaking season ticket record & Sullivan resignation.. how West Ham disaster turned into feel-good summer
Sports.content:
WEST HAM’S relegation to the Championship was supposed to be a disaster.

With debts reported north of £100m, crashing out of the Premier League was predicted to be total Hammergeddon.



Yet so far this summer there is a bizarre feel-good factor in East London — with fans already snapping up a staggering FIFTY THOUSAND season tickets.

That is 4,000 more than they sold last year in the Premier League.



And it has completely smashed the Championship record for ticket sales — beating the previous best of 37,000 set by Newcastle in 2016.

In fact, only Manchester United — and possibly Arsenal, Liverpool and Tottenham — will pull in bigger home crowds across the entire country this season. Quite some going for a second-tier club.



So why are West Ham fans flocking back to watch their team take on Lincoln and Preston rather than Arsenal and Manchester United?

Ticket prices have been reduced by 10 to 30 per cent, and with 24 Championship clubs this covers four extra games compared to the Prem.

The top non-hospitality ticket — the 1966 West Premium — costs £1,200 (£52.17 a game), a £520 reduction from last season but still the highest in the second tier.

The cheapest costs just £310 — or £13.48 a match! Only Lincoln (£273), QPR (£275), Bolton (£279) and Blackburn (£299) cost less.



SUN VEGAS WELCOME OFFER: GET UP TO £100 BONUS

TOP 10 SECOND-TIER SEASON TICKET SALES WEST HAM have smashed the season-ticket sale record in the Championship during the Premier League era West Ham (2026/27) — 50,000+ Newcastle United (2016/17) — 37,000 Sunderland (2024/25) — 35,000 Aston Villa (2018/19) — 30,000 Leeds (2023/24 & 2024/25) — 27,000 Derby (2016/17) — 23,000 Middlesbrough (1997/98 & 2024/25) — 21,000 to 22,000 Coventry (2024/25) — 20,500 Norwich City (2023/24 & 2024/25) — 20,000 Leicester City (2023/24) / Sheffield Wednesday (2016/17) 20,000 *Premier League era

West Ham’s average attendance last season of 62,347 — beaten only by Manchester United — was swelled by football tourists. These numbers will likely take a hit offering only Championship football.

But prices alone aren’t driving ticket sales.

First co-owner David Sullivan stepped down as chairman to focus on fighting serious historical misconduct allegations made by several women in a joint investigation by The Times and BBC Panorama.

Sullivan was unpopular among fans, who accused him of selling the club’s soul by moving from the Boleyn Ground to the London Stadium in 2016. He was long the subject of fan protests and boycotts.

Another huge development was Czech billionaire Daniel Kretinsky becoming top shareholder after buying 16 per cent of late David Gold’s shares from daughter Vanessa, taking him to 43 per cent — dwarfing Sullivan’s 38.8.



Crucially — with the Gold Family Trust still holding 9.1 per cent — the parties entered a voting pact, giving them ultimate 52.1 per cent power at West Ham.

Relegation usually causes a dressing room exodus, but keeping manager Nuno Espirito Santo and captain Jarrod Bowen has given instant belief and stability.

This time last year Nuno had just led Nottingham Forest into Europe for the first time in THIRTY YEARS, missing out on the Champions League by a single point.



He took over a complete mess last September — a result of shocking recruitment under Julen Lopetegui and Graham Potter.

Only after bringing in January recruits Taty Castellanos, Pablo Felipe, Axel Disasi and Adama Traore could he properly compete — and had they averaged the 25 points taken from their last 17 games, they would have finished seventh and qualified for the Europa League!

That was sensibly acknowledged and the Portuguese coach was asked to lead the charge straight back to the Prem.

Let’s not forget, Nuno led Wolves to the Championship title in 2018 with 99 points.

Bowen was predicted by many pundits to leave, with Liverpool, Chelsea, Tottenham and Aston Villa contacting his representatives.



Sources close to the player told me although his heart was with West Ham, his head urged a Prem move.

But his heartstrings pulled too much and he agreed to give the club a season in the Championship. His affinity with fans is genuine — and he is married to West Ham fanatic and actor Danny Dyer’s daughter Dani.

Yet he is a genuine Hammers legend after scoring the winner against Fiorentina to lift the Europa Conference League trophy three years ago — their first major silverware in 43 years.



Ironically, he flew to Prague — city of his heroics — to meet Kretinsky for crunch talks where the new power man persuaded Bowen the club mean business.

The deal to keep him was creative. Bowen agreed to slash basic wages so West Ham adhere to EFL profit and sustainability rules, but will claw it back in bonuses if promoted. If they don’t go up, a clause lets him leave on the cheap. A win-win for both parties.

Sales of midfielder Mateus Fernandes to Tottenham for an eye-watering £85m and Crysencio Summerville to Al-Hilal for an equally staggering £60m have strengthened West Ham’s financial hand.

Centre-half Jean-Clair Todibo — who fell out with Nuno after being subbed at Newcastle in May after 25 minutes — is set to leave for around £35m while Mexican midfielder Edson Alvarez and flop striker Niclas Fullkrug are also set to leave.

January signings Taty and Pablo are staying — as are keeper Mads Hermansen, centre-half Konstantinos Mavropanos, left-back El Hadji Malick Diouf, right-back Kyle Walker-Peters and injured Tomas Soucek.



Former Manchester United ace Aaron Wan-Bissaka reported back for pre-season on Friday — but question marks remain over his future.

Forgotten man James Ward-Prowse looks set to feature in the Championship, where his work-rate and dead-ball delivery will be crucial. Left-winger Maxwel Cornet has also featured in pre-season.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Now it’s all down to new director of recruitment Nils Koppen to bring in fresh faces. They haven’t signed anyone yet — but they need another striker as cover for Taty, and midfield reinforcement.

If they get that right, West Ham will be back in the Premier League next season.

Sports.title: Mikel Arteta sweating over Arsenal’s long throws as Premier League ban TOWELS in host of rule changes for new season
Sports.content:
MIKEL ARTETA is sweating after the Premier League banned TOWELS from being used to dry footballs this season.

Champions Arsenal kick off their campaign on Sunday with a Community Shield clash against Manchester City.



Gunners boss Arteta, who used Ben White and Declan Rice for long throws last term, said: “Not being able to use the towels is already a big one.”

The Spaniard fears his side’s threat will be reduced from long throws after protocols changed.



Stars will no longer be able to wipe the ball dry before launching missiles into the penalty box.

And Arteta joked he will send his players out in hats so they have something to dry their hands.



He added: “Let’s see what we do. Maybe we will play with hats on!”

Previously both teams have had to agree before matches over the use of towels.

Against Newcastle last season, Arsenal defender Riccardo Calafiori tried to use a towel left near Nick Pope’s goal to dry the ball before a throw-in.

Referee Jarred Gillett intervened and took the towel away — as the teams had not agreed for them to be used.

PLAY DREAM TEAM NOW!

When he was Nottingham Forest boss last season, Sean Dyche criticised the use of towels saying they are an unfair advantage.

Yet Arteta reckons the game will be better to watch and that the new laws are “really good”.

A crackdown on timewasting has been deployed throughout English football which will see countdowns for goal-kicks and throw-ins, time-limited substitutions, injured players being forced to stay off the pitch for a minute.

If a goalkeeper asks for the physio, outfield players must leave the pitch for one minute.

Asked which rule will have the biggest impact, Arteta said: “We have had the Premier League and the referees there with us to explain and go through everything.



“In pre-season we had the opportunity to see and experience some of them.

“We will have to see when the season starts and how this unfolds and what is more doable and what is less doable and what we need to adapt.

“We know that everybody is paying so much to the details, all the restarts and the countdowns, that will bring something else, a different dynamic, different momentum.

“So I am very curious to see. They are really good rules because what we are doing is trying to promote more game time and the fluidity of the games which is better and hopefully that will work.”

Yet it is Arsenal who were often criticised for their time-wasting on their way to the Premier League title.

Brighton manager Fabian Hurzeler criticised Arsenal goalkeeper David Raya after the Spaniard received treatment three times with Arsenal holding on to secure a crucial 1-0 Premier League victory.

Sports.title: Premier League’s managerial musical chairs is like never before – Arsenal couldn’t be better placed for more Prem glory
Sports.content:
ENGLISH football’s top flight has never witnessed a game of managerial musical chairs like this one.

For the first time, nine clubs have new men in charge and the main winners will surely be Arsenal.



The Premier League champions will take on Manchester City on Sunday in the Community Shield, the season’s appetiser before the main course arrives in a few days.

Regardless of the score at Cardiff’s Principality Stadium — history tells us not to read too much into the result — Gunners boss Mikel Arteta and his squad are superbly placed to successfully defend their title.



Even by recent standards, the managerial mayhem has been extraordinary.

Arteta’s big mate, Pep Guardiola, has left Arsenal’s main rivals, which is an even bigger boost than the Gunners buying a world-class striker.

Pep’s replacement Enzo Maresca could do well, but considering the amount of experience the City team has lost, there is no guarantee.

Andoni Iraola faces a massive task at Liverpool and it would be a huge surprise if he turns them into contenders again straight away.

Xabi Alonso will improve Chelsea, but the only guarantee is that they will not finish tenth again.

Michael Carrick was only confirmed as Manchester United’s permanent manager this summer and they could close the gap.



CASINO SPECIAL – BEST CASINO BONUSES FROM £10 DEPOSITS

But United are a work in progress and they will do well to really cause Arsenal some discomfort.

The other top-six boss from last season to stay in his job was Unai Emery, but he has lost players rather than improved his Aston Villa team, so it looks as though it is Arsenal’s title to lose.

Asked if so many managerial changes will help his side, Arteta said: “Every club would have their strengths. Some because they have won a lot in the last ten years, some because of the squads, some because of the money they have spent.

“We know ours and ours is related to what we have been producing for the last four or five years in a really consistent way.



“But we can be better and that is what we are focusing on to sustain that consistency — you called it stability. But I don’t want to be stable, I want to be better and more ambitious. That is what we want.”

City will still be Arsenal’s main competitors. However, Arteta claimed: “We will have a lot of challengers, looking at the squads, at the managers and at the clubs they are.

“But we know that. We need to focus on ourselves and make sure we maximise every resource we have to give ourselves the best chance.

“Then, day by day, it is going to be a long, long run.



“We know this league is full of incredible managers. It is so challenging every week to prepare games against them.

“That will elevate our level and my level for sure and we will try to be better.”

Despite being in a good position, and the pressure finally off after winning the title, Arsenal fans do have some concerns.

William Saliba, the best defender in the Prem, is sidelined with injury and Arteta is looking at Villa’s Ezri Konsa and Bayer Leverkusen’s Jarell Quansah.

After failing to land Vinicius Junior, Arsenal are still looking at a left winger but a high-profile arrival appears unlikely.



But this Gunners team is still not yet at its peak.

Declan Rice and Bukayo Saka returned last week and could be on the bench in Wales.

Saka’s absence has also allowed more game-time in pre-season for Max Dowman and it is inevitable that he will soon receive a senior call-up for the England team.



While some roll their eyes when the name of striker Viktor Gyokeres is mentioned, he is not quite as bad as you think — despite back-heeling the ball to an invisible Arsenal player against Borussia Dortmund in last week’s 3-2 Emirates Cup defeat.

An upgrade would be the dream but it is not realistic.

Gyokeres still scored 21 goals in his opening season and even though he cost £63.5million, that is still £8.5m less than flop Nicolas Pepe.

The Swede could enjoy a better second season and you would still expect him to improve on his Prem tally of 14.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Although he played 36 games in the top flight, just 26 of those were starts and he will have another major battle for a starting spot with Kai Havertz.



Undoubtedly, Arteta would like to strengthen but he has options in every department and all of the new managers this summer would love to be in his position.

Sports.title: ‘Fancy getting into boxing’ – Controversy as West Brom star appears to PUNCH ball into net during win over Norwich
Sports.content:
NORWICH fans were left in disbelief after Aune Heggebo PUNCHED West Brom in front at Carrow Road – and his goal stood.

Canaries stars and fans behind the net all screamed at the officials in unison after Heggebo, 25, latched onto Jimmy-Jay Morgan’s cross and bundled the ball in with 15 minutes to play.



The replays were even more convincing as a left-handed Heggebo jab appeared to be the telling touch.

With no VAR in the Championship, referee Tim Robinson was forced to stick by his gut feeling.



And it was particularly frustrating for Norwich that the match finished 2-1 to the Baggies, with Morgan putting the visitors further ahead before Mathias Kvistgaarden’s late consolation.

Fuming boss Philippe Clement said: “I’m really frustrated to lose points like this.



“I expect the referee to see things like what happened with that first goal.

“It’s incredible that we can see it from the bench, from 50 yards away.

“Players told him but still the goal is allowed. That is very disappointing.

“It is clearly with the arm that the player scores. The linesman had the best angle in the stadium.”



BEST ONLINE CASINOS – TOP SITES IN THE UK

Norwich fans were equally raging as they flocked to social media after the final whistle.

One wrote: “Does Heggebo fancy getting into boxing? Got a great punch on him.”

And another added: “How on earth that first goal stood is a joke.”

West Brom fans got involved as they looked to twist the knife, with one writing: “How have we got away with that?”

Another joked: “Clearly that’s hit his knee???”



And a third needled: “Great finish.”

Sports.title: Enzo Maresca has it all to do following iconic Pep Guardiola as he looks to avoid becoming another ‘Inbetweener’
Sports.content:
ENZO MARESCA knows he is in danger of being an Inbetweener.

The new Manchester City manager has probably never seen the TV series and films.



Although Maresca’s Chelsea successor Liam Rosenior was teased for his resemblance to nerdy Will, the Italian could hardly be more different from the lead characters, who are knee deep in teenage angst.

Yet, like them, Maresca is at a crossroads in his life.



Can he mature into one of the big boys of football management?

Or is departed boss Pep Guardiola too hard an act to follow, condemning Maresca to life as a stop-gap appointment while City search for an alpha male?



Maresca could take some encouragement from the example of Arne Slot, who won the Premier League in his first season after replacing Jurgen Klopp at Liverpool.

Yet that triumph did not insulate Slot from the consequences of a poor second campaign — and the feeling that his face did not fit at Anfield after all.

Maresca himself acknowledged, on the day he was unveiled as Guardiola’s replacement, that the situation was similar to when Sir Alex Ferguson left Manchester United and Arsene Wenger said adieu to Arsenal.

Ferguson’s anointed heir, David Moyes, was sacked in 2014, 10 months into a six-year contract.



SUN VEGAS WELCOME OFFER: GET UP TO £100 BONUS

Unai Emery lasted just 18 months after inheriting the Gunners from Wenger in 2018.

In each case, the fact the previous boss was a great in the history of both the club and English football cast a shadow over the next man from which he could not escape.

Which feels like an appropriate image at the end of a week that featured the most spectacular UK solar eclipse for 27 years.

While City and Guardiola were hand in glove, the sun shone out of his behind most of the time — burning so brightly it scorched rivals into dust.



Maresca’s predicament is more like that of Moyes than Emery.

Wenger left Arsenal in 2018 after a trophyless season at the end of a long period when the club had not challenged to be English or European champions.

But Ferguson pulled off the trick of going out at the top, riding into the sunset after winning one more title — his 13th overall — in the most dominant era any English club has ever enjoyed.

City then failed to be crowned champions in Guardiola’s last two campaigns, the only back-to-back ‘failures’ of his 10 seasons in charge.

Nevertheless, he left as a winner, adding another FA Cup and Carabao Cup to his Etihad roll of honour.



So City face champions Arsenal today in Cardiff.

And Maresca is up against a manager who has shown why it is usually better to be the man who comes AFTER the man who came after THE man.

Mikel Arteta returned to Arsenal after Emery was sacked in late 2019. The way things had gone wrong under Wenger’s immediate successor — and the deeper issues that were exposed — bought him some time.



Winning the FA Cup in his first season also earned Arteta patience from the club hierarchy as they attempted a full rebuild

It was patience he tested until last season, when he finally led Arsenal to their first title since Wenger’s Invincibles of 2003-04.

To do so, Arteta abandoned some of the principles he had learnt at Guardiola’s knee — as well as the Gunners’ reputation for attractive football from the Wenger era.

A team consisting mainly of big, strong athletes, who were physically dominant all over the pitch and especially at set-pieces, became champions in what felt like the beginning of the post-Pep world.

Maresca is his own man.

He even chose not to move into Guardiola’s old office to underline the change.



But at the same time, someone who was City assistant boss in the Treble-winning campaign of 2022-3 has no plans to rip up the Etihad playbook completely or go down the dead-ball route.

Even last season, the latest version of Pep-ball was good enough for City to come out on top in head-to-head battles with Arsenal.

Only Gabriel Martinelli’s late equaliser stopped Guardiola’s side winning at the Emirates.

City followed up a comfortable win in the Carabao Cup final with an April victory at the Etihad, which put them in control of the title’s destiny.

Yet as Declan Rice memorably claimed at the moment of defeat, it was not over.



City failed to press home their advantage and Arsenal’s greater consistency, especially in defence, saw them over the line. In that sense, today’s clash will tell us little about how any title race might go.

But Maresca will do well to avoid the fate of Moyes and Emery, let alone become a more successful Inbetweener like Slot.

BEZ BET IS HANDS OFF

Liverpool fans know better than to get excited about the prospect of Jeff Bezos becoming a co-owner.



But they should probably be alarmed.

As the Saudi purchase of Newcastle proved, having billionaire backers does not mean you can suddenly spend unlimited amounts.

The only real beneficiaries of the sale of 30 per cent of the Kop giants are FSG.

The club’s supremos are making a massive profit on the £500million they have spent on the Reds — and still retain their status as majority shareholders.

But for how long? The deal is believed to contain clauses which allow Bezos & Co to go for a full buyout.



And if what Bezos has done to another venerable institution is anything to go by, that is a scary prospect.

His reign at the Washington Post, who exposed the Watergate scandal, has been slammed by reporters.

What might Bezos do to the club of Toshack, Keegan and Dalglish?



DARK ARTS NOT SO FAB

It says something that the first person to make contact about new rules this season was an Arsenal supporter.

The amended regulations — especially on time-wasting — may well have an impact on the way Mikel Arteta’s Gunners control games.

Brighton boss Fabian Hurzeler will feel vindicated after complaining about the 1-0 home defeat in March.

Arsenal took 30 minutes 51 seconds to restart play in total.

Hurzeler said: “If they win the Premier League, they won’t care how — and you can see they do everything to win it.”



Arsenal are at the Amex on September 19. Bring popcorn.

BRUM BRINGS US A BIT OF RESPITE

Before the football juggernaut really gets going again and chokes every other sport with its fumes, the European Athletics Championships in Birmingham have been a breath of fresh air.

For all the doping scandals of the past — and those probably still to come — there remains ­something wonderfully pure and simple about human beings running, jumping and throwing.



And it was good to see Brits like Amy Hunt and Matt Hudson-Smith winning, especially in a summer of World Cup disappointment and Test series defeat by New Zealand.

LEIC OF THAT

FAIRY tales often have unhappy endings. And so it is with Leicester City and owners King Power.

The Jamie Vardy documentary, which came out a few months ago was a reminder of what a brilliant story their Premier League title triumph in 2015-16 was.



Just ten years later, the Thai family which bankrolled it have put the club, now in League One, up for sale.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

King Power’s core duty-free business has suffered a downturn and there is no more money to put in football.

Which is why we still need rules about owners and sustainability. Just better ones than we have now.

Sports.title: Harry Redknapp lands role in film about loudmouth fan he pulled from stands to play for West Ham
Sports.content:
HARRY Redknapp is set to cameo in a film about the West Ham fan he pulled from the stands in 1994.

The film is being made by Sir Ridley Scott and retells the moment that assistant manager Harry, 79, pulled loudmouth Hammers fan Steve Davies to play in the pre-season friendly against Oxford City.



The film was first exclusively announced by The Sun in June, where Redknapp’s appearance was teased.

Eddie Marsan, 58, has been cast as Harry in the film Halftime Hero alongside Anson Boon, 26, as angry fan Steve.



A source said: “This moment is one of football’s greatest true stories and fans will love to see it brought to life.

“Harry wanted to be part of the film and is honoured that Eddie agreed to play him.”

It is believed production is already underway.

Steve could be heard heckling striker Lee Chapman and repeatedly branded him a “donkey” for his poor performance.



Harry went into the stands and got him to play, with Steve going on to score and helping West Ham to a 4-0 win.

Explaining the substitution, Harry, now 79, said previously: “There’s a guy next to the dug-out.

“He’s got West Ham tattooed all over his arms and neck. After two minutes, he started on me, ‘We ain’t got Lee Chapman up front do we? I ain’t coming every week if he’s playing.’

“Half-time I made five subs. I was running out of players. Then we got another injury, so I said to this guy, ‘Oi, can you play as good as you talk?’”

Harry later told the stadium announcer he’d brought on “a great Bulgarian, Tittyshev”.



Steve, who went on to run a courier firm, said in 2013 of his goal: “I just hit it. It was like time stopped still. It was the greatest moment of my life.

“After that, I was exhausted. I was on 30 cigarettes a day back then. I had a couple of cigs and a couple of beers in the first half, didn’t I?”

The historic moment was never caught on camera, so now Anson, Eddie and Ellie Bamber – who plays Steve’s girlfriend – are bringing it to life.

Sun columnist Harry became the manager of West Ham United in August 1994 following the win against Oxford City.

Sports.title: Djed Spence posts emotional Tottenham farewell as England star seals £30million Inter transfer
Sports.content:
DJED SPENCE said Tottenham will always have a place in his heart as he sealed a £30million switch to Inter Milan.

Spence, 26, was a first-team regular at Spurs for the past two seasons and became an unlikely hero for England as they finished third at the 2026 World Cup.



But with Pedro Porro laying claim to the right-back starting berth under Roberto De Zerbi, and both Andrew Robertson and Destiny Udogie battling it out on the left, Tottenham were willing to cash on Spence this summer.

Inter announced his signing on Saturday evening, with the Italian giants forking out £25.6million up front and agreeing to a further £4.3m in add-ons.



But the grand unveiling was not published until Spence had posted an emotional farewell on social media, which included a special nod to Spurs’ 2025 Europa League final win over Manchester United.

He wrote on X: “A special chapter comes to an end. It’s been some journey, with plenty of memories, moments and experiences that I’ll carry with me for forever, especially that night in Bilbao.



“Thanks to all the staff members who’ve helped me along the way, the players who’ve become family & most importantly thank you to the fans.

“Time for a new chapter now, but Spurs will always have a place in my heart. COYS!!”

Tottenham paid £20m to sign Spence from Middlesbrough in 2022 after an impressive season on loan at Nottingham Forest.

The full-back quickly fell out of favour in North London and was shipped out on loans to Rennes, Leeds and Genoa – but his momentum continued to stall.



BEST ONLINE CASINOS – TOP SITES IN THE UK

Spence only began to establish himself at Spurs in 2024, and he made a combined 79 appearances across the past two seasons.

Now at Inter, a couple of years on from his last spell in Italy, Spence has the chance to show Serie A how much he has improved.

He said in a video address: “Hey, Inter fans. Djed Spence here.

“I’m excited to be here. I can’t wait to see you all. Forza Inter.”

Sports.content:
England star Djed Spence completes Tottenham exit after shining at World Cup

Djed Spence was England's surprise package at the World Cup, producing a string of impressive performances both as a starter and from the bench, but Tottenham have sold him to Inter Milan

View 2 Images Djed Spence has joined Inter Milan (Image: Rico Brouwer/Soccrates/Getty Images)

Tottenham have confirmed that Djed Spence has completed a permanent move to Inter Milan. Spence, 26, has joined the Italian giants in a deal worth €30million (£26m) weeks after his standout performances for England at the World Cup.

‌



The full-back, who can play on both sides of defence, has signed a five-year contract with Inter and links up with international team-mate John Stones at San Siro. Spence featured in all eight of England's games at the World Cup, helping Thomas Tuchel's side finish third.

‌



It came off the back of a difficult campaign at Tottenham, who he joined from Middlesbrough in 2022 for an initial £12.5m. Spurs manager Roberto De Zerbi wanted to keep him at the club but Spence has opted to leave.

‌



The ex-Nottingham Forest star made a total of 59 appearances for Tottenham and helped them win the Europa League in 2025 under Ange Postecoglou, beating Manchester United in the final in Bilbao. Spence's departure comes after first-choice right-back Pedro Porro signed a new deal in June, while left-back Andy Robertson has arrived from Liverpool.

Sports.title: Michael Carrick sends Man Utd stars demand after AC Milan loss - 'No excuses'
Sports.content:
Michael Carrick sends Man Utd stars demand after AC Milan loss - 'No excuses'

Manchester United suffered a 4-2 defeat to AC Milan in their final pre-season friendly on Saturday and Michael Carrick made no bones about their underwhelming performance

View 2 Images Michael Carrick gave an honest assessment (Image: MUTV)

Michael Carrick has told Manchester United's players that they must improve after their performance against AC Milan was 'not good enough'. The Red Devils lost their final pre-season game 4-2 against former boss Ruben Amorim's side, despite taking the lead twice through Harry Maguire and then Patrick Dorgu.

‌



Carrick had a near-full-strength squad to choose from in Wroclaw, Poland but his team faltered after he made changes on the hour mark. United's manager introduced the likes of Marcus Rashford, Kobbie Mainoo and Lisandro Martinez, each of whom were given their first minutes of pre-season.

‌



In an honest post-match interview, Carrick told MUTV: "We're disappointed with today. We didn't play well today. There's reasons for that in some ways [but] we need to learn from it, we need to improve.

‌



"Some of the boys were playing their first minutes. There's different reasons anyway. No excuses, we just didn't play very well today.

United will now return to Manchester and prepare for their opening Premier League fixture away to newly promoted Hull City at 12:30pm next Saturday. "The boys will have a day off tomorrow and then in for the rest of the week," Carrick explained.

View 2 Images Manchester United ended their pre-season with a defeat (Image: Andrzej Iwanczuk/NurPhoto via Getty Image)

‌



"Five days of training in different ways, sometimes a little bit harder, sometimes a bit more of recovery. But we'll work through the week and be better for it. We're looking forward to it."

Carrick hopes to have both Mason Mount and Benjamin Sesko available for the clash with Hull. Mount picked up a knock last week while Sesko has been out since the end of last season with a shin injury.

After facing Hull, Carrick's side will take on another newly promoted team, Ipswich Town, at Old Trafford. It's then a trip to Everton, a home derby against Manchester City and a visit to Fulham before the international break.

Sports.title: Norwich City boss fumes after officials ALLOW handball goal - 'Shouldn't happen'
Sports.content:
Norwich City boss fumes after officials ALLOW handball goal - 'Shouldn't happen'

Norwich City were beaten 2-1 by West Bromwich Albion in their Championship opener on Saturday afternoon but there are question marks over Aune Heggebo's opening goal

View 2 Images Aune Heggebo's goal for West Brom in their win over Norwich seemed to go in off his arm

Norwich head coach Philippe Clement was left feeling extremely hard done by after watching his side lose 2-1 at home to West Brom in their opening Championship fixture.

‌



Clement felt his side should have won the game comfortably with the number of chances they created – and also felt Aune Heggebo’s opener, which came against the run of play, should have been ruled out for handball.

‌



“It was clearly with the arm that the player scores – we could see that from where we were watching, 50 yards away,” he said. “It was the decisive moment in the game and should have been spotted.

‌



“There are four officials and one of them should have seen it. Maybe the referee didn’t have the best view – but the linesman on our side needs to see that. Missing game-changing moments like this shouldn’t happen – it has cost us at least two, maybe three points.”

Get YOUR Mirror Football Newsletter Get our comprehensive football coverage, with news, updates, opinions, analysis and everything that matters to you, straight to your inbox. To get it, it's a quick and easy one-two: 1. Head THIS WAY 2. Enter your email and hit Subscribe

As for his side’s performance, he added: “We should have won this game, we played well, showed good intensity and were the better side in all aspects of the game. I am really pleased with all aspects of the performance – except putting the ball in the back of the net.”

‌



Norwich were on the front foot for most of the game but could not find a way past a resolute defence, with a series of last-ditch blocks, and some excellent stops from Max O’Leary, keeping them at bay.

And they were made to pay for failing to take their chances as Albion scored two late goals to make it a dream start to the new Championship season.

The visitors went in front on 75 minutes when Callum Styles played in Jimmy-Jay Morgan, whose cross was bundled over the line by Heggebo. With three minutes remaining, Morgan made it two with his third goal since joining the Baggies in the summer, racing clear and working his way into the box before blasting the ball home.

‌



View 2 Images Heggebo's goal was the first of two late strikes scored by West Brom as they ran out 2-1 winners at Carrow Road (Image: Adam Fradgley/West Bromwich Albion FC)

Mathias Kvistgaarden nodded home a loose ball as the game entered added time, after a shot from Jacob Wright had been brilliantly saved, but it was too little, too late for Norwich.

West Brom manager James Morrison admitted his side were fortunate to come away with all three points. “We were on the defensive for a lot of the game and certainly rode our luck at times,” he said. “We weren’t good enough on the ball, especially in the first half.

‌



“We certainly didn’t play the sort of football we did in pre-season. We need to be a lot better than this, although I am sure we will be better once we get into our rhythm.

“In the end we were grateful for some good saves from Max (O’Leary), some good blocks – and a lot of hard work.

“We improved a bit after the break, and I think the substitutions helped and it was obviously pleasing to get those late goals.”

Sports.title: Marcus Rashford makes Man Utd return as Ruben Amorim gets last laugh - 5 talking points
Sports.content:
Marcus Rashford makes Man Utd return as Ruben Amorim gets last laugh - 5 talking points

MAN UTD 2-4 AC MILAN: Michael Carrick's side surrendered the lead twice and were condemned to defeat in their final pre-season friendly ahead of the 2026-27 Premier League campaign

View 6 Images Marcus Rashford is back in Manchester United colours (Image: Ash Donelon/Manchester United via Getty Images)

Ruben Amorim got one over on former club Manchester United as his AC Milan side ran out 4-2 winners in an action-packed pre-season friendly. Milan came from behind twice before running away with victory in sweltering conditions in Wroclaw, Poland.

‌



Harry Maguire gave United a dream start inside two minutes, only for Samuel Chukwueze to level the scores at the end of the first half. Patrick Dorgu put Michael Carrick's men in front again before Milan equalised for a second time through Alphadjo Cisse.

‌



The Italian giants then took the initiative, with Goncalo Ramos and Ruben Loftus-Cheek scoring within three minutes of each other. Not even the long-awaited return of Marcus Rashford could inspire United to produce a comeback, suffering defeat in their final friendly of the summer before next Saturday's opening game at newly promoted Hull City.

‌



Here are five talking points from the Tarczynski Arena.

FOLLOW OUR MAN UTD FB PAGE! Latest United news and more on our dedicated Facebook page

Get YOUR Mirror Football Newsletter Get our comprehensive football coverage, with news, updates, opinions, analysis and everything that matters to you, straight to your inbox. To get it, it's a quick and easy one-two: 1. Head THIS WAY 2. Enter your email and hit Subscribe

‌



1. Set piece success continues

No Casemiro, no problem. United said goodbye to one of their biggest set-piece threats this summer but still have the towering Maguire to count on.

Bruno Fernandes delivered a superb corner with just two minutes on the clock and it found the head of Maguire, who outmuscled his marker to score. The Red Devils became set-piece specialists after Carrick was appointed and look poised to maintain that tag in the new campaign.

Where will Manchester United finish this season? Give us your prediction in the comments section.

‌



View 6 Images Harry Maguire put Manchester United in front (Image: Ash Donelon/Manchester United via Getty Images)

2. Fernandes misses penalty - again

Five minutes after Chukwueze equalised, United were given a golden opportunity to restore their lead. Youri Tielemans was brought down in the penalty area and the referee pointed to the spot.

Up stepped Fernandes, but like in Wednesday's shootout against Leeds, he missed. The United captain went for power but Lorenzo Torriani was equal to it, making a fine save low to his left-hand side.

‌



Fernandes' struggles from the spot may well concern the Old Trafford faithful, although he's usually a safe bet when the pressure is on. His miss ensured that it was 1-1 at the break.

View 6 Images Bruno Fernandes has missed his last two penalties (Image: Ash Donelon/Manchester United via Getty Images)

3. Dorgu justifies Carrick's decision

Signed by Amorim and used primarily as a wing-back, the question of where Dorgu would feature in Carrick's system was a big one back in January. But no more. The United manager's decision to use him as a left winger has paid off.

‌



The Denmark international established himself as undroppable before suffering an injury that effectively curtailed his season, although he did return to the starting XI on the final day, coming away with an impressive goal and assist. Early in the second half here, Dorgu showed his goalscoring instinct again by capitalising on a poor back pass from Filippo Terracciano, coolly slotting the ball home with his weaker right foot.

Milan drew level soon after, though. Cisse skirted the offside line to covert Chukwueze's cross-cum-shot.

View 6 Images Patrick Dorgu punished AC Milan's defensive error (Image: Sergei GAPON/AFP via Getty Images)

‌



4. Rashford returns

After 612 days, Rashford was back in a Manchester United shirt. The forward came on as part of a raft of changes on the hour mark, with Kobbie Mainoo and Lisandro Martinez also making their first appearances in pre-season.

Rashford was sporting the iconic No.9 shirt, although United noted before kick-off that their squad numbers are yet to be confirmed. Unfortunately for the 28-year-old, his introduction coincided with his team's downfall.

6 View 6 Images Marcus Rashford wore a new squad number (Image: Ash Donelon/Manchester United via Getty Images) 6 View 6 Images Ruben Amorim faced his former club (Image: Giuseppe Cottini/AC Milan via Getty Images)

‌



5. Amorim gets last laugh

It may've only be a friendly but there's no doubt that this win will taste sweet for Amorim. It was reported in midweek that United's players and staff had spoken privately that they were fired up to beat the ex-Red Devils boss, but instead he came out on top.

And boy, did the Portuguese sorely need it. Milan's previous pre-season results and performances had done little to encourage fans following his appointment earlier this summer, but they got their first win ahead of next Sunday's Serie A opener away to Torino.

Sports.title: Scheffler retains lead in Memphis as Burns stars and McIlroy toils again
Sports.content:
Scottie Scheffler will take a two-shot lead into the final round of the FedEx St Jude Championship in Memphis as he looks to complete his first win since January.

The three-stroke advantage the world No 1 had carved out at halfway after a second-round, course-record 61 was trimmed by one as he bogeyed his penultimate hole at TPC Southwind on Saturday before signing for a two-under 68 and closing on 13 under.

Sam Burns carded a sizzling, bogey-free eight-under 62 while Sungjae Im shot a three-under 67 with those players the leader's closest challengers on 11 under.

But Scheffler is now just one good day away from his maiden trophy since The American Express in California at the start of the year, not that he hasn't threatened in that time.

How do the FedExCup Playoffs work? Only the top 70 in the season-long FedExCup standings have reached the FedEx St. Jude Championship. The top 50 then progress to the BMW Championship (August 20-23) and then only the top 30 make it to the Tour Championship (August 27-30). Winners of the first two play-off events earn 750 points apiece before the points reset to zero ahead of the Tour Championship. In the closing event, all players begin at even par, with the starting-strokes model based on FedExCup placings at that point axed in 2025. The winner of the Tour Championship becomes FedExCup champion for 2026, earning $10m (£7.4m) and a five-year PGA Tour exemption.

The 30-year-old has recorded five runners-up finishes, including at the 3M Open in his previous event, and nine top-fives in total in the intervening months.

In his third round in Tennessee, Scheffler bogeyed his fourth hole before birdies at two, 11, 12 and 16 preceded that dropped shot at 17, which came after he picked out a left-hand bunker with his second shot at the par four.

Defending FedExCup Playoffs champion Tommy Fleetwood remains in the hunt after a two-under Saturday - the highlight of which was a monster birdie putt at 13 - leaving him five strokes adrift of Scheffler on eight under and in a share of fourth with Jake Knapp.

Image: Rory McIlroy has not shot a round under par at TPC Southwind this week

Rory McIlroy, though, is languishing in tied-67th place on six over - 19 shots off Scheffler - after shooting a two-over 72 on Saturday, with the world No 2 yet to post an under-par round this week.

McIlroy, a three-time FedExCup Playoffs champion, was even par on the day heading to the 18th in his third round, only to then finish with a double bogey after finding the water off the tee.

The 37-year-old picked up back-to-back birdies at nine and 10, while his bogeys came at two and 13 before his gory final hole.

Sports.title: Djokovic knocked out early in Cincinnati after struggling in sapping heat
Sports.content:
Novak Djokovic suffered defeat and struggled physically in his first match since Wimbledon as he was upset by Thiago Agustin Tirante in a sapping three-set contest at the Cincinnati Open.

Djokovic, inactive on the ATP Tour since losing to Jannik Sinner at the grass-court Grand Slam on July 10, won the first set 6-2 but then lost the next two 6-4 as he battled the heat and humidity in Ohio, even appearing to vomit at one stage.

The 24-time major champion won an 18-minute third game of the second set, fending off four break points over nine deuces, before taking a medical timeout, while he dropped to his hands and knees at certain points in a match that lasted two hours and 45 minutes.

Tirante revels in 'best win of career'

Tirante, who can look forward to a third-round meeting with Spain's Martin Landaluce, made the decisive break at 4-4 in the decider after converting his fourth break point of the game and then closed out the win on serve.

Image: Tirante says his win over Djokovic was the best of his career

He said afterwards: "This is the best win of my career. I really did a good job inside the court. I managed very well the nerves of playing against a legend like Novak. Now I feel relieved.

"It is all so much pressure when you cannot break [serve]. I had so many points to break and I couldn't, so that was the key. Keep believing in myself with my team and think about it after the match."

Djokovic was the third seed in Cincinnati despite sitting fifth in the world rankings, with world No 1 Sinner withdrawing due to a knee injury and world No 3 Carlos Alcaraz also absent as he continues to deal with a lingering wrist issue.

Top seed Alexander Zverev plays Britain's Cameron Norrie in the second round overnight.

Sports.title: St Helens keep slim play-off hopes alive by stunning Wakefield
Sports.content:
St Helens produced a blistering second-half performance to stun Wakefield Trinity with a 46-16 victory and keep their slim Super League play-off hopes alive.

Saints, who have never failed to make the post-season, came into the match on a run of three defeats in a row and five losses in six, leaving them six points off the top six.

The visitors slipped 10-0 down to fourth-placed Wakefield and trailed 16-12 at half-time but then ran in six unanswered tries in the second period.

Wakefield falter after bright start

Wakefield, who lost Josh Rourke and try-scorer Isaiah Vagana to injuries inside the first quarter of an hour, missed the chance to move two points behind table toppers Leeds as they suffered a sixth successive defeat to Saints and slipped to back-to-back home losses after last week's narrow reverse against the Rhinos.

Tyson Smoothy's eighth-minute effort, which was converted by Jack Sinfield, and Vagana's Sinfield-aided score in the 12th put Wakefield on top.

However, Vagana was barged into as he went down and went off with a physio holding his left arm, after Rourke departed following a collision with Murphy.

Once Billy Keeley latched on to a loose ball and went over after 64 minutes, Saints dominated, with Sailor's hat-trick, sealed after a lung-busting run, prompting Wakefield's fans to stream for the exits.
