World.title: Anton Aleksejev: Putin does not know the people he lives among
World.content:
By allowing Yabloko to participate in the State Duma elections and failing to anticipate its rise in popularity, Vladimir Putin's administration has confirmed that it does not understand the people it governs, writes Anton Aleksejev.

A legend says that when Yuri Andropov came to power in 1982 after Leonid Brezhnev's death, he told a Politburo meeting: "We do not know the people among whom we live."

More than forty years later, Vladimir Putin — also with a KGB background — has clearly ended up in the same situation. He prefers to believe that people who oppose the war are marginal in number and that the overwhelming majority is actually pleased about it.

In early August, Putin quoted volunteers he had previously met. They asked the president: "When the 'special military operation'"— the official term for the war in Russia — "eventually ends, what will we do then?" Putin did not say what he answered. He likely does not know himself.

Life goes on, however, and since — unlike in Ukraine — martial law has not been declared in Russia, State Duma elections will be held on September 20. "Elections" is a conditional term, because in such cases the Kremlin has long been simply appointing the next composition of parliament.

On July 30, the Central Election Commission registered 11 parties to participate. All share unconditional loyalty to the Kremlin, but as usual only four or five will actually enter parliament. United Russia will get the majority. The Communists, Liberal Democrats, A Just Russia, and the supposedly liberal New People will divide the remaining seats the Kremlin leaves for them.

Among those who have never had access to parliamentary mandates is Yabloko, founded in 1993 and considered democratic and liberal.

"'Elections' is a conditional term, because in such cases the Kremlin has long been simply appointing the next composition of parliament."

They last entered the Duma almost 20 years ago. Since then, their chances have steadily declined — partly because the party refused cooperation with potential allies (including the then‑alive Alexei Navalny), and partly because the Kremlin decided once and for all that the Duma podium would not be given to "odd characters." Even so, Yabloko was regarded as an "old party," one Putin treated with a certain respect, and they never skipped an election.

As befits a marginal party, Yabloko entered the elections with a slogan marginal in today's Russia: "For peace and freedom!"

Sergei Kiriyenko, the first deputy head of the presidential administration responsible for elections, reasoned that Yabloko would again get its two to three percent, fail to enter parliament, and prove to all anti‑war citizens that they are vanishingly few.

But within a week of registration, support for the party rose from three percent to seven — with a month and a half still to go. The outsider and marginal force was becoming a poorly controllable threat right before the presidential administration's eyes.

Of course, according to Stalin's principle — "it doesn't matter how people vote, but how the votes are counted" — no level of public support would have changed anything. No one intended to let Yabloko into the Duma.

Still, the mere fact that during the fifth year of the war, the slogan "For peace and freedom!" would appear on television and in newspapers for six weeks could have unpredictable consequences.

Yabloko did not speak about who Crimea belongs to, did not oppose holding elections in occupied Ukrainian territories, and so on. Two words were enough to signal clearly: if you want the war to end as soon as possible, here are people who share your view. And voting would show how many of you there are.

The FSB's 2nd Service — responsible for protecting constitutional order — understood the problem first. Action had to be swift and decisive. On August 7, it filed a lawsuit with the Supreme Court to remove Yabloko from the elections.

As usual, the FSB chose a suitable executor. Official parties — Communists, Liberal Democrats — rushed to accuse Yabloko of extremism and near‑treason, but none dared go to court demanding a ban.

The role fit perfectly for State Duma deputy Alexei Zhuravlyov of the Rodina party. The party itself is not represented in the Duma, but Zhuravlyov was allowed in during the previous elections, presumably in hopes he might be useful.

So far, his usefulness has consisted mainly of appearances on propaganda TV shows, where he has called for killing at least two million Ukrainians and claimed that Europe has special zoophile zoos where perverts can pay to have sex with animals, even turtles.

"As befits a marginal party, Yabloko entered the elections with a slogan marginal in today's Russia: "For peace and freedom!""

Zhuravlyov did not disappoint his superiors. In his lawsuit, he accused Yabloko of extremism, foreign funding, and even copyright infringement. One Yabloko poster depicted a nuclear explosion as a symbol of war. Zhuravlyov claimed the photo showed the 1945 Hiroshima bombing and that the rights belonged to the U.S. Army.

Even the judge was surprised and asked whether Zhuravlyov could prove his claims. He was unfazed: the photo could not exist without the bombing, and since the bomb belonged to the United States, the image of its explosion must also be U.S. property.

By that logic, anyone wishing to use a photo of a nuclear explosion in the future must build a nuclear bomb, detonate it themselves, and photograph the blast — otherwise they risk being crushed by the Russian legal system.

Despite the absurdity, on August 10 the Supreme Court removed Yabloko from the elections — the first time in Russian history that a party was banned just ten days after being allowed to run.

As the murdered Boris Nemtsov said, in the absence of fair elections and fair polling, the only way to understand a political force's popularity in Russia is through the authorities' reaction.

Everything happened exactly in line with Andropov's words. By allowing Yabloko to run and failing to foresee its rise, the presidential administration confirmed it does not know the people it lives among. The FSB, by removing Yabloko with Zhuravlyov and the Supreme Court, clarified: we do not know them and do not want to know them.

Meanwhile, such unwillingness to know the governed is characteristic of many governments. Volodymyr Zelenskyy likely did not expect that his July decision to dismiss former defense minister Mykhailo Fedorov would bring thousands of young people into the streets in protest.

Last Monday, several hundred young Yabloko supporters gathered outside the Supreme Court in Moscow. For a city of millions, that is not many, but in a country where all unsanctioned street gatherings are effectively banned, it is a significant number.

The motivation of young Russians who do not want to go to war and fear mobilization coincides strikingly with the motivation of at least two million Ukrainians trying to avoid mobilization.

And if Yabloko's slogan "For peace!" is interpreted as a call to freeze fighting along the front line immediately and begin negotiations, then nearly 60 percent of Ukrainians today share that view.

How many Russians share it, we will not know — but judging by the authorities' reaction, enough to cast doubt on the continuation of the war. And as Vladimir Putin said: "When the war ends, what will we do then?"

World.title: Mounting public interest seeing teachers brush up on drone knowledge
World.content:
Over the next five months, 20 science and mathematics teachers will visit various companies to gain practical insights and work together to create teaching materials for the future.

The "Lae end" ("Charge Yourself") education program is aimed at middle school physics and mathematics teachers, helping them bring more practical examples and real-life connections into the teaching of science and mathematics. This year, 72 teachers applied to the program, of whom 20 were selected. Participants include both new and more experienced teachers who began the program at Metrosert's drone and defense technology testing laboratory.

"We have a whole range of laboratories here for testing subsystems. What is important about all of these laboratories is that the tests can be replicated," said Rainer Kivimäe, head of Metrosert's drone unit.

Interest in drones and artificial intelligence is also growing in schools, meaning teachers increasingly need to be able to explain these topics to students.

"Starting this academic year, as far as I know, some schools will begin talking more about drones. An educational program is also being developed in Tallinn where young people will be able to play drone soccer themselves. So young people's interest in the field is gradually beginning to grow and teachers naturally need to be knowledgeable enough to discuss it in the first place," said "Lae end" program manager Valentina Moskaljova.

For teachers, this means getting up to speed on subjects they have not encountered before.

"I knew as much about drones as I'd read in the news, basically, and as much as has recently been said about introducing a drone curriculum in schools," said Getriin Kokk, a mathematics teacher at Lodijärve School.

The program will also produce teaching materials for students in grades seven through nine.

"Young people need to understand which formulas they can use in both mathematics and physics. Right now, we're giving teachers the opportunity to work together in groups to create materials specifically designed to support that learning," Moskaljova said.

World.title: Gallery: Ukrainian children's fairytale art from Kharkiv reaches Estonia
World.content:
More than a dozen works by young artists in Kharkiv are now on display in Pärnu, blending forgotten legends and untold tales with new mythologies in large, colorful scenes.

"Lost Fairy Tales" opened at the Pärnu Museum of New Art (MONA) this week, showcasing 14 monumental original works created by about 40 children and teens ages 5–17.

Kharkiv's Aza Nizi Maza art studio continues to operate from a World War II-era bomb shelter, where kids still meet, learn and create amid ongoing drone, missile and guided-bomb strikes on the city.

The exhibition grew from the idea of a "missing museum" — a world made up of forgotten legends, untold stories and new mythologies inspired by the Baroque collections of European museums.

The young artists first drew elements found in ancient frescoes, botanical atlases, medieval maps and manuscripts before developing characters and building narratives around them.

Details like rosehips, seashells, bones, bats, lions and musical instruments meet characters ranging from beggars, saints and witches to princesses, children and those who have seen it all.

The scale of the works, which measure 2.5 x 1.5 meters, allows viewers to step into these visual worlds and become part of the unfolding narratives.

Curated by Mykola Kolomiiets and Iryna Hrytska, "Lost Fairy Tales" will remain on view in Pärnu through October 4.

World.title: Reform Party wants former EKRE MP as next Riigikogu Defense Committee chair
World.content:
The coalition Reform Party has proposed a former Conservative People's Party of Estonia (EKRE) MP as next chair of the Riigikogu's National Defense Committee, Postimees reported .

The move if successful may help the now-minority Reform-Eesti 200 coalition get votes passed at the Riigikogu.

The MP, Leo Kunnas, now sits as an independent, and Reform's secretary general, Kristo Enn Vaga, told Postimees his name had been discussed favorably.

However, Vaga said, Kunnas has not formally been agreed on within the party as candidate for the next Riigikogu Defense Committee chair to replace Kalev Stoicescu, who stepped down this week.

"He has served as deputy chair, has said he will not run for anything else, and his work there would be guided not by political interests but by national defense interests," Vaga said, noting it is not yet known whether Kunnas would agree to run for the post.

Kristo Enn Vaga. Source: Arp Müller/ERR

That a former EKRE member has been floated for the role by Reform – the parties were very much at loggerheads when EKRE was in office 2019–2021 – is likely the result of the Reform-Eesti 200 coalition now being a minority government; courting Kunnas could mean he will vote with the government on the state budget come autumn, and on other key matters.

Additionally, the current composition of the Defense Committee is such that electing a coalition MP to the post could prove complicated, while as noted Kunnas has served as deputy chair in any case. He is also a retired military officer.

The vote on the new Defense Committee chair is to take place on September 14, after parliament has reconvened from its summer break.

Kalev Stoicescu announced Sunday evening he was quitting Eesti 200, and he is stepping down as Defense Committee chief as well.

His departure and that of Meelis Kiili from the Reform Party a day later left the coalition with 50 seats at the 101-seat Riigikogu; Kiili himself told Postimees that Kunnas would make a good candidate for the Defense Committee job.

Other important votes coming up include the presidential election ballots on September 2 and 3; there are 20 independent MPs at the Riigikogu now, making them a significant demographic within parliament – 68 or more votes are required to elect a head of state.

World.title: Drone surveillance system starts work on Narva River
World.content:
A new drone surveillance system has been launched on the Narva River. Initially, border guards will be able to monitor aircraft movements along about a third of the river border, with the entire border river to be covered next year.

The first five radar masts were erected along the Narva River in the spring. They have now been equipped with surveillance equipment and for the first time border guards can monitor drone movements at and near the border. Even Russian reconnaissance aircraft flying along the border show up on the radar.

"These systems are now operational. We can see drones — not just small, civilian drones. In principle, if a military drone appears near our border, it will also show up on the radar screen. This is a significant step forward," Interior Minister Igor Taro said.

Just a few years ago, border guards said they could see about 70 percent of what was happening on the Narva River. By next year, the remaining blind spots are expected to disappear.

"We have state-of-the-art radar systems that, in addition to conventional monitoring of the airspace, can now also track different types of drone traffic. Better eyes and better systems give us a clearer picture to respond to," said Veiko Kommusaar, deputy director general of the Police and Border Guard Board (PPA).

While border guards can currently only monitor drone movements, the next step will be to counter drones both along the eastern border and inland.

"We are currently in the final stages of procuring an experimental site. Once the procurement is complete, an experimental site will be built where various counter-drone solutions will also be tested. If these solutions prove successful, they can then be deployed elsewhere across Estonia where they could be useful," Taro said.

Estonian border guards currently have drone surveillance coverage from Narva to Narva-Jõesuu. Construction of radars that will cover the Narva River as far as Lake Peipus is still underway and they are expected to become operational next year.

World.title: Demand for specialists remains high as Estonia's unemployment falls slightly
World.content:
The unemployment rate fell slightly in the second quarter, but the overall employment situation did not improve significantly. Employers say the greatest challenge is hiring specialists, for whom competition is fierce.

According to Statistics Estonia, Estonia's unemployment rate was 6.6 percent in the second quarter, slightly lower than a year earlier. The employment rate, at 68.6 percent, was also slightly below last year's level.

SEB economic analyst Mihkel Nestor said the figures are to be expected given the economy's gradual growth.

"Our economic growth is also relatively slow, which means there is no record-fast demand for new workers. I'm afraid unemployment will remain at around 6 percent for quite some time," Nestor said.

Southern Estonia and Harju County were the only regions where employment increased. Paulig is moving an entire production unit from Sweden to Saue, creating nearly 100 new jobs. Plant manager Margo Kuslap said there is no shortage of applicants.

"Our experience in Saue so far shows that people are willing to commute to work in Saue if the workplace is accessible, stable and offers opportunities for development," Kuslap said.

Kuslap added that hiring specialists is more difficult.

"There are roles that require specific expertise and those people are a little harder to find because many companies are competing for the same specialists," Kuslap said.

Martti Kork, CEO of Võru-based wood processing company Barrus, which was recently named Factory of the Year, said low investment has left the sector in a difficult position and forced his company to lay off employees this year as well. According to Kork, most local wood processing companies are in the same situation.

"The unfortunate thing is that all these companies are in rural areas, so jobs in rural areas are taking the hit," Kork said.

Barrus has created new opportunities in the region by shifting some work to computer-based roles. Kork said data specialists are now easier to recruit than machine operators.

"Our most recent recruitment process for a senior data architect position brought in 80 résumés here in Võru, which is quite surprising," Kork said.

The unemployment rate among 15- to 24-year-olds in Estonia was 22.4 percent in the second quarter. That is relatively high, although significantly lower than last year. Nestor sees this as a sign of society's growing prosperity.

"Families today can afford for young people's childhoods to last a little longer," Nestor said.

World.title: Iraq Ministry of Oil inks deal with Japan’s JGC to resume FCC project
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) — The Iraqi Ministry of Oil announced on Friday, August 14, 2026, an agreement with Japan’s JGC Corporation to officially resume construction and operational work on the massive Fluid Catalytic Cracking (FCC) complex at the South Refineries Company (SRC) in Basra.

The deal follows negotiations led by a ministerial committee under directives from Oil Minister Basim Mohammed Khudair Al-Abadi, chaired by Ministry Advisor Hamid Younis alongside SRC Director General Hussam Hussein Wali. Under the finalized agreement, JGC remobilized its technical personnel to the Basra site starting August 10 to prepare processing units for full design-capacity operations, advancing Iraq’s target of refined petroleum self-sufficiency.

Key Operational Deliverables & Production Capacity

High-Octane Gasoline: Adding 5 million liters per day to domestic fuel supplies.

Gas Oil (Diesel): Producing approximately 7 million liters per day.

Liquefied Petroleum Gas (LPG): Delivering 400 metric tons per day for commercial and domestic consumption.

Project Milestone: Mobilization of JGC engineering teams began on August 10, 2026, to finalize site preparations and run commissioning sequences.

Strategic Objective: Eliminating fuel import expenditures and converting heavy refining residues into high-value white petroleum products.

The FCC complex at the Shuaiba refinery in Basra is among Iraq’s most critical downstream modernization projects, designed to upgrade heavy vacuum gas oil into premium fuels.

By adding 12 million combined liters of daily gasoline and diesel alongside substantial LPG yields, the facility will significantly curtail state spending on imported refined fuels and support domestic market stability.

World.title: Iraq customs revenues hit 2.5 trillion IQD in Seven Months
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) — Iraq’s General Customs Authority collected 2.5 trillion Iraqi Dinars (approximately $1.9 billion) in revenues during the first seven months of 2026, matching total receipts recorded for the entirety of 2025, Director-General Thamer Qasim Al-Taie announced on Saturday, August 15, 2026.

Speaking to state-run Al Iraqiya News, Al-Taie stated that July alone generated 560 billion IQD, representing a 150% year-on-year surge compared to July 2025. With revenue collection accelerating across all federal border crossings, full-year receipts are projected to surpass 3.5 trillion IQD ($2.67 billion)—the highest annual total in modern Iraqi state history.

Key Revenue Indicators & Technical Upgrades

Seven-Month Total:2.5 trillion IQD (~$1.9B) collected through July 2026, equaling full-year 2025 custom receipts.

July Revenue Surge: Recorded 560 billion IQD, a 150% increase compared to July 2025.

Annual Projection: Forecasted to exceed 3.5 trillion IQD (~$2.67B) by year-end 2026, setting a national historical record.

Automation & Anti-Corruption: Revenue jumps were driven by the nationwide rollout of SCADA systems, automated customs processing, and integrated digital networks connecting border crossings with government agencies, drastically curbing tariff evasion and illicit clearances.

The sharp rise in customs collections reflects Baghdad’s wider push to modernize border controls, plug financial leakages, and reduce structural dependence on crude oil sales amid regional market volatility.

By implementing mandatory automated documentation and digital data-sharing across federal transit checkpoints, the Customs Authority has systematically reduced tariff evasion, accelerated cargo clearances, and fortified federal non-oil revenue streams.

World.title: Popular Lebanese restaurant Al Beiruti to open in Baghdad
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) — Al Beiruti, a popular Lebanese restaurant, is set to build its first Iraqi branch in Iraq Mall in Baghdad, adding another significant regional dining name to the capital’s growing restaurant scene.

The Baghdad inauguration will be the next chapter of Al Beiruti’s regional development, after previous launches in Jordan and Qatar, as well as its established presence in the UAE.

The restaurant announced that its Iraq Mall restaurant is about to open, with a local franchise arrangement handling the expansion.

Al Beiruti has become a renowned location for Lebanese food in the Middle East, providing both classic dishes and a more modern restaurant experience.

The menu includes Lebanese favorites, including manakish, fattoush, hummus, baba ghanouj, and grilled halloumi, as well as shawarma, wraps, and mixed grills. Larger meals include steak, chicken escalope, and grilled salmon.

Al Beiruti joins a growing number of international and regional food and beverage companies in Baghdad, as new malls and commercial expansions change the city’s retail and entertainment markets.

Iraq Mall has emerged as a focal point of that expansion, drawing new restaurants, boutiques, and entertainment ideas as consumer spending and private-sector investment continue to rise in the capital.

World.title: Baghdad and Erbil agree on unified digital customs system across Iraq
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) — Baghdad and Erbil have agreed to fully adopt the digital ASYCUDA customs system across border crossings, with non-oil border earnings shared equally by the federal and Kurdistan regional governments.

The deal is a significant step toward standardizing customs processes across Iraq and addressing long-standing disagreements over border revenues and claimed import quantities.

ASYCUDA, designed by the United Nations Conference on Trade and Development (UNCTAD), digitizes customs declarations, payments, and clearing processes, allowing authorities to better monitor products entering the nation and the income they earn.

Linking customs operations to Iraq’s banking and electronic payment systems may help limit the potential for underreporting, revenue leakage, and corruption at border crossings.

The deal comes as Iraq’s Finance Ministry and Central Bank work to digitize customs, payments, and government financial data in collaboration with UNCTAD.

A combined computerized customs system for Baghdad and Erbil might give more accurate revenue data while resolving one of the two governments’ ongoing financial issues.

The change is also significant for Iraq’s overall economy.

More open and uniform customs processes might facilitate cross-border commerce, boost governmental revenues, and enhance the business climate as Iraq pursues more foreign investment and closer integration with international markets.

World.title: Iraq’s Chief Justice Faiq Zidan meets Syrian President Al-Sharaa in Damascus
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) — Iraq’s Supreme Judicial Council President Faiq Zidan met with Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa in Damascus on Thursday, marking another high-level Iraqi outreach to a neighboring Arab state as Baghdad seeks to bolster regional relations under rising security problems.

Al-Sharaa welcomed Zidan and an Iraqi delegation to the People’s Palace, which also included Syrian Foreign Minister Asaad al-Shaibani and Justice Minister Mazhar al-Wais.

According to the Syrian president, the talks focused on extending judicial and legal cooperation between Iraq and Syria, as well as resolving mutual concerns.

The visit also resulted in more practical conversations among the two nations’ judicial officials. Iraqi and Syrian authorities agreed to set up joint judicial committees to continue working on cases involving Syrian prisoners and other cross-border legal issues.

Zidan’s visit is crucial as he is one of the most prominent persons in Iraq’s state institutions, and it coincides with Baghdad’s increased diplomatic, security, and judicial interaction with its neighbors.

The Damascus meetings come after a separate Iraqi security group visited Riyadh, where senior military official Abdul Amir al-Shammari met with Saudi Defense Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman.

Zidan had also just visited Ankara as part of a larger Iraqi effort to build ties with Saudi Arabia, Syria, and Turkey.

That approach has become more urgent in light of the regional escalation involving Iran-backed Iraqi forces.

In late July, the United States and Saudi Arabia conducted synchronized attacks against locations used by Iran-aligned organizations in Iraq, after Riyadh accused militias operating from Iraqi territory of firing drones against Saudi energy infrastructure.

The incident put Baghdad under strong pressure to prevent armed organizations from exploiting Iraqi territory to launch assaults on neighboring nations and also highlighted the potential that militia activity may harm Iraq’s improved ties with Arab governments.

Against this setting, Zidan’s encounter with Al-Sharaa is significant beyond regular court cooperation.

Iraq and Syria share a long border and confront shared concerns such as terrorism, organized crime, prisoners, and cross-border security. Baghdad also has a strategic interest in preserving stable ties with Damascus, as Iraq strives to boost regional connections and prevent unrest from spilling over its borders.

Iraq’s Prime Minister Ali Al-Zaidi’s administration sees recent diplomatic efforts as part of a larger effort to strengthen Iraq’s ties with its neighbors while keeping the nation out of the developing conflict between Iran and its regional adversaries.

Baghdad has increasingly emphasized that choices on security, armament, and relations with neighboring governments must be made by Iraqi official authorities rather than armed groupings.

The travels to Damascus and Riyadh therefore convey an essential message: although Iran-aligned militias have exacerbated tensions between Iraq and certain of its neighbors, Iraqi official institutions are working directly with those nations to restore cooperation and avoid further escalation.

Strengthening judicial, diplomatic, and security ties with Syria, Saudi Arabia, and Turkey might serve as an essential regional buffer for Iraq as it seeks to safeguard its sovereignty, control armed groups, and avoid being drawn further into the region’s crises.

World.title: Iraq’s Al-Shammari visits Riyadh to meet Saudi Defense Minister
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) — A top Iraqi security team has traveled to Riyadh for meetings with Saudi Arabia’s leadership, as Baghdad and the Kingdom work to improve security and military cooperation after weeks of heightened tensions in Iraq involving Iran-backed militias.

First Lieutenant General Abdul Amir Al-Shammari, director of the Office of the Commander-in-Chief of the Iraqi Armed Forces, met with Saudi Defense Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman on Thursday to discuss military cooperation, regional developments, and increased coordination between the two nations.

According to reports from the visit, the conversations included cross-border drone concerns, air defense, and intelligence collaboration.

The conference is especially significant in light of the combined US-Saudi attacks on Iran-linked militia locations in Iraq on July 29.

Washington and Riyadh said the operation targeted Iran-backed terrorists’ weapons and logistical facilities in response to a series of drone assaults on Saudi oil installations that they said originated in Iraqi territory.

The strikes drastically escalated tensions between Baghdad and Riyadh, highlighting the Iraqi government’s problems in preventing armed groups from exploiting its territory to target neighboring nations.

Thursday’s visit indicates that both parties are now attempting to move beyond that conflict via direct military and intelligence collaboration.

Prince Khalid underlined Saudi Arabia’s commitment to Iraq’s security, stability, and economic growth, identifying it as an essential neighbor with whom the Kingdom has strong political and social relations.

The meetings in Riyadh follow Saudi intelligence head Khalid bin Ali al-Humaidan’s visit to Baghdad last week, during which he met with Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi and reiterated an offer for the Iraqi leader to visit Saudi Arabia.

Baghdad’s security cooperation with Riyadh has grown more vital as the government seeks to prevent Iran-backed militias from drawing Iraq into a larger regional conflict.

Al-Zaidi has frequently said that Iraqi soil should not be used to attack other nations and has stepped up efforts for weaponry to be put solely under state control.

The most recent Iraqi trip to Riyadh symbolizes more than just normal defense diplomacy. It is part of a joint effort by Baghdad and Saudi Arabia to restore security trust after the July escalation and prevent militia activities from dragging the two neighboring nations into conflict.

World.title: Rare blind fish found in underground river in Iraq’s Anbar desert
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Iraqi security and environmental teams have discovered a fascinating underground water system deep under the dry Anbar desert, where rare eyeless fish thrive in total darkness.

The location is in the Al-Khasfa region near Haditha, and crews traveled through a remote desert cave and sinkhole system to access running groundwater hundreds of meters under the surface.

The expedition’s footage shows little, pale fish moving in the subterranean water in the lack of sunshine.

The fish have evolved to live in darkness by losing their eyes and pigmentation, giving them a characteristic white-to-pink look.

The crew traveled more than 500 meters into the cave system despite challenging terrain and low oxygen levels.

The difference between above- and underground has piqued interest: underneath what seems to be an isolated and very arid stretch of western Iraqi desert, there is flowing freshwater and a specialized ecology.

Initial investigations have also suggested a link between the subterranean water system and the Euphrates basin, with the watercourse possibly running for a long distance under the desert.

However, environmental experts have highlighted that the blind fish themselves are not a novel finding.

Qais Najeh, the chairman of the Anbar Environment Directorate, stated that experts first confirmed the occurrence of eyeless fish in Al-Khasfa in 2010.

Similar fish have also been discovered in subterranean water near the Sheik Hadid mausoleum in Haditha district.

According to experts, the fish may grow to be roughly 49 millimeters long and survive in rather steady groundwater temperatures ranging from 20 to 22 degrees Celsius.

Their lack of vision and pigmentation are adaptations to generations of living in perpetually dark subterranean habitats.

The recent mission is nonetheless noteworthy because it has refocused attention on one of Iraq’s least-known natural ecosystems, perhaps allowing scientists to better research the subterranean water network, its geology, and the creatures that rely on it.

The fish’s severely limited environment renders it vulnerable.

Changes in groundwater levels, pollution, or human intervention might endanger a population that has acclimated to highly particular subsurface circumstances.

The Al-Khasfa location offers a unique dimension to Anbar, a region best known for its wide western desert and the Euphrates.

Hidden under that terrain lies an environment few Iraqis have ever seen: flowing subterranean water that feeds fish who have evolved to survive their entire lives without sunshine.

World.title: Israel reopens once-closed West Bank settlement
World.content:
GANIM – Israel officially reopened the West Bank settlement of Ganim on Thursday, more than 20 years after it withdrew from the community, in a move emblematic of the current government’s policy of rapid settlement expansion.

The smell of freshly-poured asphalt hung in the air above Ganim’s new and only street, where future residents and their families — who had come to help with the move — smiled at the sight of their pre-fabricated homes.

“A month ago there was nothing here. A rocky mountain, barely any trees, barely any shade. We’re arriving now,” new resident Reut Baran, 35, told AFP in front of her new home.

In a nearby truck, dozens of brand new air conditioning units still in their boxes were waiting to be installed.

Matan Berkovitch, a 25-year-old who moved into the new settlement with his wife and child, said he was satisfied with the government’s policy towards settlements as he looked around a brand new home just connected to the electric grid.

“I’m happy to be part of a time like this where there are ministers in the government who support and guide us in the right direction and know how to get things done properly,” he said.

Berkovitch’s mother Carmit, who came from Jerusalem to move him in, said another one of her sons would soon study at the religious school in the settlement, and expressed pride at their active part in the settler movement.

“Here, this is the Land of Israel. Here, we are staying forever,” Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz said at the ceremony, after arriving by helicopter.

Ganim is one of four Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank that Israel evacuated under former prime minister Ariel Sharon’s disengagement plan in 2005.

The move came partly because of their isolated location in the north of the territory among many Palestinian cities and villages.

Under Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s government, settlement construction and expansion have soared, including with the official re-establishment of three of the four evacuated communities — Ganim, Sa-Nur and Homesh.

In Ganim, about two dozen pre-fabricated homes have already been installed, while steamrollers and other construction machinery busily created new space for future houses on the hillside on Thursday.

About a hundred people from Israel and other West Bank settlements attended the ceremony, including Katz and Yossi Dagan, head of the Israeli authority in charge of settlements in the northern West Bank.

“The era of evacuation is over — from here, we only build,” Dagan said.

In the valley below, Palestinians who spoke to AFP feared Ganim’s construction would make their lives harder, or even mean eventual displacement.

On both sides of the road leading to the settlement from Israel, the army has demolished stores in recent days and blocked several dirt roads to Palestinian communities with piles of rubble.

Israel has occupied the West Bank since 1967. More than 500,000 Israelis live in settlements in the territory, which are illegal under international law, among some three million Palestinians.

Violence against Palestinians by Israeli settlers has increased dramatically since the October 7, 2023 attack on Israel by Hamas from the Gaza Strip.

NEW DELHI: A parliamentary panel has taken note of a curious case involving emergency alert buttons in buses. While the switches cost just Rs 15-20 each, they have largely remained unused because there are no dedicated centres to respond to alerts. Bus operators told the panel they are still required to pay Rs 2,500 to Rs 25,000 per vehicle to have the switches tested during mandatory fitness tests.The latest report of the parliamentary standing committee on transport, tourism and culture, headed by JDU's Sanjay Jha, noted that the buttons were made mandatory after the 2012 Nirbhaya case as a safety measure for women passengers.The report said the road transport ministry informed the panel that in several states, the system had been connected to emergency response number 112. It also said there were many instances of false alarms, prompting some states to "disengage" them."The ministry wishes the system restored, while am-ong operators there is a feeling that it should be dispensed with," the report said. A committee member observed if the system was not effective, it was not fair to charge so much for it. One member asked why CCTV could not be installed. The ministry said cameras were being made mandatory in new buses.The committee recommended that the programme to install emergency buttons, call facilities and vehicle location tracking devices in public transport vehicles be pursued with states beyond the 16 that have made progress in implementing it.

World.title: At BCI helm for 14 years, Manan Kumar Mishra faces heat over professional conduct
World.content:
NEW DELHI: BCI's controversial decision to bar 2026 law graduates from Hyderabad's NALSAR University of Law from being registered as advocate, which it withdrew within hours, brought into focus the regulator's working which has been headed by senior advocate and BJP MP Manan Kumar Mishra for 14 years.

A statutory body established under Advocates Act, 1961, BCI is mandated to regulate legal profession and legal education. It lays down standards of professional conduct for advocates, exercises disciplinary jurisdiction, and recognises universities whose law degrees qualify a person for enrolment. Section 7(1)(g) of the Act also gives it general supervision and control over state bar councils.

But no provision of the Act gives it the power to enrol a person as an advocate which is to be done by a state bar council to admit persons as advocates on its roll.

Clearly, the regulator ventured into the area beyond its domain by taking punitive measures against students, and upset SC which observed that BCI had no business to intervene in the matter.

The controversy has put the spotlight on BCI's functioning on whether it has over the years been able to discharge its statutory duty to maintain the standard of legal profession and legal education. Going by a statement of Mishra himself, BCI has failed in its duty by a massive margin.





An outspoken man who contested polls as nominees of BSP and Congress before drifting into BJP , has said on more than one occasion that 35-40% of advocates have fake degrees, and are practicing in the courts on the basis of fabricated degree certificates. The statement, while believed to be true by many, is an indictment of regulator and clear evidence that guard rails against serious malpractice have not been working.

World.title: PM Modi puts women's quota back on table, makes fresh pitch to opposition
World.content:
PM Narendra Modi

New Delhi: PM Narendra Modi chose his Independence Day address Saturday to give a strong indication of of his govt's intent to revive the Constitution amendment bill to implement one-third reservation for women in Lok Sabha and assemblies, with a 50% jump in their overall strength from 2029, urging all political parties to ensure that it was rolled out as soon as possible.While it was widely speculated in political circles that govt was keen to revive the bill, which was defeated by the opposition in April, Modi put on record that the matter was on the agenda, boosting the prospect of Parliament being summoned as early as next month."Today, standing here beneath the shadow of the Tricolour on the ramparts of Red Fort, I pray to and urge all political parties to acknowledge the power of women. Let's step forward to uphold their dignity and ensure our mothers and sisters get 33% representation in assemblies and Lok Sabha as soon as possible," he said.What has enhanced the likelihood of the bill being passed is the defection of 20 Lok Sabha MPs from Trinamool Congress and six from Sena UBT to NDA and DMK's assiduous efforts, visible in the recently concluded session, to keep away from the opposition's ranks after Congress ditched it in Tamil Nadu to ally with Vijay-led TVK.NCP SP is being seen as another potential support.Congress accused Modi of making a "dishonest pitch" for women's reservation in his address, saying 'Nari Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam' was unanimously passed in Sept 2023, but BJP govt's "double standards" and "hypocrisy" had made sure it didn't come into effect from 2024.Congress general secretary Jairam Ramesh, in a post on X, said the party had stood firm on its stand to implement women's reservation from the 2029 Lok Sabha elections by retaining the current strength of 543 seats in LS.Modi said women served as public representatives in large numbers in panchayats to municipalities and municipal corporations, referring to their salience in local bodies on the back of reservation.Despite several efforts to reserve seats in Lok Sabha and assemblies, the idea had fallen victim to political battles for over 40 years, he said.He called it the need of the hour and told parties to join the cause. "You also take the credit, you also take the fame, but give rights to my mothers and sisters," he said, reiterating the pitch he had made before the failed bid last time.The monsoon session has not been prorogued, keeping open the possibility of govt summoning Parliament.

World.title: Army dog Tsyon that helped forces track 3 terrorists in J&K, shot in leg by ultras during op gets President I-Day honour
World.content:
NEW DELHI: New Delhi: Indian Armyâs assault dog Tyson, who is attached to 2 Para Special Forces, has been honoured during the Independence Day 2026 celebrations for showing âbravery and extraordinary courageâ during a counter-insurgency operation in J&K as part of Operation Rakshak early this year.

The name of Tyson, a German Shepherd of Remount Veterinary Corps, appeared among 89 Mention-in-Despatches (MiD) approved by President Droupadi Murmu on I-Day eve on Friday.

Tyson is the only animal hero among the 89 personnel chosen for MiD, which is an official military commendation recognising bravery and meritorious service in a combat zone.During Operation Trashi-I in Chatroo belt of J&Kâs Kishtwar district on Feb 22 this year, Tyson scouted ahead of the troops and located a hidden terrorist hideout.

Tyson is part of the elite squad of Army assault dogs, which are trained like soldiers for high-risk operations.

âTyson displayed extraordinary courage by taking the first bullet while leading the entry into the terroristsâ hideout. Undeterred by his injuries, he pressed forward and launched a fierce assault, compelling the terrorists to open fire and thereby confirming their presence. His fearless action enabled troops of White Knight Corps, J&K police and CRPF to precisely engage and neutralise three Pakistan-sponsored terrorists,â Army had said in a post on X.





Tyson was then airlifted to Command Hospital Udhampur for emergency treatment and has now recovered. âWounded yet in high spirits, alert and recovering well, Tyson exemplifies unwavering devotion to duty, a true warrior and a soldier in every sense,â Army said later.

World.title: Had Article 370 stayed, PoK may have sought to rejoin J&K: Omar Abdullah
World.content:
SRINAGAR: J&K CM

credited Kashmiris with fighting the 1947 tribal invasion before Indian troops arrived and said people across the LoC might have been protesting to rejoin J&K today had Centre not revoked

in 2019.

Speaking at an Independence Day event Saturday, Omar paid tribute to his grandfather and National Conference founder Sheikh Mohammad Abdullah, portraying his role in resisting the Pakistan-backed tribal invasion as central to J&Kâs history.

âBefore Indian Army reached here, it was the people of J&K who fought the tribal invaders, who fought the infiltrators sent from across, who fought the soldiers sent from across,â Omar said.

âThousands of brave peopleâ sacrificed their lives, he said.

Omarâs remarks came as his govt continues to press for restoration of J&Kâs statehood, while Sheikh Abdullahâs legacy remains a political fault line after the abrogation of Article 370.

Recent unrest in PoK sharpened Omarâs argument. âWhen I see the situation today across the LoC, I realise that the decision taken by our leaders 80 years ago for us was the right decision,â Omar said, underscoring Sheikh Abdullah preferring Indiaâs secular ideals over Pakistan and supporting J&Kâs accession in 1947.





Pakistani security firing has killed dozens following protests demanding abolition of 12 seats in the 53-member PoK assembly reserved for refugees from J&K who settled there after 1947. Protesters say the seats let Pakistani parties wield influence in PoK.

Omar said the condition of PoK made him wonder what might have happened had J&Kâs situation not changed in 2019. âPerhapsâ¦ people of that part of J&K would be protesting to rejoin us today,â he said.

âThat part of J&K Kashmir is ours. We consider those people as our own. No one is a stranger. No one is an outsider.â

Omar also made federalism a central plank of his speech. âFederalism suffers when central agencies start interfering in the affairs of the states,â he said. Restoring J&Kâs statehood should be part of a broader effort to strengthen all states rather than federalism being reduced to âonly wordsâ, he added.

World.title: 'How was leak overlooked?' Uttarakhand Congress chief demands probe into Pipalkoti tunnel tragedy
World.content:
NEW DELHI: Uttarakhand Pradesh Congress Committee president Ganesh Godiyal on Saturday criticised the Pushkar Singh Dhami government over the Pipalkoti tunnel accident in Chamoli district, questioning how a reported leak at the site was allegedly overlooked despite workers claiming it had persisted for some time.

The criticism came as the death toll in the under-construction THDC tunnel accident rose to eight, with two workers still trapped and rescue operations continuing.

Godiyal said workers injured in the accident had told him that water leakage had been occurring at the same spot for a considerable period before the tunnel was inundated by a massive surge of water.

"When I spoke to the injured, I learned that a leak had been occurring for quite some time at the very spot where the incident took place.

How this was overlooked or why there was such apathy towards it is a matter for further investigation. NTPC provided Rs one lakh, but that amount is insufficient. I will discuss what arrangements can be made to ensure the families can sustain themselves properly," Godiyal told ANI.

He also questioned the compensation announced for the families of those killed in the accident.

"The CM announced compensation of Rs four lakh, though I believe that amount is not sufficient," he said.





Congress leader Harikrishna Bhatt echoed the criticism, saying the compensation did not reflect the value of human life and calling for safety audits across all ongoing infrastructure projects in the state.

"Regarding the announced compensation of Rs 4 lakh, a human life cannot be valued at merely Rs 4 lakh," Bhatt said.

"Safety audits should have been conducted for all such ongoing projects. The entire population of Uttarakhand is bearing the brunt of these disasters which are man-made.

There is a need for a thorough analysis to determine what actual interests the people of Uttarakhand have in these large-scale projects," he added.

The death toll increased to eight on Saturday after rescue teams recovered another body from the tunnel. Two other workers remain trapped inside the under-construction THDC tunnel, where operations by the National Disaster Response Force, State Disaster Response Force, District Disaster Response Force and the Indo-Tibetan Border Police are continuing.

Rescue efforts have been complicated by water and accumulated sludge inside the tunnel, restricting movement and slowing the search for the remaining workers.

THDC India Limited executive director Ajay Verma said the massive inflow of water appeared to have originated from a pre-existing natural cavity.

"Regarding the leakage and the massive influx of water in the tunnel, it appears there was a pre-existing natural cavity.

During the rainy season, this cavity filled with water. The volume was so great that it found a weak point, specifically where we were excavating the tunnel from below, leading to the leakage," Verma said.

He described the scale of flooding as unprecedented for a hydro-tunnel project.

"The inflow consists mostly of water, with very little debris. Historically, such a massive influx of water, enough to fill the tunnel for a stretch of 1.2 kilometres, is unprecedented in hydro-tunnel projects.

This level of leakage is highly unusual and unexpected. It is a matter requiring investigation," he added.

Verma said authorities had lowered the water level by around 1.5 metres and were continuously increasing the number of pumps.

"We have managed to lower the water level by about 1.5 meters. We are continuously increasing the number of pumps in operation. Running these pumps requires laying pipelines and ensuring a power supply; we are managing all these tasks simultaneously," he said.

He added that less than a metre of water remained inside the tunnel.

World.title: 'Not a matter of ego': BCI chairman apologises to law students after row over NALSAR diktat
World.content:
NEW DELHI: Bar Council of India chairman Manan Kumar Mishra on Saturday apologised to law students following the council's controversial decision to briefly halt the enrolment of National Academy of Legal Studies and Research (NALSAR) University of Law's 2026 graduating batch as advocates, Bar and Bench reported.

In a letter issued on Independence Day, Mishra said he regretted any words or communication connected to the controversy that may have hurt the feelings of law students.

"If anything connected with the present controversy, any of my words, or letter, has hurt the feelings of our law students, I sincerely regret and apologise for the same. There should be no hesitation in saying so," the letter reads.

"An expression of regret is not a matter of prestige or ego. It is simply an acknowledgment that the feelings and concerns of our students matter," he added.

The apology comes after the BCI directed all state bar councils not to enrol NALSAR's 2026 graduates as advocates until further orders. The council withdrew the directive within hours following an uproar on social media.

The BCI had initially said it was examining allegations regarding a campaign against Chief Justice of India Surya Kant's participation in NALSAR's convocation and had sought a report identifying those responsible.





The council later modified its decision to allow the enrolment of the university's 2026 graduates before withdrawing the notification altogether. The revised notification said the "vast majority" of students were innocent and should not be made to suffer for the alleged "misconduct" of a few.

The controversy began after around 450 graduating NALSAR students urged the university to reconsider inviting CJI Kant as chief guest at its convocation.

The students cited his alleged refusal to hear pleas concerning "police brutality" against students who had marched to Parliament on July 20 seeking the resignation of then-Union education minister Dharmendra Pradhan over the NEET-UG question paper leak in May.

The Supreme Court later expressed "strong disapproval" of the BCI's now-revoked order.

A bench headed by CJI Kant, and comprising Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana, said students have the right to protest peacefully and described the episode as a "dialogue" between him and the students.

"If students are protesting peacefully, who is BCI to take action? It is the right of the students to protest peacefully. It is a dialogue between students and me. No one else has to step in," the CJI said.

The Supreme Court also stayed any coercive action against students or faculty by the BCI or state councils.

"It (the letter) was absolutely uncalled for," the bench added.

World.title: ‘Sharma Ji Ka Beta Toh…’: Why some Indian careers are judged before they are chosen?
World.content:
âWhat do you do?â

Sounds like a simple question. But in India, the answer to this question determines your social status.

Is there any scope?

How much will you earn?

What will people say?

Some careers in India instantly earn respect.

Others invite questions.

So when a young person chooses a career, are they really choosing what they want or are they going for what society considers worth choosing?

What are the top careers in India?

A 2018 Global Education Census by Cambridge International, based on responses from nearly 20,000 teachers and students across the world, including 4,400 teachers and 3,800 students in India, found that medicine and engineering continued to dominate career ambitions.

The survey found that 23% of Indian students wanted to become doctors or dentists, while an equal 23% aspired to become engineers. Another 16% wanted to become software engineers, the highest proportion for this career among all countries surveyed. The findings also showed India's strong interest in scientific careers, with 8% of students saying they wanted to become scientists.

Now, letâs figure out why that is so.





What role do parents & society play?

While some students choose these careers out of genuine interest, others pursue them under pressure from parents and society.

Another 2020 study published in the Int J of Indian Culture and Business Management found that parents, peers and societal expectations significantly influence career choices among Indian youth.

TOI also conducted a survey to understand how society perceives different professions and whether certain careers continue to command greater respect than others.

75 % of respondents selected yes when asked if their relatives ever suggested them a âbetterâ career

Among respondents from sectors including journalism, medicine and PR, we received 100% response in âyesâ, agreeing that society accords greater respect to certain professions, with over 80 % respondents selecting both doctors, and IAS/IPS officers emerging as the most prestigious career choices, in second position was engineering.

Around 74 % of them agreed that often-overlooked professions like nurse, police constable, mechanic, cab driver do not receive the same respect as traditionally prestigious careers in medicine and engineering.

Somdeb Dhar Choudhury, one of the respondents and a PR consultant, said, âI grew up in an environment where engineering was considered the more conventional professional route. Many people in my extended family came from engineering backgrounds, and after Class 12, there was an expectation that I would follow a similar path.â

When asked why he thinks PR receives less social recognition, he said, âIn India, professions such as medicine, engineering and civil services have had a clearly understood social identity for generations.

Families know what those careers involve, there is a visible educational path leading to them, and society has established benchmarks of success around them. PR operates very differently. Much of the work happens behind the scenes.

â

Is it affecting mental health?

When asked if the respondents ever felt pressured to choose a career mainly because of its title or status, half of them responded with yes. More than half chose yes when asked if their relatives ever suggested they choose a particular career.

Rashmi N, former Army public school counselor, while speaking to TOI, says, âPeer comparisons lead to self doubt and career indecisions. Falling behind in academics and comparing grades with peers may also trigger withdrawal from friends, low self esteem and or lack of interest to improve.â

On the other hand psychologists say the pressure to choose a socially accepted career may not always be obvious.

Explaining the same, a Delhi-based psychologist Radhika Goyal said, âwhen motivation is driven mainly by fear, fear of failure, criticism, comparison or disappointing the family, rather than genuine enthusiasm.

A student may perform well but still experience burnout, frustration or disengagement.â

Factors influencing parentsâ decisions

While parents may want the best for their children, itâs important to discuss what drives them to push certain careers over others.

1. Job security

For many Indian parents, a âgoodâ career is still closely associated with stability, authority, financial security and social respect.

Rashmi said that this may be because of job stability and authority.

âAuthority, financial stability & fame are the major factors influencing the perception of any career paths.â

âFor more affluent families, social status, community approval and family reputation can weigh heavily on career choices, while for families with fewer financial resources, immediate income and financial security may take precedence,â she said.

Poll Vote & Share your view What do you value more in a career? Social Status Job Satisfaction Financial Security 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

2. Unfinished ambitions leading to societal comparisons

Goyal pointed to an often-overlooked factor: parents projecting their own unfinished ambitions or past experiences onto their children.

âParents may sometimes project their own unfinished ambitions, disappointments or experiences onto their childrenâs career choices, often with good intentions. A parent who could not pursue a particular career may believe they are protecting their child from the difficulties they experienced.â

However, this dynamic appears to be changing among a newer generation of parents.

Savita S, a parent of a 24-year-old daughter working in an HR firm, said, âI believe my children are satisfied with my support.â

When asked about the typical âSharma ji ka betaâ comparison, she said that parents are becoming more mindful of how their children respond to such pressure.

âThis kind of comparison is reducing day by day.â

Now, if youâve had your parentsâ support, overcome societal pressure and chosen a career based on your own dreams, are you truly happy with that choice?

What happens when youth passion meets reality?

1. Paycheck

For some young professionals, the pressure around career choices continues even after entering the workforce, with questions of money, job security and growth becoming important factors in deciding whether to stay or change paths.

Aayushi, a journalist, while sharing her experience said, âI was satisfied with choosing a career outside the conventional mainstream, but was disappointed by the financial returns. I am satisfied in terms of doing something different from the generic league. But in terms of money, way too underwhelmed.â

Join conversation Commentsâ Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines

She also sometimes considered changing her career.

Around 56% of respondents selected Low salary, lack of job security and growth as their main reasons to reject a career.

2. Women face another layer of pressure

A 2025 study published in the

International Journal of Trends and Innovations in Business & Social Sciences

found that women were more likely to change careers because of social expectations, especially after marriage, while men more often cited personal interests and changes in the job market.

The gendered perception of careers can also influence how professions are valued.

3. When your profession needs an explanation

For some professionals, however, the pressure is less about being forced to leave a career and more about constantly having to explain its worth.

Somdeb recalled that this became apparent after he entered the industry. âIf someone says they are a doctor, engineer or lawyer, people immediately understand the profession. In PR, you often have to explain what the job involves before people can understand its value. That lack of familiarity created more pressure for me than any direct opposition to my career choice.â

Perhaps the real measure of progress is that there has been a shift, but still there is a long way to go.

World.title: Super Chennai brings a ‘fresh vibe’ to Medavakkam
World.content:
For residents of Medavakkam, last Sunday morning began a little differently.

From fitness and games to music, traditional performances and creative workshops, the first edition of Super Chennai Community Vibes brought residents and families together for a morning of shared experiences at Navin’s Starwood on August 9.

An initiative by Super Chennai, Community Vibes is conceived as a neighbourhood-led platform that brings together fun, fitness, culture, creativity and learning.

The first edition, held between 6 a.m. and 9 a.m. on August 9 saw enthusiastic participation from residents and families from Navin’s Starwood as well as the wider Medavakkam neighbourhood., says a press release from Super Chennai.

The idea behind the initiative is to take community experiences beyond large city-wide events and into the neighbourhoods where people live.

The morning offered something for different age groups. Families and children had an opportunity to rediscover traditional and native games, many of which are becoming increasingly unfamiliar in today’s urban environment, the release adds.

Children were also at the centre of several hands-on activities. Crochet, live abacus and art workshops gave them opportunities to learn, create and interact in an informal setting, while allowing parents and children to participate together.

The main stage added to the festive mood with a mix of contemporary music and traditional performances. Popular music band Maayavisai performed for the audience, while a Bharatanatyam team from the local community showcased its talent.

Traditional Thappattam and Mayilattam performances brought the sights and sounds of Tamil folk culture to the morning, giving both children and adults an opportunity to experience these art forms up close.

A dedicated music zone further added to the atmosphere, creating a relaxed space for residents to gather, listen and spend time with one another.

The first edition at Navin’s Starwood marked the beginning of what Super Chennai hopes will become a series of such community experiences across Chennai, says the release.

World.title: West Asia war highlights: Iran fires back at Trump’s threat to declare Hormuz a U.S. territory
World.content:
Iran on Saturday (August 15, 2026) fired back at U.S. President Donald Trump’s claim that he would soon declare the Strait of Hormuz part of U.S. territory, saying the crucial energy waterway it has blockaded “will remain Iranian”.

Mr. Trump has repeatedly insisted that the strait, which Tehran effectively closed at the start of the war in West Asia in late February, is under U.S. control despite traffic remaining throttled.

Also read | What does the U.S.-Iran agreement say? | Explained

Iran demanded that Qatar release three of Tehran’s pilots whose aircraft went down early in the war, though the Gulf state denied it was detaining them. Iran had previously reported one pilot killed and others missing after a sortie to Qatar in March, but news of their alleged capture was not publicised at the time.

Also read | No progress on reviving peace deal with U.S.: Iran

Lebanon said Israeli strikes on the south killed 11 people including three children on Saturday (August 15, 2026), the deadliest raids since deals in June eased hostilities between Israel and Hezbollah. Lebanese leaders condemned the strikes, which Israel’s military said were in retaliation for an attack by the Iran-backed militant group, with one targeting a Hezbollah commander it accused of using his family as “human shields”.

World.title: Mamallan reservoir project: documentation as advocacy
World.content:
Water moves in two directions across the Nemmeli coastal wetland — freshwater flowing east from inland lakes and tanks, and seawater moving inland through Muttukadu estuary. Spread across more than 8,500 acres between Kelambakkam and Mamallapuram, the wetland is a meeting point of these two water systems, shaped by tides, rainfall and the seasons.

That landscape is now being reshaped into a freshwater reservoir. The first phase of Mamallan reservoir project covers 4,375 acres. A second phase is proposed for the remaining wetland.

The proposed reservoir will occupy a landscape marked by marshes, mudflats, shallow waters, salt pans and seasonal grasslands, spanning freshwater and brackish-water habitats. The wetland is also a seasonal stopover along the Central Asian Flyway, drawing migratory birds, while its waters support fish, prawns, crabs and other species that sustain fishing activity in the surrounding villages.

The wetland is also being documented from the ground up. Environmental groups and naturalists are recording its biodiversity through field surveys, documentaries, signature campaigns, rallies and a coffee-table book.

Nemmeli’s Last Tide, a documentary conceptualised by Deepak Venkatachalam of Suzhal Arivom, a grassroot level, volunteer-driven environmental education, research, and conservation group and produced by the Wetland Conservation Network, brings together voices from naturalists, scientists, maritime researchers, educators and fisherfolks to document what the wetland holds and what could be lost.

According to Deepak, making people see the landscape is central to conservation. “We try to break that barrier by bringing in people and increasing the footfall to these places,” he says, describing the need to reconnect people with nature through direct experience and visual storytelling. “The landscape has so much life. It is a very complex, intricate ecosystem. It cannot be recreated at any cost once it is depleted.”

That life is reflected in the numbers. Suzhal Arivom’s documentation records 232 species in the Nemmeli Wetland complex, with nearly 45,000 birds counted during the 2025–26 peak season. A count of 16,000 migratory ducks, spread across half-a-dozen species, was recorded.

The wetland is also an important node in the Central Asian Flyway, with 88 migratory species recorded.

The documentation extends beyond birds. In January 2026, Suzhal Arivom recorded a established colony of Burmann’s Sundew (Drosera burmannii) at five GPS-verified locations. The tiny carnivorous plant survives in acidic, nutrient-poor, seasonally waterlogged soils making its presence an indicator of relatively undisturbed wetland conditions.

A parallel effort has come from the Palluyir Trust, a group for Nature Education and Research, founded in 2021 by naturalists, through its coffee-table book Kovalam–Nemmeli Coastal Wetland: A Biodiversity Montage. Combining photographs with species information, the book records the wetland’s birds, insects, benthic life, mangroves and other flora. Crucially, it was printed and sent to bureaucrats, MLAs and government authorities, accompanied by letters highlighting the wetland’s ecological importance and concerns over the proposed reservoir. A digital version is also available on their official website.

The documentation also places these species within the wider wetland ecosystem, its mudflats, marshes, shallow waters and vegetation which provide feeding and breeding grounds for aquatic life and habitat for migratory birds. It also records the wetland’s links to fishing livelihoods and flood protection.

“The idea is we are trying as many strategies as possible to make people feel for that place and be moved by the life there,” Yuvan says. For him, the question is also whether a freshwater reservoir can ever be considered an “alternative” to this landscape. “A freshwater body does not belong by the beach,” he argues, pointing to the difference between inland reservoirs and tidal wetlands.

Fewer fish, less income

Fisherfolk from more than 16 villages depend on the Kovalam–Nemmeli wetlands, with nearly 7,000 families relying on its shallow waters to collect prawns, crabs, oysters and other species. Unlike mechanised fishers, they work largely by hand and foot, following Iral Thazhuvuthal, the traditional practice of catching prawns and fish by hand. The Paraval, as they locally call the coastal wetland, has 18 distinct habitats, with the Purattasi season (mid-September to mid-October) bringing the highest catch. During this period, a family can earn ₹1 lakh–₹3 lakh, an income that can sustain them through much of the year.

The proposed reservoir threatens this livelihood system. About 5,000 acres of the wetland is proposed to be converted into an impounded freshwater reservoir, with Phase I covering 65% Kazhuveli marshland and 35% Uppangazhi salt pans. Forfisherfolk who have depended on these waters for generations, the loss could mean shrinking incomes and a shift to unfamiliar and precarious work.

For Kovalam R. Narayanan, the impact of the Mamallan Reservoir Project can be measured in the distance between what fishing once earned his family and what it brings in today. A fisherman from Kovalam, Narayanan began fishing at 11 and has continued in the occupation for decades. The earnings have now dwindled considerably. Narayanan links the decline partly to what has happened to fishermen who once worked in the coastal wetlands. As access to the wetland has reduced with the progress of the reservoir project, he said, many of those fishermen have moved to the sea.

That has changed the arithmetic of fishing. “Earlier, there were around 500 fishermen fishing in the sea and another 500 depending on the wetlands. Now all 1,000 are going to the sea,” he said. More boats and more fishers are consequently chasing the same marine catch, he said, leaving each fisher with a smaller share.

“The wetlands earmarked for the project are not an empty expanse waiting to be developed. They are a living ecosystem supporting an intricate network of species and livelihoods” said Narayanan.

Link to the documentary https://tinyurl.com/NemmeliDoc

Palluyir Trust - @palluyirtrust.org

World.title: Madras Day 2026: an old market in Mylapore puts on a brave front
World.content:
At the point where Kutchery Road is “amputated” by Metro Rail work , two streets peel away in opposite directions. The workaday realities of these two streets, Devadi Street and Bazaar Road, are also on contrasting trajectories ever since this work took over a section of Kutchery Road shutting it down for regular traffic. Devadi Street has become overly industrious working indefatigably shoulder-to-shoulder with Nadu Street to funnel vehicular traffic from North Mada Street into Kutchery Road towards Santhome High Road. It also entertains wheels from Appu Street. While wheels have increased on Devadi Street, the footfall has simultaneously reduced on Bazaar Road.

Shopping is a languid, leisurely experience; hive off the comfort factor and you detract a vital component from that experience. When Kutchery Road was fully available to motorists and pedestrians, shopping on Bazaar Road felt natural. Now, with diversions and circuitous detours, it feels forced. Unless there are strong reasons to transact business over a shop counter, people are going to find alternatives; and digital pathways keep those alternatives flowing freely.

But Bazaar Road is attractive on account of enterprises that have established a strong presence over decades of retail commerce. Amidst shops that have regularly changed their name board and trade are a multiplicity of enterprises that have persisted with one trade and built immense social capital, installing an emotional hotline with its customers. Examples abound. Picking a handful: Jayakumar Mill, around 70 years old; New Shiva Country Drugs and Herbals, nearly 90 years old, though the old name board pegs it at 80; and there is then the seller of pots Gunasundari N., the third generation entrepreneur in this business.

As anywhere else, a strong USP principle works like a charm. For A. Bhaskar, who runs Sri Jayakumar Flour Mill and also Sri Jayakumar Oil Stores along with his brother A. Kumar, his grinding machines stay heard on Bazaar Road above the subterranean rumble of tunnel-boring machines on Kutchery Road because of certain unique offerings. The machines grind the familiar. To name a few, rice, gram and wheat flour, turmeric, vermilion and ragi and health mixes for young mothers after childbirth. And one machine grinds nalangu maavu (herbal bath power), and that has made a huge difference.

Besides, as Bhaskar points out, his customers value the fact that this mill dedicates a grinding machine to each variety of items to be ground. So, business keeps plopping into those wide funnel-shaped feed hoppers. The challenge, Bhaskar observes, is more from people’s increasing preference for packaged foods than the reduced access caused by Metro Rail work. While packaged foods have changed the way people buy, impacting the mill store’s business, Metro Rail work has made reaching the shop harder. Bhaskar believes opening even one access route on the Metro Rail-impacted section of Kutchery Road could bring back some of the footfall.

A similar disruption has affected New Shiva Country Drugs and Herbals on Bazaar Road, says its owner R. Prakash. Nearly 90 years old, the store began as a herbal medicine shop under Prakash’s grandfather and gradually expanded into pooja articles, dry fruits, and bamboo products. With monsoon comes sniffles and a rush of customers, but through the year, there is a steady flow of commerce, thanks to older customers who grew up relying on country remedies and younger ones who have inherited that faith from their families. Close to New Shiva Country Drugs and Herbals, there are other country medicine shops run by relatives. The concentration of shops of this stripe helps. Prakash notes that New Shiva has branches at Thanithurai Market and North Mada Street, also in Mylapore. Scattered presence helps, particularly in these times. Prakash observes that online business of country medicine is a greater challenge to ford.

For seller of earthen pots Gunasundari N., the going is palpably tough. But her resilience is tougher still, which explains her continued presence at Bazaar Road despite mounting odds. Unlike a flour mill or one selling herbal medicine, her business is largely seasonal, the need for pots largely being felt during festivals and functions at home. The thinning of the customer base, she believes, has resulted largely from changing lifestyles, the earthen pots she sells cracking under the magnetic pull of ever-silver wares. The pots, once a familiar presence in Mylapore homes, are in an unequal battle with ever-silver and aluminium vessels that promise convenience and durability. Obviously, the challenge glowering at Gunasundari is not only a metallic shift in tastes. The road itself poses a challenge now, as it now draws fewer people stopping to browse or buy. Even during festivals such as Pongal and Deepavali, when sales used to be on the higher side, there is lukewarmness from potential buyers.

The fact that she cannot not afford a setting and resources to make these pots, only source them from Thiruneermalai in Chengalpattu district and Arani-Periyapalayam area in Thiruvallur district does not help cost management. She observes that her father-in-law is a potter, but being advanced in years, he cannot work at the potter’s wheel anymore. “In any case, making pots is an impossibility as we do not have space for that activity,” adds Gunasundari wistfully.

Her voice drops to a plaintive murmur when she says, “There are days I go home without earning anything.” But bringing the curtains down on the business does not enter her mind. That steely resolve pretty much sums up the attitude of the old shops at Bazaar Road in Mylapore.

(Ahead of Madras Day, Resilience Series tracks old markets in the city that are under the shadow of a major civic infrastructure work but are soldiering on with inimitable poise.)

World.title: Taken by one of the big four: Snakebite at Maharashtra tribal school
World.content:
Eight-year-old Anu Koreti’s eyes twinkled as she raved about the performances put together to celebrate World Tribal Day on August 9. She clapped to the dance performances and later raved to her older brother about how much she had enjoyed them. That was the last conversation she had before going to bed at a tribal residential school in Dhanora, Gadchiroli district, in Maharashtra. The programme honoured tribal culture, and gave a call for tribal empowerment.

For Anu and her two older siblings studying here, their only hope for a better future away from poverty was this tribal residential school. For them, and for the two generations of Gonds, a Scheduled Tribe, who studied in the private, aided primary and secondary Ashram School in Japtalai in Dhanora, empowerment meant a window to education.

On the intervening night of August 9 and 10, as Anu and 111 girls in the school lay on the hostel floor, a common krait found its way into the dormitory. It bit six girls, all between 8 and 14 years, killing three. Anu was one of them.

One of the girls was airlifted to a hospital in Nagpur, Maharashtra’s no. 2 capital. She is now home and recovering. One continues to be serious, on ventilator support, at a hospital in Gadchiroli, but out of danger. Another is on her way to recovery.

Residents question the lack of medical and general infrastructure in one of the most underdeveloped and remote parts of Maharashtra, Gadchiroli. Chief Minister Devendra Fadnavis is its guardian minister. Gadchiroli, earlier a part of the Red Corridor, is the eastern-most district of Maharashtra.
