World.title: Myth Detector: 230 fake social media accounts created to create illusion of support for Georgian PM’s statements
World.content:
Fake accounts created to support Georgia’s prime minister

1On 2 August, marking the 18th anniversary of the 2008 August War, Georgian Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze held a briefing. He focused in particular on what he described as the spread of “Russophobia” in Georgia and the role of the so-called “deep state” in this process.

After the briefing, pro-government messages began circulating widely on social media. Various media outlets also published visual materials promoting these messages.

According to a study by Myth Detector, 230 fake accounts took part in the campaign. The organisation analysed likes on social media posts, as well as the photos and activity of the profiles that shared them. It identified signs of coordinated and suspicious behaviour that, according to the study, aimed to increase support for specific government narratives.

The study also says the profiles were designed to appear as if they belonged to different socio-demographic groups. Some accounts used photographs depicting idyllic family life to make themselves appear more trustworthy.

Profile photos were generated using artificial intelligence (AI)

According to Hive Moderation, a tool for detecting AI-generated images, there was more than a 90% probability that all 230 profile photos had been generated using AI. In some cases, the probability reached 100%. A visual inspection also identified features typical of AI-generated images, including unnatural shapes of hands and fingers, as well as certain distortions.

The photos repeat the same settings and compositions

Some accounts use identical or very similar photos, including the same images with minor changes. The visual design of different accounts also repeats similar photography styles and details. These include photos with a consistent aesthetic, featuring Tbilisi in the background, a glass of wine or a cup of coffee, a hand touching the head, or similar compositional choices. The accounts also use images showing people having fun, relaxing or taking part in sports to create an impression of authenticity. In some cases, different accounts use the same first and last names.

An illusion of broad support is created through artificially diverse social and demographic profiles

The campaign creates the impression that it brings together people of different ages, appearances and interests. The profiles include young and older people, supporters of conservative and alternative views, as well as religious people, family-oriented users, sports enthusiasts and people who enjoy outdoor activities.

AI-generated accounts use real workplaces and educational institutions to make their profiles appear more credible

Most profiles list places of education and employment, including the Tbilisi Transport Company, various Georgian insurance companies, commercial banks, microfinance organisations, government agencies and municipal services.

Different accounts show identical behaviour

Most profiles list a date between 20 and 24 July 2026 as the date they began living in Georgian cities, although some accounts appear to have been created earlier.

Profile activity focuses on the same messages

The activity of the suspicious accounts, particularly their likes, is concentrated on posts featuring conspiracy claims by the ruling party’s chairman about the “party of global war”, the “deep state’s plan” and the “opening of a second front”. They also engage with the narrative about “Russophobia”, suggesting an artificial increase in the level of support.

Fake accounts created to support Georgia’s prime minister

World.title: Russia no longer attracts Armenian migrant workers as they look for new opportunities in Europe
World.content:
Armenian workers turn to Europe instead of Russia

The geography of labour migration from Armenia is changing. Russia, which until recently remained the main destination, has become less attractive. The main reasons are Russia’s economic downturn, driven by the war in Ukraine, and the depreciation of the rouble.

Many migrants are now returning from Russia to Armenia. Some are trying to find work in their home villages or in the capital, while others are looking for new opportunities, particularly in Europe. The direction of labour migration is changing, with European countries becoming increasingly popular.

Work visa for Poland

After two years working at a meat-processing plant in Poland, 40-year-old Serob (name changed) returned to Armenia for a month. He came to prepare all the necessary documents and take his wife and children with him to Warsaw.

“I received a three-year residence permit and the right to work. Living away from my family is difficult. I decided that we should be together. I should also say that Poland has become one of the first steps towards the European labour market for many people. Many of my friends work in the Czech Republic, the Netherlands and other countries on legal work visas. I was also offered a job in the Netherlands, but I decided to stay in Poland,” he says.

Serob is a butcher. He was also in demand in Armenia. However, he says his salary there was not enough to support his family:

“I had friends who worked as butchers in Europe. They told me that the profession was in demand there and well paid. Gradually, I started thinking: why not try going to Europe and working there? I also had a lot of debts and loans. I went to Poland on a work visa. The process moved slowly. The Polish embassy invited me for an interview a year after I submitted my application.”

A recruitment agency then sent his details to a meat-processing company. Representatives of the company interviewed Serob online. During the video call, he demonstrated his professional skills to the employer, including how he deboned meat.

“The employer liked my work and sent me a contract and the necessary documents. The embassy then approved my work visa. At first, I lived in a house in Poland with people of different nationalities. They all worked for the same company and lived in separate rooms. Later, when my financial situation improved, I moved into a separate flat with a friend from Armenia. I sent most of my earnings to my family to help resolve our financial problems. I did not work in a shop or at a market. I worked at a specialised meat-processing plant with refrigerated storage facilities. It is physically demanding work,” the butcher says.

He notes a shortage of butchers in the European labour market, which creates demand for migrants with the necessary skills. Meat-processing plants employ workers from Ukraine, Argentina, Azerbaijan and Armenia.

“Many Armenians are now going to European countries for work. And not only to meat-processing plants. When I flew to Poland, I met some women who worked as pastry chefs on the plane. They were also travelling to Poland under legal employment contracts. Many Armenians also work in shops. These are people who speak foreign languages. In any case, I am happy. I will return to work in a month, this time with my family,” Serob says.

Working at a German medical clinic with an Armenian degree

Doctors, teachers and highly skilled professionals in various fields are also in demand on the European labour market. Dentist Edgar Mirzoyan has been living and working in Germany for nine months.

Edgar Mirzoyan

“One day, my nurse told me that her friend worked in Germany and that they might need a dentist. I simply gave her my contact details and forgot about it. Some time later, they contacted me. At the same time, I started learning German. The whole process took two years: learning the language, preparing documents and taking exams. Finally, I moved to Germany. By the way, getting my Armenian degree recognised in Germany seemed more realistic and achievable than in other European countries,” Edgar says.

At the same time, the 30-year-old dentist studied not only the professional requirements but also the overall situation in the country, including its economy, level of safety and even happiness index.

“Geography also influenced my final decision. It was important for me to stay connected to Armenia. You can get from Germany to Armenia in just a few hours. In this sense, Europe was a much more convenient destination for me than, for example, Canada. Before moving to Germany, I had a completely different idea of what it would be like. Of course, everyone’s experience is different. Some doctors who arrived at the same time as me had a much harder journey. A lot depends on which city you move to, who your employer is and who you interact with. Everyone has their own experience,” he says.

Edgar started working two days after arriving in Germany. Some time later, his wife also joined him.

“Before moving to Germany, I registered in advance to take a language exam. They tested my knowledge of medical German. I passed the exam successfully. After that, I received a temporary licence valid for two years. I can work during this period, but I must work under the supervision of an experienced doctor.

However, the process of having my degree fully recognised is still under way. The authorities compare my entire university curriculum, the number of hours I completed and the subjects I studied with the German curriculum. I applied for this process while I was still in Armenia. They only started reviewing my documents after two years of waiting. If they find differences between the curricula, I will have to make up the gaps. It is not yet clear how significant those differences will be,” the doctor says.

According to Edgar, working in Germany has its own particularities. Berlin is a multicultural city, and his patients include not only Germans. About 30 per cent are Armenians and Yazidis, while another 30 per cent are Russians and Ukrainians.

Edgar continues to practise in Armenia as well:

“I can take leave twice a year. I come to Armenia, mainly perform implant procedures and surgeries, and then return to Germany. I have many patients who wait for me to come back. They book appointments in advance, I come and perform the surgery, and the next stage of treatment takes place three to six months later, when I can return again.”

When labour migration is a family choice

For many people who move to Europe, leaving is a decision about their family’s future, improving their living conditions and trying to build a new life in a different environment.

Vergine (name changed) chose this path. She has lived in the Czech Republic with her husband for seven years and now has two children.

“First, my husband moved to Prague on a work visa. He started working in the security department of a shopping centre. Two years later, I joined him. We made the decision consciously, after carefully considering everything. We wanted to settle down and continue our lives in a European country. In this sense, the Czech Republic seemed like a suitable option, and we are very happy with our choice,” Vergine says.

Before moving to the Czech Republic, the couple worked at Zvartnots Airport.

“At first, I worked at a language centre as an English teacher. Then my second child was born here. Of course, there were many difficulties. We lived in a foreign country without support from relatives and with a small child, but we managed. I now work as an English teacher at a school,” she says.

The young family does not plan to return to Armenia for now, but they regularly visit their relatives.

“We have the right to live and work here, but I am sure that one day we will definitely return,” Vergine says.

Changing migration patterns

According to Tatevik Bezhanian, an expert with the migration programme of the charitable organisation Armenian Caritas, Armenia currently has no statistics showing how many people leave for European countries to work.

One reason is that Armenia has no intergovernmental labour migration agreements with EU countries. Bulgaria is the only exception. In addition, most people who leave for Europe find jobs through private recruitment agencies, and the state does not register this process.

“You will not find this data in official statistics. On the other hand, we also do not have a migration card system under which people have to state when entering or leaving the country that they are going abroad to work. They may not indicate the purpose of their departure at all,” Bezhanian says.

She says this problem is not unique to Armenia. Internationally, governments mainly register migrant workers arriving in their countries because they can manage these migration flows. Countries that pursue targeted labour migration policies, sign bilateral agreements and organise the recruitment of their citizens abroad usually have comprehensive data on those who leave. The Philippines and Uzbekistan are among them, for example.

Tatevik Bezhanian notes that even when Armenian authorities want information about labour migrants leaving for Russia, they have to rely on official Russian statistics:

“If the geography of labour migration expands, we will have to approach the relevant authorities in countries such as Poland, the Czech Republic and the Netherlands. We will need to obtain data and determine how many Armenian citizens work there.”

Armenian workers turn to Europe instead of Russia

World.title: Opinion on Georgian petrol in Abkhazia: ‘If needed, it’s possible’
World.content:
The indirect consequence of Ukrainian drone attacks on Russian oil refineries has been a fuel crisis in Abkhazia, which in recent years has been buying petrol from Russia.

After struggling with shortages for two weeks, Abkhazia decided to buy petrol from Georgia. Given the unresolved Georgian-Abkhaz conflict, this was a rather “unorthodox” move, but at the same time the only viable way out of the situation.

In a blog post, Inal Khashig, editor of the Abkhaz outlet Chegemskaya Pravda, discusses whether Abkhazia can trade with Georgia.

Inal Khashig: “Abkhazia has been grappling with a petrol shortage for the past two weeks. There is virtually no fuel left in the country. Government assurances that the situation is under control and that a new shipment of petrol is about to arrive have done little to reassure people — if anything, they have only deepened the pessimism. Queues at petrol stations stretch as far as the eye can see.

And then petrol arrived from an unexpected source — Georgia.

Tbilisi says the government has nothing to do with it and that it is entirely a private business matter. Sukhumi, for its part, says that when the country is facing a fuel shortage, it will not prevent petrol tankers from entering from Georgia. After all, there is precedent for this kind of economic contact: during the difficult 1990s, we supplied Georgians with relatively cheap fuel.

This particular fuel crisis has once again brought an enduring Abkhaz question to the fore: should we trade with an enemy state or not?”

To me, it is quite straightforward: if this kind of cooperation is vital for the country as a whole, its economy and the well-being of its people, then it is justified. Sukhumi has, after all, cooperated with Tbilisi in the energy sector throughout the post-war years, and no one objects because there is no alternative. This cooperation is vital to both Abkhazia and Georgia.

And now, when the whole of Abkhazia — and with it the country’s economy — has ground to a halt because of the lack of petrol, refusing to buy fuel from the Georgians looks like outright posturing.

Incidentally, I think the government’s argument that Abkhazia actively sold petrol to Georgia in the 1990s is a very good one. At the time, war-ravaged Abkhazia was under a severe blockade: Russia under Boris Yeltsin had effectively sealed us off on all sides. Nothing could be brought in or taken out. About the only thing permitted was taking mandarins across the border in handcarts, with Abkhaz women effectively serving as beasts of burden.

Abkhazia’s tiny budget was funded by selling timber and scrap metal to Turkey, as well as by smuggling fuel into Georgia.

The latter involved considerable risk and loss of life, as fuel tankers had to travel towards the Georgian border through the Gali district, which was unstable at the time. But there was effectively no other way of bringing even a little money into the state coffers. Whatever anyone may say, those modest revenues helped Abkhazia survive at the time.

And yes, we traded with Georgia then because we had to.

And we need to do so now to protect the country from a fuel crisis.

And in future, we need to take similarly responsible steps, even if they run counter to established dogmas. Rigid dogma is not the best guide to action in crises like the one we are facing now.”

The terminology, place names and views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial position of this website.

World.title: Analysts say Ukraine is preparing a large-scale offensive
World.content:
Ukraine Launches Large-Scale Offensive

Based on reporting by Novosti Donbassa

Ukrainian defense forces have liberated 19 settlements across several sectors of the front, according to DeepState, a Ukrainian battlefield monitoring project, which reported the advances after updating its combat map.

According to the analysts, Ukrainian forces have regained control of Zelenyi Hai, Novokhatske, Hrushevske, Tolstoi, Zirka, Yalta, Piddubne, Myrne, Voskresenka, Sichneve, Vorone, Ternove, Berezove, Stepne, Kalynovske, Pryvillia, Zlahoda, Rybne and Krasnohorske.

In addition, Ukrainian troops pushed Russian forces back in six other settlements: Novopavlivka, Novoheorhiivka, Novomykolaivka, Novohryhorivka, Zaporizke and Pryvilne.

The Ukrainian military also released video footage from settlements it said had been liberated in the Donetsk, Dnipropetrovsk and Zaporizhzhia regions.

exchange

World.title: Georgian Constitutional Court judge issues dissenting opinion on cases involving protests on pavements
World.content:
Judge on protests on pavements in Georgia

A dissenting opinion by Constitutional Court judge Giorgi Kverenchkhiladze has been published on the punishment of people for holding protests on pavements.

Kverenchkhiladze believes that imposing administrative detention on people for peaceful protests and assemblies could cause harm that may later prove impossible to remedy.

The Tbilisi City Court began hearing the so-called “pavement cases” in December 2025. Since January 2026, dozens of demonstrators have faced administrative detention for holding protests on the pavement outside parliament.

Several people petitioned the Constitutional Court to challenge the ban on protests on pavements. They also asked the court to suspend the disputed provisions until it issued a final ruling. The Constitutional Court began hearing the cases but refused to suspend the provisions. Judge Giorgi Kverenchkhiladze believes the court should have suspended them.

However, according to lawyer Giorgi Burdjanadze, Kverenchkhiladze was in the minority among the judges of the Constitutional Court’s First Chamber when they considered the issue.

Judge Giorgi Kverenchkhiladze’s dissenting opinion

“If the threat of administrative detention or imprisonment forces a person to repeatedly refrain from taking part in an assembly or publicly expressing their position, that opportunity can no longer be restored,” the judge wrote.

He said this was why such a restriction could cause “irreparable harm”.

Giorgi Kverenchkhiladze’s dissenting opinion also includes arguments that lawyers raised before the Tbilisi City Court when it considered cases related to protests on pavements. However, the judges did not take those arguments into account.

One such argument concerns the temporary disruption of people’s normal movement in their daily lives.

Judge Giorgi Kverenchkhiladze

Kverenchkhiladze notes that pedestrian movement on pavements can be disrupted for various reasons, including parking violations, commercial or construction activities, and other circumstances. However, the state has never considered imprisonment a necessary measure to protect freedom of movement in such cases.

“Temporary restrictions on pedestrians’ freedom of movement do not represent an interest for which a democratic state would normally resort to imprisonment as a means of protection,” the judge wrote.

Kverenchkhiladze also drew attention to the severity of the sanction. He said harsh punishment not only demonstrates the state’s attitude towards a particular action, but can also discourage people from taking part in protests altogether.

“The severity of the sanction provided for by the disputed provisions indicates not only the degree to which the act is considered reprehensible, but also the strength of the ‘deterrent effect’ it may have on the exercise of freedom of expression and freedom of assembly,” Kverenchkhiladze stressed.

Context

Georgia has seen continuous protests since 28 November 2024. Thousands of people took to the streets after Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze of the Georgian Dream party announced that the government would not put EU accession talks on the agenda for the next four years.

Since then, Georgian Dream has repeatedly restricted freedom of expression through new laws. These measures have included bans on wearing masks and using pyrotechnics at rallies, as well as criminal liability for repeatedly blocking roads during protests.

The most far-reaching of these repressive legislative initiatives came with amendments banning assemblies on pavements. Under the new rules, organisers of any assembly or demonstration on a pavement must notify the Interior Ministry five days before the event. The ministry can also propose an alternative time and location for the protest.

The new rules also introduce administrative detention as the initial penalty for violations, except in certain special cases.

Judge on protests on pavements in Georgia

World.title: Menopause and music: pioneer women's health doctor dies at 94
World.content:
Dr Margaret Smith was fond of describing herself as "not famous, but well-known".

The renowned Perth obstetrician and women's health advocate delivered some 6,000 babies throughout a decades-long career, during which she had to battle the sexism rampant in the male-dominated hierarchies of medicine in the 1950s and beyond.

Dr Smith died on July 14, her 94th birthday.

In his eulogy, family friend Julian Dowse said she often paraphrased the famous quote that described golden-age Hollywood actors Ginger Rogers and Fred Astaire dancing together.

"I have to do everything he does backwards and in high heels, but fortunately I can make it look twice as easy," Mr Dowse quoted her as saying.

Margie, as she was often called, was a twin, born four minutes before her identical sister Joan.

Their mother, attended by just a midwife and expecting a single baby, had picked out one girl's name: 'Margaret Joan'. Such was the shock at the multiple birth that the girls were only given one name each. Their sister Nancy completed the family four years later.

Margaret and her sister Joan were so alike they were sometimes referred to as `Margaretorjoan’ by schoolmates (Supplied)

As a child, she became determined to pursue a medical career when a favourite cousin died in her teens in the era before antibiotics. Later her grandmother's death from ovarian cancer steered her towards women's health.

No residencies for women

Margie graduated from the University of Adelaide in 1956, one of only four women in her class of more than 100 men.

Initially, she was refused a residency in obstetrics because she was female.

Mr Dowse said her classmates made sure she got what she wanted.

"There was a famous act of solidarity by her fellow students, who refused to take up their residencies unless the talented Margie was offered a rightful place," he said.

Loading...

The lead campaigner was Frank Smith, who was to become Margie's husband. The couple had no children.

"Margie once said to me, reflecting on the dilemmas that professional women of her era faced:

'I could not have had children, otherwise I could not have done what I did for other children'," Mr Dowse said.

A pioneer in women's health

Margie spent five years training as a specialist in Edinburgh, winning a gold medal in her postgraduate examinations in 1963 for the highest-performing student in the realm.

In the 1970s, she and Frank spent seven years in the highlands of Papua New Guinea, where Frank worked as a surgeon, and Margie delivered babies.

But her role in the remote location went far beyond obstetrics, and she was often a physician and anaesthetist, practising in difficult circumstances without the support of specialist teams.

"During this time, Margie was most proud of safely delivering a set of triplets," Mr Dowse said.

Margaret Smith delivered about 6,000 babies during her long career. (Supplied)

After Papua New Guinea, the couple moved to Perth, where Margie was one of the few female practitioners at the time. She worked both at King Edward Memorial Hospital and in private practice, as well as lecturing at the University of Western Australia.

"Margie revolutionised the treatment and care of women," Mr Dowse said. "She put women first from birth to menopause."

Treating the silent suffering

In the 1970s, menopause was rarely discussed in public but Margie recognised the challenges faced by many women in midlife.

She founded WA's first menopause clinic in 1978, later named in her honour. She was also a founding member of the Australasian Menopause Society.

Colleague Dale Hamilton said she was passionate about teaching women to take better care of their own health.

"She ran a lot of public seminars for education about the menopause and … she was a very clear and passionate speaker, and very, very popular," she said.

" She had a good sense of humour, she was clear about the information, so she imparted a lot of power to women by educating them on what was possible. "

Community recognition

Margie was named a WA Citizen of the Year in 1994, and was appointed a Member of the Order of Australia in 1996 for service to medicine and women's health care.

Dr Margaret Smith working at her desk in 2010. (ABC News)

In 2011, she was inducted into the WA Women's Hall of Fame.

Margie also wrote several books, including a memoir, as well as more than 30 published medical papers.

Throughout her career, she mentored countless young doctors, inspired many colleagues and assisted thousands of patients, all with patience, encouragement and humility.

"Her work was the Hippocratic Oath writ large," Mr Dowse said.

"She safely brought life into the world and sought to make life better for countless others."

Music and medicine

Margie loved classical music, and was a choral singer well into her 90s.

Margaret Smith loved music and poetry (Supplied)

She also loved poetry, and considered Norton's Anthology of Poetry an "indispensable reference book", Mr Dowse said.

"She introduced me to Keats's observation that 'a thing of beauty is a joy forever'," he said.

Late in life, Margie learnt to play the cello and to paint.

"She had a wonderful energy ... no matter what was going on," Dr Hamilton said.

Margie is survived by her twin sister Joan, nieces and nephews, as well as more than one generation of deeply grateful women.

World.title: Hurricane Lala threatens to make landfall on Hawaii's Big Island
World.content:
Hawaii's Big Island is bracing for its first possible direct hit from a hurricane in 155 years after the tropical system, Hurricane Lala, roared in the Pacific Ocean and battered the region with gusty winds, waves and rain.

The US National Hurricane Center said Lala's maximum sustained winds reached 120 kilometres per hour, making it a category one hurricane.

The National Weather Service also warned of dangerous surf and localised flooding.

The Hawaii Department of Transportation said it was closing Hilo International Airport and would close Ellison Onizuka Kona International Airport at Keahole at 2pm Saturday local time (Sunday, 10am AEST).

The US National Hurricane Center has advised residents on Hawaii's Big Island to expect damaging winds and rain. (Zoom Earth)

The department also closed the Hawaii Island, Maui County, and Kaua‘i commercial ports.

The eye wall was forecast to move over or near Big Island's southern end by Saturday evening local time, lashing its worst winds at volcanic slopes thousands of feet above sea level.

Governor Josh Green, noting rainfall of 5 centimetres an hour, said "people should be sheltering in place now".

Forecasters said higher elevations on the island, dominated by the towering Mauna Kea volcano, could get as much as 63cm of rain.

That could cause life-threatening mudslides in a mountainous area where people live off the grid in improvised housing.

Earlier the governor called it an "enormous storm", capable of destructive flooding and even the possibility of wildfires kicked up by strong winds across the island chain.

Residents prepare for Lala

Electricity was knocked out for nearly 20 per cent of customers on the Big Island, according to PowerOutage.us.

Resident Bobby Camara, 75, said he planned to "hunker down, cross my fingers, hope the lights don't go out" at a care home just outside Hilo.

He said gas stations were busy as people sought fuel for chainsaws and vehicles.

"I think stocking up is part of life over here … you learn to be self-reliant," Mr Camara said.

Mike Caputo, who lives in Keaau, near the Big Island's east coast, said the main concern was flash flooding and fallen trees, especially albizia, a common tree.

"They're not very sturdy, but they grow extremely large," said Mr Caputo, 50, a local fire captain.

"They can make roads impassable. I made sure my trees were trimmed a few days ago."

The Big Island was under a hurricane warning, and tropical storm warnings were issued for the islands of Maui, Molokai, Lanai, Kahoolawe, Oahu, Kauai and Niihau.

Hurricane hit Big Island more than a century ago

A category three hurricane hit the north-east corner of the Big Island in 1871, according to research by a University of Hawaii atmospheric scientist.

The latest forecast has Lala striking "very close to the southern tip of the Big Island", said Vanessa Almanza, a National Weather Service meteorologist in Honolulu.

Shelters were opened, events were cancelled and ranchers were urged to leave their cattle in pastures, rather than structures that might collapse.

"It doesn't take landfall to create destruction," Ms Almanza said.

The hurricane centre predicted about 20 to 30cm of total rainfall across Maui and the lower elevations of the Big Island, and 10 to 15cm across the island chain.

About 20 to 30 centimetres of rain is predicted across Maui and the lower elevations of the Big Island, and 10 to 15cm across the island chain. (Supplied: National Hurricane Center)

Kauai, which is several islands north-west up the archipelago from the Big Island, is where Hurricane Iniki made landfall as a category four hurricane in 1992, an El Nino year like this one, when a warming of the Pacific near the equator increases Pacific hurricane activity and affects weather patterns across the globe.

"It did $3 billion worth of damage. It destroyed thousands of homes, and it did kill six people," said Steven Businger, a University of Hawaii scientist.

"We just can never know if a storm is going to turn."

ABC/Wires

World.title: Live: Australia in desperate need of runs with Bangladesh closing in on famous win
World.content:
(Getty Images)

Ah, hindsight.

The airwaves and internet forums reek of it in the post-toss wash up from a poor decision.

Ponting bowling first at Edgbaston in 2005, or Joe Root doing the same in Adelaide in 2017. Poor decisions that have come back to bite Australia.

Will Pat Cummins' call to bat first on a green pitch in Darwin similarly go down in folklore?

"Hindsight is wonderful but I tend to not look at wickets too much," Josh Hazlewood said. "I leave it up to whoever is making the decisions. I honestly think people get cricket wickets wrong more than they get them right — but you tend to bat first."

Bangladesh made the most of the friendliest bowling conditions on day one to bowl Australia out for 198.

The visitors then made hay as the wicket flattened out to post 426 in their first innings before the hosts made a better fist of batting the second time around to be 4-161 at stumps on Saturday's day three.



Australia did bat poorly in the first innings and with more application could have fought harder to cash in on day two.

Did captain Pat make the right call? (Getty Images)

In Hazlewood's view "the wicket looked decent", unlike some of the controversial bowler-friendly pitches of recent Australian summers.

Marrara Stadium has a drop-in split pitch but it has proved a good cricket wicket.

"It wasn't a raging green seamer. I still think 'runs on the board and put the pressure on'," Hazlewood said. "Drop-in wickets can be a little bit different. You can think it is still going to be a decent wicket on days four and five. Adelaide is still pretty good day and four and five. "Darwin is not your traditional 'win the toss and bat' but it was still discussed. I still think it was the right choice at the time." Bangladeshi's seamers, led by Hasan Mahmud who took 6-55, bowled in the right areas and stuck to their plans. "I think they have bowled very well to the conditions and got the most out of the wicket on day one," Hazlewood said. "They bowled a nice full length and the ball seamed around for a bit longer on day one that it has since."

With AAP

World.title: Memory of late partner blooms in sharing wildflowers
World.content:
Leonie Aspin travels from New Zealand to Western Australia's Mid West each year as a kaleidoscope of colourful blooms emerges after winter rains.

For months, she volunteers as a wildflower tour guide in Morawa, 360 kilometres north-east of Perth, in memory of her late partner,Ray Fraser, a former shearer who died from brain cancer in 2022.

A variety of blooms have emerged near Morawa. (ABC Midwest and Wheatbelt: Chloe Henville)

It was Mr Fraser who taught her about wildflowers during long drives around the region.

"[Ray] would sometimes in the morning say, 'Do you want to go hunting for orchids?' and it was just like, 'Yes please,'" Ms Aspin said.

"He was just the best in that aspect."

Leonie Aspin and Ray Fraser would often hunt for orchids together. (ABC Midwest & Wheatbelt: Chris Lewis)

Grief-stricken, Ms Aspin moved to New Zealand after Mr Fraser's death, before the lure of wildflowers brought her back.

"It got to a point where I just missed the wildflowers, and it got to the point where I had to test my little heart again," she said.

Ms Aspin now returns each year to continue their shared hobby, guiding tourists to carpets of blooms and pointing out the more understated, hidden gems.

"I know he'll never be there again, but it just helps fill that little empty hole in my heart," she said.

Loading...

Ms Aspin draws parallels between her grief and the seasonal blooms.

"We all have to get off the boat at some time, don't we? And just like wildflowers, well, it's a complete circle of life," she said.

"To see the red dirt transform after the rains into absolute colour; you can't explain it, you need to see it."

Red dirt is hidden under a carpet of wildflowers. (ABC Midwest & Wheatbelt: Chris Lewis)

Business behind the blooms

Ms Aspin said tourists were starting to flock to the Mid West.

"It's starting to amp up now, so it will only get busier, so the next month will be absolutely probably crazy," she said.

She said the annual influx was an important boost for the small communities scattered across the wildflower region.

"People are going to need food, coffees, accommodation, obviously fuel," she said.

"It just benefits the whole town."

Tom Pilkington travels every year to see wildflowers. (ABC Midwest & Wheatbelt: Chris Lewis)

Tom Pilkington travels from Perth annually to see WA's wildflowers, this year making the four-hour journey to Morawa.

He said the hospitality of the small town was a real drawcard, along with the abundance of blooms.

Some visitors travel to see small, elusive orchids. (ABC Midwest & Wheatbelt: Chris Lewis)

"It's a lovely little place … everybody's really friendly and helpful," he said.

"They're just over the moon with giving you information [about] which way to go."

'Other-worldly' scenes

Carla Read and Ray Hatton also travelled from Perth, camping in Morawa while on a five-day journey to Lake Ballard.

The pair said they had not done much wildflower touring before, but were considering making it an annual tradition.

Ray Hatton and Carla Read say they hope to travel during wildflower season again. (ABC Midwest & Wheatbelt: Chris Lewis)

"I never used to understand the gold and green thing, and now driving here, I fully get it because everything is gold and green," Ms Read said.

"Being in nature and seeing the flowers … it just takes you somewhere else out of who you normally relate to being.

"It's just other-worldly really.

"It's just that nature. The colour, freedom, the open skies, it's just beautiful, and the red dirt. I love that."

Pink everlastings draw tourists to the Midwest. (ABC Midwest & Wheatbelt: Chloe Henville)

World.title: The bush artisan saving craftmanship one stockwhip at a time
World.content:
On a warm winter's day, sunlight spills through the tall timber doorframes of the memorial hall where Bill Webb is gently folding one strand of kangaroo leather over another.

Dust dances in the beams of light as five women carefully follow his practised movements, cutting, braiding and conditioning at workstations dotted around the hall.

Conversation ebbs and flows as they laugh about husbands, children and the joys found living in rural north Queensland.

The room smells faintly of kangaroo hide and fresh country air.

There is no rush.

For the next three days, they have traded family and farm for sharp knives, leather gauges and sheets of finely cut kangaroo skin.

The master leather plaiter is teaching them to make one of Australia's most iconic bush tools — the stock whip.

Bill Webb hopes to keep the art of leather plaiting alive through workshops. ( )

Softly spoken and quick to laugh, Bill roams from one student to the next, quietly correcting a hand position here, tightening a braid there.

"Lean on it with your body," he reminds them.

It is advice repeated dozens of times throughout the workshop.

Not because leather is difficult, but because patience is.

While few Australians may know the name Bill Webb, plenty know the man who taught him about craftsmanship and legacy.

Keeping RM's dream alive

Those immersed in the world of leather plaiting regard Bill as one of the country's finest craftsmen, whose work has travelled to Brazil, England, Italy and the United States.

He has won multiple Dame Mary Durack Awards for Outback Crafts, which Bill describes as "the Melbourne Cup" of leatherwork.

Bill favours kangaroo skin for making whips because of its strength and durability. ( )

Working with leather requires patience and time. ( )

Tools of the trade used by Bill and his workshop attendees to craft leather into different designs. ( )

But ask him what he is proudest of, he does not mention the awards.

He talks about teaching.

"My mission in life is to try and keep the art form of leather plaiting alive," he says.

" That was RM's dream and I'm trying to do the same. "

'Boy'

Long before Bill became the teacher, he was simply "Boy" to legendary bushman Reginald Murray Williams, now famously known as RM Williams.

The pair first met when Bill was a teenager spending school holidays mustering on neighbouring properties.

His payment was not money — it was two weeks learning beside the man whose name would become synonymous with craftsmanship and Australian bush culture.

RM Williams affectionately nicknamed a young Bill Webb "Boy." ( )

RM Williams (left holding hat) took Bill Webb under his wing when he was a young man at Rockybar station. ( )

Bill Webb grew up on cattle properties where bushcraft was part of everyday life. ( )

"He was such a generous man," Bill says.

" If you were fair dinkum, he'd give you the shirt off his back. "

RM also demanded perfection.

A piece that looked finished to everyone else often wasn't finished to him.

"He'd say, 'You can do better than that. Start again,'" Bill recalls.

Bill's leather plaiting skills were passed on to him by the famous RM Williams when he was just a boy. ( )

Catherine McNamara learns the skills to continue the trade long after the workshop has finished. ( )

Bill trims the conditioned kangaroo leather so it is ready for plaiting. ( )

Rhonda Walton patiently braids the thin strands of kangaroo leather for the body of her stock whip. ( )

More than half a century later, Bill still hears RM's words every time he starts a new piece.

"He was always just saying, 'Try and make the next one better than the last one and be the best that you can be,'" he said.

At the Bloomsbury Soldiers Memorial Hall, about 90 kilometres north of Mackay, the ladies are starting to understand why.

Making a whip involves focus and steady movements to perfect not just what is seen on the outside, but also to establish the foundations and finally the finishings on the inside too.

Bill tells them 70 per cent of the job happens before the first strand is ever plaited.

Raelene Miller conditions her hand-cut leather strands before she begins the plaiting process. ( )

"Each strip must be cut to exactly the right width," he says.

" Every strand stretched. Trimmed. Bevelled. Prepared. Only then can the leather start to take shape. "

"Look after it, and a good whip can last a lifetime … or two."

Saving the trade

For Jane Henley, the journey to Bloomsbury started more than a decade ago.

The hairdresser from Tully first met Bill at a Lost Trades Fair in Victoria, which is dedicated to showcasing artisans who practise lost arts, rare trades and forgotten crafts.

Tully farmer Jane Henley has been waiting years for Bill Webb to host a leather plaiting workshop in north Queensland. ( )

When she found out Bill was heading north for a workshop, she packed the car and convinced three girlfriends, Catherine, Rhonda and Raelene, to come too.

"We've been stalking Bill Webb for years," she laughs.

Her handmade whip is destined for her husband, who still uses one while mustering cattle on their small property near Tully.

Jane had never worked with leather before, but now she'll have the knowledge to make another.

That, Bill says, is exactly the point.

He says for generations, leather workers closely guarded their techniques, but now he believes the great risk is that nobody learns at all.

"They wouldn't show you because you're going to take business away from them," he says.

The work starts with the right piece of leather. ( )

" Now … we're trying to tell everyone as much as we can so we can keep it alive. "

Workshop organiser Kimberly Carey grew up surrounded by horses, dogs and stockwhips on a cattle property near Clermont in central Queensland.

She worries practical bush skills are slowly disappearing beneath screens and keyboards.

Kimberly Carey tests her newly made stockwhip in her backyard. ( )

"If we don't keep any of these old skills alive, they're going to be gone," she said

" It builds character, it builds patience, and unreal craft. "

Spreading the craft

By the final afternoon, everyone has a finished whip.

Some are a little tighter than others, some braids are more even, but none of that matters much to Bill.

He knows they have learned enough to make another or to teach someone else.

Kimberly Carey's whip collection now includes her own handmade addition. ( )

Some of the many uniquely handmade leather products crafted by Bill Webb. ( )

The fine strands of Kangaroo leather tightly plaited show the intricate work needed to make the butt of a stockwhip handle. ( )

Bill travels to crafts markets to sell his work and meet others people who appreciate bush craftsmanship. ( )

Kimberly turns her whip over in her hands.

"It's pretty awesome," she says.

"I didn't realise how much was involved in building one.

" They're works of art. "

It will take pride of place in her home, the first of many she intends to make.

Raelene Miler, Jane Henley, Rhonda Walton, Catherine McNamara and Kimberly Carey with their handmade stockwhips and teacher Bill Webb (centre). ( )

For Bill, her confidence to try more is the greatest compliment a teacher can receive.

When asked what Bill would like his legacy to be, he pauses for a moment.

World.title: Teen obliterates men's world record in 1,500m freestyle first
World.content:
The world record for the men's 1,500m freestyle, an event once dominated by Australians Grant Hackett and Kieren Perkins, has been obliterated by 19-year-old German star Johannes Liebmann.

The teenager smashed the record at the European Aquatics Championships in France on Saturday, knocking almost four seconds off the previous record in a dominant display.

The new world-best mark of 14 minutes 26.79 seconds eclipsed the previous record set by American Bobby Finke at the Paris Olympics two years ago by 3.88 seconds. He also became the first man to complete the distance in under 14 minutes 30 seconds.

"I'm just amazed, the time is incredible. I didn't think it was possible for me … I'm just speechless," Liebmann told Olympics.com.

"The race was hard. I started fast, it was planned to just get rid of the others to swim my own race. Halfway through the race, I saw I was way ahead of the others, and I felt good … I guess in the last 200 or 300 metres, I saw the crowd standing up and it just gave me another burst of power."

The teenager said he knew he was going to post a good time, but he had no idea how fast he was going.

"When I saw the crowd standing, I knew probably a European record, maybe a world record, but I thought it was close, so I was a bit overthinking it, and the last 100 metres were so hard, but then just seeing the 14:26 is incredible."

Saturday also saw another world record fall as American Kate Douglass reclaimed the women's 50 metres freestyle world record by registering a time of 23.49 seconds in the preliminaries at the Pan Pacific Swimming Championships in Irvine, California.

Reuters/ABC

World.title: Blind surfer stuns locals at Queensland beach
World.content:
Steve Fox is legally blind but that does not stop him from jumping on a board while visiting the Queensland town of Agnes Water.

The 60-year-old para surfing champion from Gerringong, in New South Wales, has stunned onlookers with his skills while on holidays at the coastal community, nearly 500 kilometres north of Brisbane.

Wearing a rashie with the words "blind surfer" across his chest, Steve carved up the waves with the help of local instructor Shayne Silver.

"What he does is something really, really amazing," Silver said.

Steve Fox and Agnes Water surf instructor Shayne Silver. (ABC News: Johanna Marie)

Fox was diagnosed with retinitis pigmentosa as a child and completely lost his eyesight about 10 years ago.

Instead of giving up the sport he loves, he has learnt to listen and feel the ocean.

"Because I lost my sight over a long period of time I kept making small adjustments," he said.

" You just rely on the movements of the ocean, which way the wind's blowing, which direction the swells and the sounds are coming from. "

Adaptive surfing

Adaptive, or para surfing, is an inclusive sport enabling people living with a disability to surf using specialised equipment and modified surfboards.

Fox also relies on assistance from other surfers to direct him and call him into the waves.

Instructor Silver said it was an "amazing experience" to work with him.

Shayne Silver helped blind surfer Steve Fox into the waves. (ABC News: Johanna Marie)

"We've got a bit of a system where we use the clock, and he knows where 12 o'clock is and that's the direction that he's got to paddle into the wave.

" I'm looking forward to working with other people that want to come down to the beach and do this, be it blind or any other kind of disability. "

Surfing Australia, which has established a Para Surf Committee with the aim of having the sport included in the Brisbane 2032 Olympics, says the sport is growing in popularity.

Fox was crowned one of 12 national champions at the Australian Para Surfing Titles in Byron Bay earlier this year and he has also competed in the World titles.

He is eager to encourage more people in the blind and vision impaired community to "give it a go".

"It's good for the spirit, good for the soul," he said.

"There's a growing para surfing community and whether you're blind or whether you're in a wheelchair, whether you're an amputee, you can still get out there and surf."

World.title: Experts warn H5N1 bird flu spread to the Northern Territory 'inevitable'
World.content:
Veterinary authorities say it is "inevitable" H5N1 bird flu will spread to the Northern Territory, almost two months after the first case of the disease was identified in Australia.

The virus, first detected in Western Australia in late June, has now been found in all six states, leading to bird vaccination programs in some of them.

Senior Director of Species Management at the NT Department of Lands, Planning and Environment Tony Griffiths said the disease's arrival in the territory was imminent.

Tony Griffiths says it's only a matter of time before the H5N1 bird flu strain arrives in the NT. (ABC News: Tristan Hooft)

"It's definitely going to happen," he said.

" It could be weeks, it could be months, but it's a national event, it's the biggest national disease event that has ever occurred in Australia for wildlife. "

For bird owners like Darwin local "Datto", who frequents Nightcliff Jetty with his galah Buddy, the threat of the flu has created a looming sense of anxiety.

The NT is home to 450 species of bird, 37 of which are considered threatened. (ABC News: Tristan Hooft)

"It's going to take away a lot of privileges of me taking [Buddy] where the other birds are, and we're going to lose a lot of good birds over it," he said.

Datto said an outbreak in Darwin's northern suburbs, where wild birds routinely flock along the coastline, would devastate locals who come to enjoy the wildlife.

"We get all myriads of birds here — the firebirds, the honey eaters and everything else — and it'll be a shame to see all of them in a little pile of feathers on the side of the road," he said.

The NT's Chief Veterinary Officer Sue Fitzpatrick said it was not just wild species that were at risk, urging backyard poultry farmers and other bird owners to be vigilant against the disease.

Sue Fitzpatrick says the Territory's backyard poultry owners can do their bit to help stop the spread of bird flu. (ABC News: Tristan Hooft)

"While we don't have a commercial poultry industry, we certainly have many backyard poultry owners," she said.

"We're looking for bird keepers to protect their birds from wild birds, enclose their runs and put some roof over their runs, protect feed and water sources from wild birds."

Birdwatchers essential to response

Dr Griffiths said the plan to combat H5N1 in the NT would largely rely on wide-scale surveying of areas where birds are known to flock, such as the Top End coastline and Barkly Lakes.

He said while experts had been rigorously sampling faeces and water supplies to identify contamination, vaccination of native species was not on the cards.

The masked lapwing has small spurs on its wings which it uses to protect its chicks. (ABC News: Tristan Hooft)

"We have 450 species of bird in the territory and 37 of those are threatened, but we don't rely on captive breeding programs to support the management of those species," he said.

"The threatened birds we have are dispersed over very large areas and it's very difficult to catch them to vaccinate."

With a vast network of birdwatchers across the NT, Dr Griffiths said the government was looking to harness the power of the territory's avian enthusiasts to tackle the tyranny of distance.

Keen birdwatchers are being urged to use their skills to help monitor the spread of bird flu in the NT. (ABC News: Tristan Hooft)

Biodiversity Watch NT's Graeme Sawyer said having boots on the ground would be essential to the mitigation effort.

"The authorities' problem is always that they haven't got any staff in most places," he said.

" By using bird-watching fraternities, Indigenous communities and ranger programs, you've got people right across the country, and a lot of them know a heck of a lot about their birds. "

Mr Sawyer said anyone with a passion for birds and wildlife conservation could help to slow the spread of the virus.

Graeme Sawyer says the NT's bird-watching fraternities, Indigenous communities and rangers "know a heck of a lot about their birds". (ABC News: Tristan Hooft)

"I would just urge anybody who's got a remote interest in birds to sharpen up their eyes and get their binoculars out," he said.

"It is a big unknown and the more information we can get early, the better."

World.title: Antarctic grass an ominous sign of how the world is warming
World.content:
EnvironmentClimate changeClimate crisis Editorial Antarctic grass an ominous sign of how the world is warming The Herald's View Editorial August 16, 2026 — 10:00am

August 16, 2026 — 10:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A few decades ago the prospect of icy Antarctica catching fire may have seemed like science fiction, and rather far-fetched science fiction at that. It’s now a live option, according to Australian scientists who have found evidence of grass spreading across parts of Antarctica in response to human-induced climate change. Science reporter Angus Dalton details the new research in The Sun-Herald today that shows invasive grasses are competing with native vegetation in the Antarctic region. The findings “raise the prospect of a dramatically and rapidly changing Antarctic region, and in particular this prospect of fire”, said Professor Melodie McGeoch, an ecologist from Monash University who supervised the research. Grass growing across western Antarctica. Noemi Sheppard



Fires are already striking the Antarctic, Dalton reports. In January 2025, a wildfire burned 55 per cent of Amsterdam Island, an island of the French Southern and Antarctic Lands, and in 2024 a fire also burned on Bird Island in the sub-Antarctic. The complexity of the world’s climate systems means that it’s not a simple story, and the Antarctic isn’t necessarily “greening”. There won’t be sheep farms at the South Pole any time soon. “Every single island is undergoing its own mini-climate change,” said Monash University PhD student Noemie Sheppard, who led the research. “Some are drying, some are wetting, some are increasing in temperature, so all the grasses across these islands are undergoing different changes.” The local effects of global warming are diverse but a common thread is the natural world straining under the stress of rapid change, more wild weather and more heat.



The expanding Antarctic grasses are one part of the puzzle showing the effects of rising temperatures. Another piece is the unprecedented heatwave that swept Europe last month, leaving thousands of people dead. Another, the huge El Nino that is likely to drive temperatures even higher later this year. It is perhaps understandable that some people might look at the bigger picture of advancing climate change and feel resignation, even despair. But the best response to risk is to take action. Multinational efforts to slow climate change by cutting emissions and adapting to some of its effects continue, despite setbacks. In recent years, gains in renewable energy deployment have often been wiped out by sudden policy reversals. Progress is too slow. How is Australia faring in this effort? It is a mixed picture. As a major exporter of fossil fuels, the nation is helping to fuel the crisis. It has sometimes played a laggard role in international negotiations, holding back stronger action.



On the plus side, Australia has made some strides in cutting its own fossil fuel use. It has proved that emissions can be “decoupled” from economic growth. Since 2005 – the baseline year for measuring emissions under the Kyoto Protocol – Australia has cut back its total carbon pollution by close to 30 per cent. There are millions more Australians today than there were in 2005, millions more cars on the road, manufacturing output per person has stayed steady, and average net wealth per person has more than doubled. This serves as an encouraging reminder that the naysayers were wrong, and their wild claims that cutting emissions would destroy our way of life were just so much hot air. Yet most of the work remains to be done. Australia is again starting to veer away from the net zero trajectory it has pledged to achieve, and the next few years remain crucial.



Later this year Australia will co-lead the next round of international climate talks, alongside Turkiye. It is an opportunity to galvanise global efforts to tackle climate change and make sure voices of those most directly affected – including those from Pacific island nations – are heard by policymakers. Australia has a chance to make a real difference, and the world will be watching. Jordan Baker sends a newsletter to subscribers each week. Sign up to receive her Note from the Editor.

World.title: Star professor’s death leaves Cambridge exposed to hard questions on race and hiring
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Cambridge, England — When Cambridge University interviewed Jason Arday for one of the most prestigious sociology positions in the world, he was an early career scholar and underqualified, by the school’s own standards. Cambridge’s requirements, reviewed by The New York Times, called for “an outstanding research record of international stature” and a “proven successful track record” supervising doctorate students. Arday had a modest publication record and had bounced from one university to the next — not staying long enough to oversee a full three-year-or-more doctorate. At 37, Jason Arday became the youngest black professor at the University of Cambridge in its history. Cambridge hired him anyway in 2023, making him, at 37, the university’s youngest black professor at a time when the school was under pressure to diversify. In doing so, Cambridge thrust him into the international limelight, giving him a platform at one of the world’s elite universities to champion academic diversity and making him a target for critics. Arday was found dead in London on Friday, days after resigning his job amid accusations that he had plagiarised chunks of his papers, embellished parts of his recently published memoir and fabricated aspects of his life story. The controversy exploded along cultural fault lines — race, neurodiversity and academic hiring. In his August 5 resignation letter, he wrote, “I no longer wish to feel as though I am living under a constant spotlight, where every aspect of my life is subject to public examination and judgment.” He added, “This is not the end of my work. It is simply the end of this chapter.” His family said that, since starting at Cambridge, Arday had faced a campaign of scrutiny intended to undermine him. That became too much for him, they said.



Questions about Arday’s career are unlikely to end with his death, however, because they were as much about Cambridge as they were about him. The centuries-old alma mater of Isaac Newton, William Wordsworth and kings and queens, Cambridge now faces deep scrutiny about its decision-making, even from its own faculty. Too good to be true While Arday was underqualified for his job, he had a remarkable story: a tale of being diagnosed early with autism and having such significant developmental delays that he spent his entire childhood in a special-needs school. In his account, he did not speak until age 11 or read until 18, yet he managed to earn his doctorate and begin giving keynote speeches on the academic circuit. Also, he had run 30 marathons in 35 days for charity, a feat that would have placed him among the world’s elite athletes. King’s College, Cambridge. Supporters say Jason Arday is a victim of racially motivated attacks. Bloomberg If, in hindsight, elements of Arday’s story seemed too good to be true, Cambridge ignored repeated warning signs. A review of internal Cambridge documents and interviews with former colleagues and associates shows that, in addition to passing over more experienced candidates for the job, administrators gushed publicly about Arday’s scholarship and privately disregarded complaints about his work. They declined to investigate plagiarism concerns and accused his critics of a “vile campaign” to discredit him.



Arday’s claims about not speaking were false, a former classmate and a speech professional who worked with him told the Times. His supposedly remarkable trajectory from non-verbal preteen to PhD had no precedent in medical literature, experts in developmental and speech delays say. That should have set off alarm bells for the Cambridge hiring committee, which included a child psychiatrist who had done research on autism, experts said. ‘DEI Kool-Aid’ Before Arday’s death, conservative commentators seized on his fall as evidence of diversity-and-inclusion efforts run amok. They said that Cambridge had been so eager to diversify that administrators let their judgment be clouded. Related Article Diversity Diversity programs ‘must die’: Trump pushback gathers pace in Australia “They seem to have drunk the DEI Kool-Aid,” Jacob Rees-Mogg, a former Conservative lawmaker in Britain, said early this past week on The Telegraph’s “Daily T” podcast. Prominent academics on the left agree that Cambridge must answer for its decisions. They say the ordeal has fuelled racism and cast unjustified aspersions on accomplished scholars of colour.



Cambridge said on Friday that it was “desperately saddened” to hear of Arday’s death. An administrator, in a letter to the faculty on Tuesday, called the misconduct accusations “an aberration” and “troubling”. A spokesperson separately declined to answer a list of questions about his hiring and his time there, citing a planned independent investigation — a difficult inquiry that will likely be made even more uncomfortable following Arday’s death. Arday, for his part, had worked hard to silence any questioning of his credentials. When a journalist for Times Higher Education, a respected academic industry publication, asked about plagiarism last year, a prominent British defamation law firm had helped kill the article, the journalist said. Arday later reported the journalist to the police. When a scholar from another university questioned his work, Arday turned the tables and filed a racism complaint with the other school, according to someone with direct knowledge of the complaint. That person, like some others who spoke to the Times, spoke on the condition of anonymity to avoid being dragged publicly into the controversy. Arday never squarely addressed the questions of plagiarism and fabrication. But what is clear from interviews and public records is that elements of the story would have been easy for Cambridge to check. ‘It just stretches credulity’ Arday, the child of Ghanaian immigrants, grew up in public housing in an ethnically mixed, working-class quarter of South London. Early on, he was identified as having learning difficulties.



Arday has claimed that before age 11, he could understand language but not speak. In 2022, before interviewing with Cambridge, he said that he had been educated exclusively in a special-needs school “with other pupils that had very severe learning difficulties and physical disabilities”. Jason Arday was Cambridge University’s youngest black professor. Joe Giddens/PA via AP In his memoir, published on Tuesday, he gave a different account, saying he attended a mainstream school but spent time sequestered alone in a classroom, again without speaking. Both tales are false, according to people who knew Arday as a child and spoke with the Times before his death. A speech professional who worked closely with the young Arday recalled him having a language delay but speaking with both children and adults. One former schoolmate, Jonathan Stewart, recalled Arday cracking jokes and putting on playful accents in a minivan on the way to church activities as children. While non-verbal children could certainly learn to speak, even at a late age, the rapid development described by Arday had no precedent in clinical literature, three experts on autism and speech said.

World.title: Polar wildfires? Scientists warn of grass spreading across parts of the Antarctic
World.content:
Exclusive EnvironmentClimate changeClimate crisis Polar wildfires? Scientists warn of grass spreading across parts of the Antarctic Angus Dalton August 16, 2026 — 9:45am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Grass is spreading across some regions of the Antarctic as ice retreats, threatening Southern Ocean islands with the prospect of wildfires in another sign of how human-caused climate change is warping the polar wilderness. Australian scientists systematically reviewed a raft of existing datasets and papers, and found an overall increase in grass populations in the icy but fast-warming region. They presented the preliminary findings this week at the Scientific Committee on Antarctic Research (SCAR) conference in Oslo. Grasses and moss – pictured here on Heard Island – grow naturally across sub-Antarctic islands and parts of the continent, but there’s evidence grass populations are expanding under climate change. Naomi Monk Professor Melodie McGeoch, an ecologist from Monash University who supervised the research, said the different strands of evidence come together to “raise the prospect of a dramatically and rapidly changing Antarctic region, and in particular this prospect of fire”. A wildfire in January last year ripped across 55 per cent of Amsterdam Island, an island of the French Southern and Antarctic Lands, and in 2024 a fire also burnt on Bird Island in the sub-Antarctic.



“They’re cold, wet, boggy, icy, and the vegetation across many of these places is pretty sparse, and so the idea of fire in these areas is quite remarkable,” McGeoch said of the islands. Grass is more flammable than other types of vegetation in the region, and both invasive bluegrass and native species seed and spread rapidly after a fire. “Grass-dominated systems are more likely to burn,” McGeoch said. Grass growing across western Antarctica. Noemi Sheppard Native hairgrass grows naturally on the Antarctic continent, particularly on rocky parts of the western Antarctic Peninsula – the part that branches off the continent like a tentacle – and the nearby South Shetland Islands. But the area is one of the fastest-warming regions in the southern hemisphere, and increasing temperatures have likely driven grass growth on the peninsula and nearby islands normally dominated by hardy mosses and lichen.



“Suddenly, we’re starting to see grasses do well, or better than they used to,” Monash PhD student and research leader Noemie Sheppard said, as ice retreats and exposes soil, grass can colonise. While the overall trend implies a net increase in grass across the region, the story is complex and it varies between different locations, particularly between sub-Antarctic islands. Invasive grass growing on Marion Island. Naomi Monk Grasses and moss growing on Heard Island. Naomi Monk In some places grasses are decreasing, while different factors including the eradication of invasive rabbits from some islands have also influenced vegetation cover, Sheppard said.



“Every single island is undergoing its own mini-climate change. Some are drying, some are wetting, some are increasing in temperature, so all the grasses across these islands are undergoing different changes,” Sheppard said. The researchers turned their attention to grass after noticing Azorella macquariensis, a species of cushion plant, was doing poorly on Macquarie Island while other grasses seemed to thrive. A once healthy cushion plant suffering from dieback on Macquarie Island due to warming. Dana Bergstrom via antarctica.gov.au Antarctic hairgrass is increasing at a faster rate than invasive bluegrass, according to the preliminary research which is yet to be peer-reviewed. However that could change as the climate grows warmer. Climate change, driven primarily by the burning of fossil fuels, has warmed the Antarctic peninsula by 3 degrees and amplified rare atmospheric warming events such as one in 2024 that saw temperatures in east Antarctica shoot 28 degrees above average.



Related Article Climate crisis A crying glacier and a shivering ice shelf: A beautiful, tragic story The idea of whether Antarctica is “greening” in response to warming, and to what degree, however, is hotly debated by scientists. A 2024 Nature paper reported vegetation cover on the Antarctic Peninsula had grown from less than 1 square kilometre in 1986 to 12 square kilometres in 2021, and the “rate of greening” had accelerated by 30 per cent between 2016 and 2021. Other scientists said the study over-egged the trend, and used satellite imagery critics deemed unreliable because of persistent cloud cover and poor resolution not suited to capturing Antarctic’s small and patchy vegetation, which may have led to an overestimation of greening. Researchers argued in a new Nature comment paper published on Friday the reported greening rate was theoretically impossible and, while vegetation cover was expected to increase with warming, it was likely to do so at a more moderate rate.



McGeoch, a chief investigator with the Securing Antarctica’s Environmental Future research group, said more boots-on-the ground research across Antarctica was desperately needed in a crucial region that’s notoriously difficult to study. Related Article Climate crisis In the Trump era of America first, scientists fear for the future of Antarctica “We’re at a point in time where there’s this awful acceleration of very rapid changes that are difficult to anticipate the ultimate consequences of,” she said. “But at the same time, we’re at a point where all our technologies, our data capability, our high-performance computing, the advances in AI and so on are accelerating, which excitingly gives us the opportunity to answer some of these questions quite rapidly.” Get to the heart of what’s happening with climate change and the environment.

World.title: Ella has finally found a community of friends. NDIS cuts mean she could soon be alone again
World.content:
NationalDisability Ella has finally found a community of friends. NDIS cuts mean she could soon be alone again Grant McArthur August 16, 2026 — 9:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Ella jolts around in her chair playing pigeon simulator. She laughs, then screams with delight as her bird takes to the sky and wreaks havoc. Her best friend Jen* is playing Animal Crossing on a screen beside her, and the two chat, joke and help each other navigate their respective virtual worlds. Ella, centre, is worried that losing her NDIS package means she will no longer be able to see her friends. Simon Schluter Behind them, with his back turned so he can concentrate on the cards on the table in front of him, Tim* is too focused on a game of Magic: The Gathering to notice their laughter. But the real magic here is that the three are not only gathered, but have become friends.



Brought together by the National Disability Insurance Scheme – or, more in particular, genU’s NDIS-funded Gamer program – the unlikely Geelong friends have intensely different personalities but a very similar need: to build social skills, confidence and ways to navigate the world outside. Related Article Disability Labor-led committee warns of human rights risks in NDIS reform They also hold the same fears: that community service cuts to the NDIS will mean the end of their Gamer funding – and their pathway into the world. Seeing the benefits Gamer has for Ella – who has a rare chromosome abnormality, resulting in intellectual disability, global developmental and cognitive delay, speech delay, restricted growth, and low muscle tone – her mother Debbie is distressed by its potential loss. “Over the years, we have tried many different programs that haven’t worked, [but] she just loves Gamer. All the kids are open-minded and have accepted Ella for who she is and what she is, they are very understanding,” Debbie said.



“She comes out beaming most days and lets me know she loves it. She is very, very excited to get up and motivated get to Gamer on time. “If Ella’s funding was cut, even just a little bit or altogether, it would be just devastating for the whole family. She would probably just spend all her time in her room, and I wouldn’t be able to get her out, which would affect not only her physical health, but her mental health.” Run by care provider genU, the Gamer program is like tens of thousands of other programs designed to provide formal social and community participation opportunities for up to 350,000 NDIS-funded participants across the country. Debbie (left) is worried what will happen to her daughter Ella if she loses the Gamer program. Simon Schluter When The Age attended Wednesday morning’s Gamer session, there was another, larger group of participants playing games at the back of the room, separated from Ella’s gathering by tables covered with jigsaws, 3D printers and dozens more activities waiting in boxes.



But much of the talk throughout the room centred on events in another far less colourful room, 730 kilometres away in Canberra, where a Senate committee was preparing to hand down its final report on how $150 billion can be cut from the bloated NDIS over the next decade. Loading Like hundreds of other NDIS providers, genU had earlier made a submission to the inquiry outlining its impacts on real people, including Ella and her friends, and warning that community programs served a far greater purpose than fun and games. “Where community participation supports are withdrawn, the evidence in this submission shows the resulting pressure does not disappear – it moves to hospitals, families and carers, mental health services, and in some cases justice and crisis response systems. This is inappropriate and ineffective substitution of services,” the genU submission to the senate committee states. When the Senate inquiry’s report was handed down late on Friday, it all but confirmed those fears. While a Labor-led human rights committee will continue to push for ways to stop vulnerable people falling through the cracks, the report paved the way for the government to rein in the NDIS by removing 240,000 participants over the next five years, and to slash the social and community participation budgets of those who remain.



Debbie, Ella and her friends are all too aware that the Gamer program looks like an easy target for those cuts, at least on paper. The genU program focuses on young people and attempts to engage them in interests they already have, by setting up games and drawing people in to play together, while its workers then fade into the background and subtly try to steer the interactions when needed. Its success is that from week to week participants such as Ella, Tim and Jen increasingly need fewer interventions during their Gamer sessions, and far beyond. “The NDIS is important because it gives me access to communities that I would normally not have,” Tim told The Age, after winning his Magic: The Gathering game.



“I suffer mass anxiety, depression, and I am autistic, which doesn’t help making friends and all that. Here [Gamer] can bring a lot of frustration because I don’t always agree with people, but that is necessary. Related Article Opinion

Healthcare NDIS overhaul must look beyond the balance sheet The Age's View Editorial “It is the only reason I went out and got a job – actually, I got two jobs – because this reduces all my stress and allows me to be natural when I am outside.” As Ella returns to Pigeon Simulator, surrounded by all her friends and carers, Debbie just hopes the NDIS cuts don’t hurt too deeply. “It’s a worry. But we have been blessed. Ella joined up on the NDIS pilot and was one of its first participants, and we’ve been very happy. We’ve never asked for anything we didn’t need – and we’ve had that back in return,” Debbie said.
